SIMPLIFIED INTERPRETATION OF THE REAL ESTATE LAW 

1. The Real Estate Act was created by State Legislature in 1919. 

2. The penalty for paying a commission to any other than a licensed Real Estate Broker is a fine of Fifty Dollars. 

3. Any person who presumes to act for another for a compensation in connection with a Real Estate Transaction, whether or not the transaction is consummated, is subject to a fine of $500.00 and/or six months in jail. 

4. The selling of lease subdivisions comes under the jurisdiction of the Real Estate Commissioner. 

5. The members of the State Real Estate Board serve as such without compensation. 

6. The fee for a Broker's license of one who acts only as an officer of a corporation is $2.00. 

7. The Commissioner and all members of the State Real Estate 

Board are appointed by the Governor. 

8. No one is eligible to the office of Real Estate Commissioner, or membership in the State Real Estate Board unless they have been a Real Estate Broker actively engaged as such for five years in the State of California. 

9. The State Real Estate Board consists of seven members, including the Real Estate Commissioner, who shall act as chief. 

10. The salary of the Real Estate Commissioner is set by the 

State Legislature at $7,500.00 per annum. 

11. Three members of the Real Estate Board shall be appointed from the Northern part of the State and three from the Southern. 

12. Only two members of the Real Estate Board can be appointed from any one County, any vacancies on the Board are filled by the Governor. 

13. The Real Estate Division of California is a Division of the Department of Investments. 

14. The Real Estate Board shall meet at least once every three months at such a place as they designate in the State of California, and shall meet oftener upon five days' written notice signed by the Real Estate Commissioner or a majority of the members of the Board. 

15. The Real Estate Commissioner is required to furnish a bond in the sum of Ten Thousand Dollars, 16. All clerks and deputies in the Division of the Real Estate shall be employed by the Real Estate Commissioner, who shall set -47-

their salary and assign their duties, subject to the approval of the 

Department of Finance. 

17. No employee of the Division of Real Estate shall be employed or connected directly or indirectly, with any real estate firm during his term of office. 

18. The Real Estate Commissioner shall cause to be published on or about the first of October of each year a Directory of Licensees, which shall be free to licensed Brokers, but not free to licensed Salesmen. 

19. All deputies and employees of the Division of Real Estate are subject to the Civil Service Law, except two deputies who shall be designated by the Real Estate Commissioner. 

20. The Commissioner shall establish branch offices in such cities as he may deem necessary, subject to the approval of the 

Department of Finance. 

21. The Division of Real Estate is supported by fees paid under the provisions of the Act, which fees shall be turned into the State Treasury at least once a week, and credited to the Real Estate 

Fund. 

22. All money in excess of $100,000.00 remaining to the credit of the Real Estate Fund on June 30th of each year shall, not later than the 15th of July, be transferred to the general fund of the State. 

23. A complete transcription of formal hearing in the Real 

Estate Commissioner's office shall be made, and copies of all records and papers in said office shall be available to the public, and may be received as evidence, if certified under the hand and seal of the 

Commissioner, the same as the originals. 

24. The Attorney General acts for the Commission in an advisory capacity only. Prosecutions under the Act in Court shall be made by the District or City Attorney. 

25. The Real Estate Commissioner is charged with the enforcement of the Real Estate Act, but acts only in an Administrative capacity. His authority is limited to suspension or revocation of the licenses. 

26. The Commissioner is charged with certifying by written examination that licensees have a fair knowledge of the Real Estate Law of the State of California, that they understand the English Language, have a fair knowledge of elementary arithmetic, spelling, land ecomonics, land measurements, appraising, leases, deeds, land contracts, etc. 

27. All licensed Brokers must secure a branch office license for any location other than their main office, from which they operate in the Real Estate Business. -48

28. Real Estate Salesmen must, at all times, be in the employ of a licensed Real Estate Broker, and can only work for one 

Broker at a time. 

29. Changes of address, changes of Broker, duplicate license for lost license, branch license, etc., all require a fee of One Dollar. 

30. The Commissioner may call any Broker or Salesman for hearing as to his acts whether or not there is a complaint issued against the licensee. 

31. The Real Estate Act provides that the Real Estate Commissioner may require any licensee to take a qualifying examination before issuance of a renewal license at the beginning of any license period. 

32. The State fee for Broker's license is $5.00 per annum; for 

Salesmen, the fee is $2.00. If not renewed before midnight on June 

30th, the fee will be double. 

33. The examination fee is Fifteen Dollars for Brokers, Three 

Dollars for Salesmen. One fee shall pay for any number of examinations necessary prior to the issuance of the original license. 

34. Failure to renew license during the year succeeding the last license period, shall place the applicant in the same position as if he never had been licensed. 

35. All licenses issued under the Act shall be prominently displayed in the office of the employing Broker. Failure so to do may result in suspension or revocation of Broker's license. 

36. Change or abandonment of office location shall automatically cancel the license unless the Commissioner is notified 

IMMEDIATELY. 

37. A definite place of business is required to be maintained by each licensed Broker. A sign must be prominently displayed. 

38. The Real Estate Commissioner may call a hearing regarding the conduct of any licensee for violation of the Real Estate Act, or other violation of the law, and may cause such licensee to be punished in accordance with the provisions of the law, where such conduct or violation occurred within three years. 

39. The action of the Commissioner in suspending or revoking a license shall take effect ten days after its date. 

40. The decision of the commission in suspending or revoking a license is subject to review by the Superior Court upon application therein by the aggrieved party. 

41. When a Salesman shall have been discharged by his

Broker for a violation of any of the provisions of the Real Estate Act, the Broker must immediately notify the Commissioner in 49

writing, with a verified statement of facts relating thereto. (10 days permitted.) 

42. The license of the Real Estate Broker cannot be revoked for the wrong-doing of a Salesman, unless it is shown that he had guilty knowledge of such wrong-doing. 

43. Any person presuming to act as a Real Estate Broker or 

Salesman without first securing a license is subject to a fine of $500.00 and/or six months in jail. If a corporation, the fine is $5,000.00. 

44. Any firm or corporation shall, prior to the opening of any subdivision, or the offering for sale thereof, notify the Commissioner and supply him with details thereof, together with a copy of a recorded map, copies of all forms to be used, history of the title to the property and all facts pertaining thereto, and shall get the written approval for the sale thereof from the Real Estate Commissioner. 

45. The cost of filing application for the sale of a subdivision in the State of California shall be borne by the applicant, and an initial fee of $50.00 minimum shall be paid. 

46. In cases where an application has been made to the Commissioner for the subdivision permit, and such permit has been denied, the party who feels the decision unfair shall be entitled to review of the case by the Superior Court. 

47. Any and all changes in the set-up of a subdivision sold in the State of California shall be submitted to the Real Estate Commissioner before such a change goes into effect. 

48. Any subdivided lands sold in the State of California which is subject to liens or encumbrances securing or evidencing the payment of money thereon, shall not be sold or offered to the public unless such liens or encumbrances have a covenant providing for the release of such land or parcels thereof free and clear from such lien or encumbrance. 

49. The Real Estate Act provides that land divided or proposed to be divided into five or more parcels to be sold now or in the future shall constitute a subdivision. 

50. The penalty for misrepresentation of a subdivision by an individual Broker or Salesman is a fine of $2,000.00 and/or two years in jail, or if a corporation, the penalty is a fine up to $5,000.00. 

51. A Provisional license may be secured by making application to the Division of Real Estate, paying a fee of $3.00 and taking a written examination therefor. Such Provisional license shall be good for a maximum of four months from date of issuance and cannot be transferred or renewed. -50-

QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON CALIFORNIA REAL ESTATE LAW 

Q. If you are assisted by your grocer, who has no real estate license, on a sale of a property on which you received a brokerage commission, what if any, portion of the commission would you pay the grocer?

A. It is unlawful to pay any portion of commission to the grocer since he is not licensed. 

Q. May a salesman or broker be deprived of his license for conviction of falsely promising purchaser something which induced the transaction, but which is not mentioned in the written contract? Explain. 

A. Yes. For making false promises or for misrepresentation. 

Q. To whom may complaining buyer look for relief before

State Real Estate Department when he dealt solely with the salesman? 

A. To the broker under whom salesman is licensed.

Q. The Real Estate Commissioner denied renewal of license to agents who refused to quit selling under certain guises, branding such practices as dishonest and untruthful. What phrase or words in the Act justify such an interpretation? 

A. "A continued and flagrant course of misrepresentation.' 

Q. Smith & Co., licensed brokers, made sales through solicitor and salesman whose licenses, though applied for, had not been received. Sellers upon hearing that latter were not yet licensed, refused to pay commission. Could Smith & Co. collect? Explain.

A. Presuming that authorization was given in regular form and was properly signed by the sellers, Smith & Co. could collect commission. This was purely a contract between sellers and broker and as such, sale had been made and commission was collectable. 

However, on the other hand, Smith & Co. could not pay any part of this commission to this solicitor and salesman, as it is unlawful to pay such to any unlicensed persons. Furthermore, Smith & Co. are subject to serious reprimand from the Commissioner for permitting unlicensed persons to work from their office. Simply because licenses had been applied for is no positive assurance that same will be issued, therefore, nothing should be done in the capacity of solicitor or salesman, until licenses had actually been received. 

Q. Smith & Co., licensed brokers, were selling their own lots through salesman not yet licensed. The real estate commission sought to revoke broker's license. Why?

A. For paying commissions or compensation to salesman not permitted by law to receive them. 

Q. If a real estate broker fails to perform his duties as such, explain fully what procedure, if any, a person can take to recover damages. 

A. Bring civil suit against broker for recovery of damages. -51-

Q. (a) What must a broker do with his license certificate? (b) What, if anything, must be done with his license if he changes his business location?

A. (a) License certificate of broker (and of all his salesmen) must be prominently displayed in broker's office. (b) Broker shall return his license certificate (and also those of all his salesmen) to the Commissioner, accompanied by written notice of change of business location, the fee of one dollar, for each certificate so sent shall accompany request. Commissioner will then issue new licenses for the unexpired periods at the new business address. 

Q. Give three causes for revocation of license, other than for bad faith with client or customers, or matters of ethics, or character of licensee. 

A. (1) Failure to notify commissioner of change of business address. (2) Failure to display proper sign at place of business. (3) Paying commissions to any person other than a duly licensed broker or salesman. ..

Q. Name the three paramount qualifications necessary for applicant for broker's or salesman's license, as set forth in Real 

Estate Act. 

A. Honesty, truthfulness and good reputation. 

Q. When salesman wishes to transfer to another broker, what must he do to satisfy the demands of this Law? 

A. Have broker return his (salesman's) license to the Real 

Estate Commissioner for cancellation. Regular transfer forms are supplied by the Real Estate Department, one of which is to be filled out, signed by the salesman and both the old and new employing brokers. This is sent to the commissioner at Sacramento accompanied by the fee of one dollar ($1.00) who will then issue new license. 

Q. Name six moral delinquencies for which the commissioner may suspend or revoke an agent's license. 

A. (1) Making any substantial misrepresentation. (2) Making any false promises of a character likely to influence, persuade or induce. (3) Acting for more than one party in a transaction without the knowledge of all parties thereto. (4) Procuring a license under this act, for himself or any salesman, by fraud, misrepresentation or deceit. (5) Willfully disregarding or violating any of the provisions of Real Estate Law. (6) Willfully use word "Realtor" without the legal right so to do.

Q. What has the Commissioner to say about the size and placement of the sign which the broker is required to display? 

A. Size and place of such sign shall conform to regulations that may be adopted by the Real Estate Commissioner. The department rules that sign shall be of a size and in a place to be easily seen and read, and further that it shall clearly show name of broker, together with the words "Licensed Real Estate Broker." Department further rules that in event broker is a member in good stand- -52-

ing, of the local Realty Board, said Board being affiliated with the National Association of Real Estate Boards, broker is then permitted to use simply the word "realtor" folowing his name on sign. This in lieu of the four words as above. 

Q. May a real estate broker licensed by the Real Estate Division bring an action for malicious prosecution against one who files a verified complaint with the Real Estate Commissioner accusing the broker of misconduct, where the broker believes the charges were maliciously filed, and where the Commissioner dismisses the same after hearing?

A. No, not successfully. Of course, any complaint may be filed, but the question evidently means bring an action with success. The negative answer is because the action for malicious prosecution arises where the damages sought to be recovered are caused by the institution of a judicial proceeding. Although the question implies that the other elements are present, to-wit, the filing of the charges from wrongful or improper motives and without probable cause to sustain them, yet the action referred to must arise in a judicial proceeding. The Real Estate Commissioner, and similar commissions and boards, are held to be engaged in enforcing ADMINIS- 

TRATIVE determinations and not exercising JUDICIAL functions. 

Q. (a) What does the Real Estate Law require a broker to do with his license and those of his salesmen when received from the department? (b) On what date do all real estate licenses expire?

A. (a) Display them in prominent position in broker's office. (b) Midnight on June 30th, of each year. 

Q. If a broker produces a purchaser ready, able and willing to perform where the broker has a signed listing, but no written contract is actually entered into between the owner and the purchaser, can the broker nevertheless collect his commission? 

A. Yes. A written contract between the seller and the purchaser is not essential to the recovery of the broker's commission if he has produced to the seller a purchaser who was ready, willing and able to purchase upon the terms proposed by the seller and who has agreed to those terms and is willing and offers to enter into a binding written contract. 

Q. What penalty may salesman suffer for promising buyer something not authorized in the contract; or for persuading buyer to enter into transaction on representation not authorized by the salesman's employer, or which are not certain to be true? 

A. License may be suspended or revoked. 

Q. What penalty may owner or subdivider suffer for falsely advertising his project by radio or in writing? 

A. Imprisonment in County Jail not exceeding two years or fine not exceeding $2,000.

Q. What does the act require owner or subdivider of property to do before offering it for sale? -53-

A. Prior to time when subdivided lands shall be offered for sale the owner, his agent, or subdivider shall notify Real Estate Commissioner in writing of his intention to sell such offering. Such notice of intention to include all information and data relative to the property, ownership, size, legal description, title, encumbrance thereon, how it is to be sold, copies of contracts, etc. 

Q. Can a salesman legally split with, and pay commission to, another salesman? Explain.

A. No. Salesmen employed by same broker may agree to split commissions and broker will pay as agreed to them. Brokers only can pay commission to salesmen and then only to salesmen licensed under him.

Q. Can salesman lawfully accept payment of a commission from another salesman or broker other than his employer? 

A. No. See answer to question above.

Q. It is lawful for salesman to complete deal and collect in his own name the commission, and then to give his broker his agreed share? Explain.

A. No. Unlawful for any person, firm or corporation to pay any commission to other than licensed broker.

Q. What penalty may salesman suffer for transacting the business of a broker without fully accounting to him for his acts. and his representations made to buyer and seller? 

A. License may be suspended or revoked. 

Q. What penalty may broker suffer for his failure to properly supervise the acts of his salesmen? 

A. May lose license or be defendant in suit. 

Q. What classes of property come under inspection review of the commissioner? 

A. All subdivided lands.

Q. Name ten different things, the performance of which requires person to holder broker's or salesman's license. 

A. (1) Sell or offer to sell. (2) Buy or offer to buy. (3)

Lease or offer to lease. (4) Rent or offer to rent. (5) Negotiate sale, purchase, or exchange of real estate. (6) Negotiate sale, purchase or exchange of leases. (7) Negotiate loan on real estate. (8) 

Solicit for prospective purchasers. (9) Collect rent. (10) List property. 

Q. May person who has once held broker's or salesman's license secure license without examination?

A. Not unless less than a year has elapsed since expiration of permanent license. Department requires all licenses to be renewed yearly.

Q. Is it lawful to sell a lot in a projected subdivision whose map is not yet filed or recorded? Explain fully. 

A. No. It is unlawful to sell, or offer contract to sell, any subdivision or portion thereof by reference to any map other than a recorded map. -54-

Q. Agent signed deposit receipt as "seller." Buyer complained that he represented himself to be agent in sale of the property. 

Discovered that agent was really optionee and had his own price on the property. Explain why agent's license was revoked. 

A. Agent procured deposit through misrepresentation and deceit. He should have made his position as optionee known to buyer. 

Q. What penalty may commissioner impose upon licensee for his failure to save purchaser from harm when promise of resale was broken? 

A. Suspend or revoke license.

Q. What penalty may a realtor suffer for transgression of the code of ethics?

A. Member is liable to expulsion from his Realty Board. This does not automatically affect his Real Estate license.

Q. Real estate agent assured buyer that the acre would likely yield the income which the subdivider indicated. State Real Estate 

Department warned that the estimates were too high and should not be expected. In due time the expected high income failed to materialize and agent stood trial before the department for conduct constituting dishonest dealing. Assuming that purchaser relied upon the agent's assurances, was this sufficient cause for revocation of license? Explain. 

A. Yes. For reasons see Real Estate Law.

Q. Real Estate Broker failed to maintain a sign at his place of business indicating that he was a licensed real estate broker. 

Did he violate any of the provisions of the Real Estate Law and if so, what penalty was he subject to for such violation? 

A. Failure to maintain a sign indicating that he was a licensed real estate broker together with the name under which he was operating was in direct violation of the Real Estate Law. The 

Broker in such case was subject to temporary suspension or permanent revocation of his license.

Q. Tom Brown had a Broker's license in the State of New 

York and moved to California. He decided to go in the real estate business in Los Angeles, and solicited a listing on the residence of his next door neighbor and sold the same, representing himself to both buyer and seller as a licensed real estate broker, although he did not have a California license. Did he violate the provisions of the Real Estate Law and if so, what was the penalty of such violation?

A. Yes, this was a direct violation of the Real Estate Law and was punishable by a fine of not to exceed $500.00, or by impris onment in the county jail for a term not to exceed six months, or by both such fine or imprisonment.

Q. A corporation doing business in Denver and licensed in the State of Colorado as real estate brokers opened a branch office in San Francisco and without securing a real estate license in the State of California, advertised for sale in California, certain prop- -55-

erties located in Colorado. Their advertising literature and stationery represented them to be licensed real estate brokers. Did they violate the California Real Estate Law, and if so, to what penalty were they subject?

A. Yes, this was a direct violation of the Real Estate Law and is punishable by fine not to exceed $5,000.00. 

Q. Mary Jones was a licensed real estate sales lady operating under the license of John Doe & Co., Realtors, as her broker. She secured a client for a four-family flat building. Her broker not having a suitable property listed, she secured the listing she wanted from another broker and sold it to her client. The second broker paid her a commission for the sale. Did Mary Jones or the second broker violate any provision of the Real Estate Law, and if so, to what penalty were they subject?

A. Yes, both the second broker and Mary Jones were in direct violation of the Real Estate Law. Such violation was a misdemeanor and each of them was subject to a fine not exceeding $50.00 for any one such offense. In addition to this, each was subject to temporary suspension or permanent revocation of their real estate license. -56

Section III 

Agency

Agency taken from word "ego," meaning a doer, a force, a power that accomplishes things. Occupies a fiduciary position, one of trust. 

Q. What constitutes agency? 

A. In real estate when one person authorizes another to act for him or in his behalf, the relation of principal and agent is established. The old maxim of the law applies, i. e. "Qui facit per alium facit per se," meaning he who does a thing through another does it himself, and "Respondeat superior," meaning let the superior or principal answer. This constitutes the fundamental principles of the law of agency. 

Q. Define agent's apparent authority.

A. Agent's apparent authority is the authority which an agent apparently has, judging from the circumstances of the agency, i.e., such authority as a prudent person with reasonable diligence and discretion might use on behalf of the principal.

Q. What warranty is included in an authority given to an agent to sell and convey real property, and in an authority to sell personal property?

A. Section 2323 of the Civil Code of California provides that an authority to sell and convey real property includes authority to give the usual covenants of warranty, and that an authority to sell personal property includes an authority to warrant title of a principal and the authority and quality of the property. (Reprint, "California Property Laws.")

Q. When may an agent delegate his powers to another person to act for him in the agency?

A. Section 2349 of the Civil Code of California provides that an agent, unless specially forbidden by his principal to do so, can delegate his powers to another person in any of the following cases, and in no others: (a) When the act to be done is purely mechanical. (b) When it is such as the agent cannot himself, and the sub-agent can, lawfully perform. (c) When it is usage of the place to delegate such power. (d) When such delegation is specially authorized by the principal.

However, Section 2349 of the Civil Code of California above cited is the only exception to the general rule that a delegated authority cannot be delegated unless the agent is specially authorized to do so. (Reprint, "California Property Laws.") 

Q. When must the authority of the agent be in writing?

A. Generally speaking, any authority of an agent to enter into real estate contracts (except contracts to be performed within one year) must be in writing. The authority to enter into leases -57-

for more than one year, or the authority to enter into contracts for the sale of real property (at any time) or the conveyance of real property, must be in writing. The only exception to this is the case where the transaction is executed in the presence of the principal, and with his acquiescence. To collect commissions all contracts should be in writing.

Q. A gives B an exclusive agency in the sale of A's parcel X property. Subsequent to the granting of said authority, A sells parcel X property himself; B sues A to recover commissions. Is 

A liable to B?

A. A is not liable to B for commissions by reason of the fact that A himself sold the property, thereby not violating his agreement with B to the effect that B was his exclusive agent. If, however, A had given B an exclusive right to sell as distinguished from an exclusive agency, the liability of A to B would take effect even though A himself sold the subject matter of the agency, as the latter authority obviously deprives the principal of making the sale himself.

Q. Is a husband always the agent of his wife in a real estate transaction?

A. No, he is not presumed to be her agent unless he has authority to act as such from her. 

Q. A allows B, his wife, to enter into numerous transactions in his name for a considerable period of time. State whether the wife is the agent of the husband and also state in what manner the husband may terminate such agency.

A. In such a case the wife is the agent of the husband by implication, and with regard to the termination of such authority by the husband, he must give actual notice to those with whom she has dealt in his name, save and excepting that he cannot relieve himself from liability for her necessaries when it is his fault that she is in need of them. Notice may be given by advertising. 

Q. What conditions will terminate the agency relationship?

A. (A) Death of Principal or Agent. (B) Insanity of Prin cipal or Agent. (C) Bankruptcy of Principal or Agent. (D) Revocation by Principal or Agent. (E) Accomplishment of object. (F) Change in Conditions. (G) Lapse of time.

Q. What effect has the death of an owner of real property on his duly signed authorization to a broker to sell property? 

A. Death of principal revokes authority of agent, except in very rare cases, say where agent holds an interest in the property involved. Complete answer depends upon circumstances. General rule is that authority of broker is terminated by death of principal. 

CLIENT 

Q. What is the difference between a client and a customer?

A. A Client is one who employs you to represent him. A Customer is one with whom you may do business but do not represent. -58-

BROKER  

Q. When a broker has written authority to sell property for a stated price, does that also give Broker (agent) authority to execute the contract of sale? Explain fully.

A. Broker cannot execute a binding contract on behalf of his principal unless authorized by a written instrument sufficient in its terms to constitute it a power of attorney. The common form of written authorization given to a broker authorizing the sale of a property is merely an authorization to the broker to negotiate a sale by finding a buyer. He has authority to take a deposit and give a deposit receipt.

Q. Is a broker justified in withholding from the purchaser of real property, information which if disclosed would probably defeat the sale of the property? Give reasons for your answer.

A. No, it is the duty of every broker to protect the public against fraud, misrepresentation, or unethical practices in connection with real estate transactions. Property should be offered by broker solely on its merit without exaggeration, concealment, or any form of deception or misleading representation. See Section 

12 of the Real Estate Act.

Q. Under what circumstances, if at all, may a real estate broker buy for himself or acquire an interest in property listed with him by a client?

A. When he has made his true position clearly known to the listing owner. 

Q. Can a president of a corporation licensed under the Real

Estate Act transact business as a broker in his individual capacity? 

A. No. Under latest ruling, a license issued to an individual an an officer or a member of a particular corporation or partnership does not authorize him to act as an officer or member of another corporation or partnership, or as an individual broker. A license issued to a broker as an individual does not authorize the holder to act as an officer or member of a corporation or partnership. 

A separate license must be procured for each capacity but only one examination is required.

Q. Is it ethical and lawful for broker to sell his own property to customers? If so, under what conditions?

A. Yes, when the broker makes it clear to the buyer that he (the broker) is selling his own property. A broker selling his own property is not acting in capacity of a broker, he is an owner. 

REALTOR 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. What does the term "Realtor" denote?

A. That the person using such term is a member of a local, State, or National Realty Board, which is affiliated with the National 

Association of Real Estate Boards. 

-59-

Q. John Brown took a real estate broker's examination, and upon receiving his broker's license, opened an office and put up a sign reading "John Brown, Realtor." Did he violate any provisions of the Real Estate Law, and if so, to what penalty was he subject? 

A. Yes, this is in violation of Sec. 10300 of the Real Estate Law, and makes the licensee subject to suspension or revocation of his license.

COMMISSIONS  

Q. Seller refused to pay commission, but gave agent net price. 

Broker added 10% commission to the net list price, though 5% commission was the custom. Purchaser discovered this and sued broker for difference. Why did he win suit?

A. In absence of an agreed rate of commission, the broker should add or charge the customary rate, that is, the equivalent of the Realty Board Schedule unless net listing specifically gave broker "all over and above" the net. 

Q. Owner in distant state listed his property for sale with broker in California at a stated price. Shortly thereafter a new oil, field was brought in close to the property. Agent found ready buyer at listed price and submitted to owner. Latter accepted, but while deal was in escrow he heard about the oil discovery and thereupon wired cancellation of deal. Was broker entitled to his commission? Explain.

A. No; his action constituted a breach of good faith. Suppression of true facts constituted deceit on part of broker. 

Q. A broker secures a purchaser who signs a contract to buy within the time provided in the broker's contract for the payment of his commission from the owner. The broker did not notify the owner of the purchaser's acceptance within the time provided, but the owner did learn of the purchaser's acceptance before the time expired. Can the broker recover his commission?

A. Yes. It is immaterial that the broker gives no notice of having found a purchaser if the principal knows from other sources that a purchaser has been secured. 

Q. The only written provision for paying agent a commission was in the escrow agreement between buyer and seller. For some reason they cancelled these escrow instructions but later made a deal leaving out the agent. Where does agent stand with reference to the commission?

A. Statute of frauds involved in question. It requires written evidence of "agreement to pay commission" for sale of real estate. 

In this instance (a) Escrow instruction sufficient had escrow not been cancelled and buyer had complied with his part of agreement. (b) Agent's right (at law) to collect commission would involve why the escrow was cancelled; if presumption was strong enough that -60

cancellation of escrow was to avoid liability for payment of commission, court would probably rule escrow instruction sufficient. 

If deal as subsequently closed was on entirely different terms agent would probably have difficulty in collecting commission. 

Broker could have protected his interest by having had separate agreement (deposit receipt) signed by both parties previous to "taking them to escrow. 

Q. Owner wrote letter to agent saying, "I will take $10,000 cash for the property." The agent at once procured a purchaser who offered to take it for price named, on terms of half cash, balance at $100 per month. Owner not only refused to accept, but also decided not to sell at all. What recourse has agent?

A. Agent has no recourse for collecting commission, since he did not find a buyer ready, willing and able to buy on the terms authorized by owner.

Q. If a licensed real estate broker has a duly signed authorization to sell real property as the agent of the owner and actually sells same, how can he collect his commission if the owner refuses to pay?

A. By suit against owner for breach of contract. He should have protected himself by having commission paid through escrow. 

Q. Owner assured broker that there were no restrictions against building store on lot; relying upon it, deal was made, but it was discovered that the city had banned stores by a zoning ordinance. Buyer refused to go on with deal and demanded return of his money. Was the broker blamable, or did he earn his commission, and could buyer recover? Explain fully.

A. Assuming word "restrictions" as used in question refers to all things that would prevent building store, such as building restrictions, zoning or other ordinances, broker is not to blame. He earned commission. Principal must act in good faith; his failure to do so will not deprive broker of his commission. Buyer can recover since conditions were found to be different from those represented by owner, provided sale was made clearly on understanding that there were no "restrictions" of any character (see assumption above) that would prevent buyer building store.

Q. How is the amount of compensation or commission which a real estate broker has earned determined? 

A. Amount of commission is dependent upon agreement between broker and party who agrees to pay commission. Any amount may be agreed upon; not fixed by law. In absence of definite agreement as to amount, commission should be in accordance with schedale of local or nearest realty board. 1 -61-

SCHEDULE OF COMMISSIONS 

Principles and Definitions Governing the Following Schedule 1. Inquiries regarding the application of any portion of the schedule to specific deals must be in writing, addressed to the Board by each principal involved, and will be answered only in writing. 

2. Usually a Transaction is logically identified as belonging to a definite district, in which case the deal automatically becomes subject to the Commission's computations applying in that district. 

However, should a transaction lack the outstanding features identifying it as being in a particular district, then the use of the following definitions will assist in properly classifying the deal. 

Wherever possible, the contracting agreements should stipulate the uses to which the property is to be put, thus avoiding a later controversy as to the proper classification of the transaction. 

3. Business Property shall be defined as that property used or available for use for commercial purposes, and not included in classifications set out in paragraphs 4 to 9, inclusive. 

4. Industrial Property shall be defined as that property used or available for use for the commercial production of raw materials into more refined, or into finished materials. 

5. Wholesale Property shall be defined as that property used by an occupant whose business is 75%, or over, storage and wholesaling. 

6. Residence Property shall be defined as that property designed and erected for purpose of single family residences. 

7. Apartment House Property shall be defined as a building containing separate apartments for three or more families, and having the street entrance common to all.

Hotels shall be defined as buildings in which 10 or more rooms are available to the public for living purposes, operated under one management or ownership.

Bungalow Courts shall be defined as three or more buildings on a single lot, each containing a complete residential unit. 

8. Flat Property shall be defined as a building of two or more stories, containing individual residences, each having its own street entrance. 

9. A Duplex House shall be defined as a building of two stories, accommodating two families, each having its own street entrance; or any other multiple unit dwelling not otherwise herein defined. 

10. Commissions in full shall be payable in cash and become due when the broker has completed his services according to law. 

11. Leasing Commissions shall be payable at the same time and in the same manner as sales Commissions. 

12. There being no legal definition in California for the term "Ground Lease," its use is discontinued in this schedule. 

13. Leases shall be divided into two classes: Ordinary Leases and 

Long Term Leases. A long term lease shall be defined as one for a period of more than twenty-five years. All leases for twenty-five years and under shall be defined as ordinary leases. -62

14. Commissions on ordinary leases shall be computed on the basis of the gross rental, or the sum total obligation of the lessee. 

15. Commissions on long term leases shall be computed on the basis of the valuation of the leased premises. (See 144.) 

16. Where, for the purpose of figuring Commissions, the rental as stated in the lease must be adapted to either a gross or net rental, such rental shall be determined by adding or subtracting, as the case may require, to each yearly rental a sum equal to 2% of the value of the land and improvements thereon, or agreed to be placed thereon by the lessor, according to the lease. 

If the valuation of the land and improvements is not stated in the lease, the valuation shall be that sum, 6% of which equals the average stated net annual rentals, and 72% of which equals the gross average stated annual rental. 

17. The item of 2% of the valuation of land and improvements thereon in paragraph 16 is used as being the nearest approximation to the actual taxes applying against a given property. 

18. The term "Gross Rental" includes taxes, insurance and the like. 

19. The term "Net Rental" excludes taxes, insurance and the like. 

20. Percentage lease shall be defined as a lease where the rents are to be computed or made payable on the basis of future commodity sales or other proceeds.

City and County-Improved or Vacant 

21. Business Property: 5% upon the first $50,000 of the purchase price. 212% upon the balance of the purchase price. 

22. Industrial, Wholesale and Manufacturing Property: 5% of the total purchase price. 

23. Resident Property, Including Flats, Duplex Houses: 5% of the total purchase price. 

24. Hotel, Apartment Houses, and Bungalow Courts: 5% of the total purchase price. 

25. Sale of Leasehold. See Leaseholds under Leases, ¶45. 

26. Sale of Leased Property to Lessee: Should a lessee, during the term of occupancy, purchase all or part of the demised premises, pursuant to a right conferred in the lease, or a subsequent modification thereof, then a regular sales fee as computed from this schedule, on the respective class of property involved, shall be paid to the original leasing agent at the time such right is exercised, deducting however any fee previously paid for leasing. 

27. Equipment, Fixtures and Stock in Trade: For negotiating the sale of a Commercial Business, including equipment, fixtures, stock in trade, good-will or similar items: 10% on the first $5,000; and 

5% on the balance of purchase price. $50 minimum. 

28. Furnishings and Hotel or Apartment House Equipment: For negotiating the sale of the furniture, fixtures, equipment, good-will

and the like, of a Hotel, Apartment House, Flat or Bungalow Court: 

10% on the first $3,000 and 5% on the balance of the purchase price. $50 minimum. 

29. Subdivisions: Each subdivision shall be treated separately and, at the time of assuming agency, the fee shall be fixed, recognizing any or all of the following factors: distance of property from urban centers, utilities, transportation, advertising, drawing of papers and any other service or services to be rendered. 

30. Acreage: 5% of the total purchase price. 

31. Ranches: 5% of the total purchase price. 

32. Exchange Fees: Each party to an exchange shall pay the full fee based upon the consideration for his respective property so exchanged, the same as if a sale had been made by each party. (See 

Schedule of Sales Fees.) 

33. Permits and Franchises: Where it is necessary in connection with the sale or leasing of property to procure a permit for operating and conducting a specific business, a fee of $25.00 and up shall be charged, according to the service required. Where it is necessary to procure a railway spur track franchise, a fee of $50.00 and up shall be charged, according to the service required. 

SCHEDULES-LEASE COMMISSIONS 

City and County-Improved or Vacant 

34. Minimum charge for negotiating new written lease $25.00. 

35. Business Property: (A) 3% of the total rental for the first five years. 12% of the total rental for the balance of the term. (B) 

Where the negotiation of a lease or leases is the originating cause of a new structure or requires structural changes to the leased property costing in excess of $1,000. 3% of the total rental for the first five years. 2% of the total rental for the balance of the term. 

36. Industrial, Wholesale and Manufacturing Property: (A) 32% 

of the total rental for the first five years. 22% of the total rental for the second five years. 12% of the total rental for the balance of the term. (B) Where the negotiation of a lease or leases is the originating cause of a new structure or requires structural changes to the leased property costing in excess of $1,000. 4% of the total rental for the first five years. 22% of the total rental for the second five years. 12% of the total rental for the balance of the term. 

37. Residence Property Leases, Including Flats and Duplex Houses: 

5% of total rental.

38. Hotel, Apartment House and Bungalow Court Leases: 3% of the total rental for the first five years. 12% of the total rental for the balance of term. 

39. Rental Listing Fee: For listing each dwelling or apartment for rent $1.00, this to apply on Commission, if rented by agent.

40. Month to Month Tenancy (All Residential Types): 25% of the first month's rent. No fee less than $10.00. If the property is furnished for residence purposes, and the agent shows property: 35% of the first month's rent. Such tenancy shall extend for a period not exceeding six months. If tenancy exceeds six months, commission shall accrue as in paragraph 48. 64

41. Month to Month Tenancy (Business, Industrial, Wholesale and 

Manufacturing Property): 50% of the first month's rent, where the monthly rental does not exceed $50; minimum fee, $10. 25% of the first month's rent where the monthly rental exceeds $50; minimum fee, $25. Such tenancy shall extend for a period not exceeding six months. If tenancy exceeds six months, commissions shall accrue as in paragraph 48. 

42. Crop Rental (Country Property): 5% of the rental for the entire term of lease; Commissions to be paid at the time, or from time to time, when crop is harvested and marketed, due diligence to this end to be used. 

43. Cash Rental (Country Property): 5% of the rental for the entire term of lease; Commissions to be paid upon payment of rental. 

44. Long Term Leases, More Than 25 Years: For the purpose of computing the Commission on a Long Term Lease, the valuation of the leased premises shall be that sum, 6% of which equals the average stated net annual rentals, and 72% of which equals the average stated gross annual rental. The Commission on properties classed in paragraph 21 shall be a sum equal to: 5% upon the first $50,000 of said valuation. 22% upon the balance of said valuation.

The Commission on properties classed in paragraphs 22, 23, and 24 shall be a sum equal to 5% upon the total valuation. 

N.B. This computation will result in the fee being identical with a sales Commission were the property sold at a valuation, which is that sum, 6% of which equals the average stated net annual rentals. 

45. Leaseholds (Long Term Leases): On a sale of a leasehold, compute the valuation of the property from the rentals applying during the unexpired term (See paragraph 44), to such valuation add the cash bonus paid. The total will represent the total valuation involved in the leasehold transaction. Having determined such valuation, compute the commission as in paragraph 44. (See example 

No. 5.) 

46. Lease Subject to Cancellation by Lessee Upon the Payment of a 

Bonus: The regular leasing commission shall be charged for the full term of the lease, provided the bonus agreed to be paid as consideration for cancellation be an amount sufficient to cover that portion of the commission applicable to the cancellation period; otherwise the broker shall be entitled to a commission based upon: (a) The period from the beginning of the term to the date the right to cancel accrues or (b) The period from the beginning of the term to the date the right to cancel is actually exercised by lessee, whichever of such periods is the longer. 

47. Renewal of Lease: Where an agent negotiates the renewal of a lease to the same tenant, the regular Commission shall be paid by the lessor, the same as though an entirely new lease had been negotiated. 

48. Extension of Lease or Additional Space Taken: Should the term of a lease be extended or the lessee occupy additional space at the same or additional rent, by virtue of optional rights conferred in the lease, or through subsequent modification of such rights, then -65-

the regular leasing commission as computed from this schedule, on the respective class of property involved, shall be paid to the original leasing agent at the time such rights are exercised. 

49. Where a percentage lease provides for a minimum rental a partial payment on account of commission shall be made, based upon the minimum rental, and the balance of commission, or if no minimum rental is provided for, the entire commission shall be payable as follows: (a) Where rents are to be computed and payable upon future commodity sales, or other proceeds, the estimated amount of such sales, or other proceeds shall be computed by agreement of lessor and agent from the best information obtainable, and commission shall be payable thereon according to the above schedules for lease commission, without subsequent adjustment. (b) As an alternative to such agreement the agent may at his option elect to await the actual determination of rents from such proceeds during the first year of said term, or any consecutive series of years thereof, including said first year, and upon such year or the average of such years be entitled to commission thereon according to the schedule for leasing commissions. 

50. Sale of Leased Property to Lessee (See [26, Sales Fees). 

51. Reappraisal of Rental: Where a definite rental is stated for a portion of the term and a reappraisal or reappraisals are provided for in the lease to determine the rental for the balance of the term, the Commission shall be figured on the basis of the average stated rental applied to the full term. 

52. Assignment, Transfer or Sale of Lease (Ordinary Leases): On negotiating an Assignment, Transfer or Sale of Lease or Sub-Lease, the regular Commission shall be charged for the unexpired term of the lease computed from the rentals applying over the unexpired term, the same as though a new lease were negotiated. In addition a Commission of 5% should be charged on any cash bonus involved. 

If the said lease or sublease includes an extension of time beyond the period named in the original lease, or specifies additional rental, or if the lease or sublease grants an option for an extension of time beyond that named in the original lease, the regular leasing Commission shall apply and shall be paid by the lessor. It is logical, therefore, to use computations resulting in a fee identical with a fee for the sale of a property at $300,000.

CONTRACTOR 

Q. Why do not owners pay contractors immediately after a building job is completed?

A. So that if the contractor does not pay his bills and allows liens to be filed against the property, the owner may withhold the amount of the liens from the contractor's remuneration. 

Q. When is owner safe in paying contractor in full for work done? A. 

When contractor has furnished a "Contract Bond” or a "Lien and Completion Bond"; when he is supplied with waiver of mechanics liens signed by all persons contributing labor or material on the job. If neither of the above have been supplied to the owner he should not pay the contractor in full until thirty days after notice of completion has been filed, and he has ascertained that no mechanics liens have been filed. 

ORIGINAL CONTRACTOR 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. Define an original contractor.

A. An original contractor is one who contracts directly with an owner to do work and furnish materials for a building project or some particular portion of the entire project. 

Notice, pursuant to Section 1187, Code of Civil Procedure, must be filed within 10 days after completion-recording fee $1.00.

CONTRACTS 

Q. Name four essentials of a real estate contract. 

A. (a) Parties capable of contracting. (b) Mutual consent of parties. (c) A lawful object. (d) A sufficient cause of consideration. Contract must be in writing.

Q. In California if a contract for sale of real estate is executed and delivered on Sunday, can it be enforced if one of the parties refuses to abide by the terms of the contract? 

A. Yes. There is no provision in California laws rendering a contract invalid because it has been made and executed on Sunday or any holiday.

Q. In California, what, if any, contracts concerning conveyance of an interest in real estate need not be in writing? 

A. All must be in writing, with the exception of lease for one (1) year or less. 

Q. Is it necessary that a contract for the purchase, sale or lease of real property be in writing?

A. Yes, with the exception of lease for one (1) year or less. 

LISTINGS 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. A broker has an exclusive listing from a nonresident owner authorizing the broker to sell the property for $10,000 and agreeing to pay 5% commission on sale price. Recent developments in the vicinity have caused values to double. Is it the duty of the broker to notify the nonresident owner of this condition, or is he justified in selling at the price listed?

A. Broker owes a moral duty to the owner to advise him honestly and intelligently regarding the true value of his property. 

Should, therefore, inform him of rise in value. -71-

Q. Owner orally asked agent to lease his store. Agent found tenant to take it for three years. Owner refused to accept tenancy for longer than one year. What recourse had agent for his commission?

A. There being no definite agreement as to period for which stores would be leased, owner has right to refuse to accept tenancy for longer than one year, and therefore, did not avail himself of broker's services. Broker could not collect commission in any amount.

Q. (a) Define an option to purchase. (b) Define an exclusive listing. (c) Define an "open" listing.

A. (a) An option is an agreement whereby one party, called optioner, for a consideration, gives another party, called the optionee, the right for a period of time, to purchase certain property at a certain price but does not bind the optionee to buy it. (b) An exclusive listing is one which gives the broker the right to sell over all other persons except the owner; in other words, an exclusive listing simply excludes other brokers. It cannot prevent the owner from selling his own property. (c) An open listing is a form of listing whereby a number of brokers are employed to sell a given property. The one who first finds a buyer is entitled to commission. 

Q. Owner gave agent, on usual form, exclusive right to sell his property for 90 days. Without knowledge of owner's death, agent sold the property. Can buyer enforce delivery of the property, and can agent collect the promised commission? Explain. 

A. No; agency terminates with death of principal, the owner. 

Q. If a husband authorizes, in writing and over his own signature, a real estate broker to sell the separate real property of his wife, and the broker finds a purchaser ready, able and willing to buy in accordance with the authorization, but the wife refuses to sell, is the broker entitled to his commission? If so, from whom?

Can purchaser successfully sue wife for specific performance? Explain.

A. Broker is entitled to commission and can recover from husband since husband authorized broker to act. Purchaser could not successfully sue wife for specific performance since wife did not agree to sell nor did she employ the broker. 

Q. When broker takes property for sale on a net listing, with whom must he deal for his commission? 

A. When broker is authorized in writing by an owner to sell property and authorization expressly provides that, in lieu of a fixed commission, the broker is to receive all over a stated price, the broker, upon finding a buyer who is ready, willing and able to buy, is entitled to receive and recover from the owner the amount which the buyer was willing to pay in excess of the price stated by owner. If broker sells property for the net price specified by owner, and no more, broker is not entitled to commission. 

On the other hand, when owner lists property with broker at a net price to owner and listing does not expressly state that broker -72-

is to receive all over the net price, the broker is not entitled to the excess, but is merely entitled to receive a reasonable commission which must not exceed the amount of the excess. 

All agreements involving a net price should be specific as to what, if any, part of the conveyance charges, other than incidental to deed, are to be paid by owner.

Q. Broker took listing of property as sole agent. Did that exclude the owner's right to sell it? Explain.

A. No; any contract depriving owner's right to sell his property would be void, but the owner is liable for a commission if he sells property on which he has given broker exclusive right to sell. 

So-called exclusive or sole listings may be either of two kinds. 

An exclusive or sole agency listing or contract only binds the owner to refrain from listing with other brokers during the life of the contract under which the broker receiving listing is employed. In other words, an exclusive and sole agency simply excludes other brokers. Owner himself may sell without liability for commission if prior to time owner entered into agreement for sale he had not been informed broker had procured a buyer on exact terms set out in broker's authorization. Broker under contract would not be entitled to commission if he finds buyer after owner himself had sold. If, during life of listing another broker should sell property, broker under exclusive agency would be entitled to commission.

An exclusive right contract confers upon the broker the sole and exclusive right to sell the property during the term of his contract with owner. Broker is entitled to commission, and owner is liable for it, whether sale is made by owner, or another broker, in fact, by any person or agent.

AGREEMENT OF SALE 

Q. Is an agreement to sell real property binding on the seller?

A. Yes, if the conditions contained therein are complied with prior to withdrawal. 

Q. Must an agreement for the sale of real estate be in writing? 

A. Yes. California Law provides that all agreements affecting real property must be in writing. (Exception-leases for 1 year or less.) -74-

Q. What actions may be brought by the vendee upon failure of the vendor to perform the contract of sale?

A. The vendee may elect either (a) to rescind the contract and recover the price paid (85 Cal. 110), or (b) to sue for damages for breach of contract (C. C. 3306,) or (c) for specific performance of the contract (C. C. 3387), or (d) for liquidated damages stipulated for in the contract (C. C. 3389; 52 Pac. 729), or (e) to foreclose upon his purchaser's lien. (C. C. 3050; 87 Cal. 49; 103 Cal. 

287; 113 Cal. 656.)

DEPOSITS  

Q. State fully how real property should be described in the deposit receipt or contract.

A. Description for the purpose of a contract may be by house number, by reference to a recorded map, by metes and bounds, or by any combination of these. City, County and State in which property is located should be stated. (Legal description from recorded map, most safe and preferred.)

Q. What are the successive steps to take when a broker makes a sale? 

A. Take deposit, draw sale deposit receipt. Have buyer and seller sign three copies of receipt so each party and broker may retain copy. Close transactions through an escrow. (See Escrows.)

Q. Buyer changed his mind and demanded of agent return of his deposit before owner had signed agreement of purchase and sale. 

In absence of time limit allowed agent to procure acceptance, what were purchaser's rights in premises?

A. Purchaser has right to withdraw deposit any time prior to written acceptance or ratification by seller. If there is time limit in agreement within which broker must procure seller's acceptance, buyer cannot withdraw deposit and offer until after time expires.

Q. Deposit receipt did not mention building restrictions on lot being sold, but agent says he told buyer all about them. Certificate of title disclosed that four-family flats could not be erected, and buyer demanded return of deposit. Explain why agent lost this deal.

A. Building restrictions should have been written into the deposit receipt, buyer would then have been bound by them. 

Q. When a broker accepts a deposit subject to owner's approval, from a purchaser ready and willing to buy, then is offered more for the property by another customer, whose offer should the broker first submit to the owner?

A. Broker is bound to protect best interest of the owner. He must get all he can for the property. He should present offer and deposit of first purchaser and fully acquaint owner with offer at higher price. 

Q. What should a real estate salesman do with deposit money received from a purchaser of real estate? 

A. Salesman should turn it over to his employing broker. All checks should be drawn to order of broker and all receipts for deposit should be executed in his name as "agent for Seller," followed by "By (name of salesman)." The words, "subject to acceptance and approval of seller" should be added. -77-
