PROTECTION TO BUYER 

Q. What is the usual and safe way of protecting buyer against a loss in event of destruction of improvements by fire before conveyance to him is completed?

A. Incorporate in sale deposit receipt clause to effect that in the event the improvements should be destroyed or materially damaged between date of receipt and date of delivery of deed to buyer, the contract shall, at the election of the buyer immediatly become null and void and any deposit paid shall be returned to buyer on demand.

EXCHANGE TRANSACTIONS 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. Must the wife of a party to an agreement of exchange sign the contract to enable the real estate broker conducting the exchange to collect his commission?

A. No, since the committee is due when both parties sign the contract. C. C. 172a does not apply to agreements of exchange. (Goodrich v. Turney, 44 Cal. App. 517.)

Q. When is a commission for an exchange earned? 

A. The commission is earned when the broker secures an acceptance of the offer to exchange. It occurs the instant the second party signs. (Goodrich v. Turney, 44 Cal. App. 517.)

Q. Is the party who signs the memorandum liable for the commission even when he does not own the property which he promises to exchange?

A. Yes, the principal is liable, for the broker has performed his part of the contract by securing the acceptance, and it makes no difference whether his principal performs his agreement with the other party. (Rucker v. Hubler, 56 Cal. App. 771; Jauman v. McCussick, 166 Cal. 517-see also 28 Am. St. Rep. 546, 19 Am. St. Rep. 225,

Annotated Cases 1914 D. 395.) 

Q. What is a sufficient description in an agreement of exchange?

A. Any description by which the property described may be exchanged. The courts are liberal in allowing property to be identified in this kind of agreements as the contract with the broker is purely an agency appointment. (Goodrich v. Turney, 44 Cal. App. 

517; McKnight v. Davitt, 27 Cal. App. Dec. 116, 27 L. R. A. (N. S.) 

786; Tolosano v. Will, 62 Cal. App. 625; Ontario D. F. G., Assn. v. 

Cutting, etc., Co., 134 Cal. 25; Marriner v. Dennison, 78 Cal. 270; 

Tooney v. Dumphy, 86 Cal. 639; Sanchez v. Yorba, 8 Cal. App. 495.) —79—

Q. In an agreement of exchange, must the broker procure a purchaser ready, able, and willing?

A. No, as the usual "Agreement of Exchange" provides the commission shall be due on securing an acceptance of the offer to exchange. (Rucker v. Hubler, 56 Cal. App. 771; Goodrich v. Turney, 44 Cal. App. 517.) 

Q. Must the plaintiff broker, suing for his commission, sign the agreement to make it obligatory? 

A. No. (Goodrich v. Turney, supra.)

Q. Is the liability of the parties to an agreement of exchange the same whether both sign one instrument or two instruments? 

A. Yes. (Goodrich v. Turney, supra; Beverly v. Blackwood, 102 

Cal. 83.)

Q. Must the agreement be consummated if it is so provided? 

A. Yes, the extent of the performance of the broker in earning his commission depends upon his authorization. (Jennings v. Jones, 31 Cal. App. 335.)

Q. In a contract containing both printed and written matter, which controls?

A. The written controls the printed matter. (C. C. P. 1862; 

Ferren v. Western, etc., Inc., 49 Cal. App. Dec. 371.) 

Q. Is a written instrument presumptive evidence of a consideration? 

A. Yes. (C. C. 1614, 3105; Weban Est., Inc., v. Hewlett, 193 

Cal. 675; Allen's Collection Agency v. Lee, 73 Cal. App. 68; Cole v. Low, 52 Cal. App. Dec. 674.) 

Q. Must want of consideration for the execution of an instrument be specially pleaded in order to offer proof of want of consideration? 

A. Yes. (Rivera v. Cappa, 29 Cal. App. 496.) 

Q. Is a name typewritten in the body of instrument a signature? 

A. No. (Little v. Union Oil Co., 47 Cal. App. Dec. 689.) 

Q. Must the plaintiff broker, suing for his commission, sign an agreement of exchange to collect?

A. No, it is sufficient if he is properly appointed. (C. C. 1624; 

C. C. P. 1073; Goodrich v. Turney, supra.)

Q. May a broker accept commission from both parties to the agreement of exchange?

A. Yes, for in such a position he acts as a mere middlemanthe rule is that an agent stricti juris may not accept a commission from both parties to a deal as he must use his discretion in bringing about a consummation of the bargain and hence represents conflicting interests-but in acting for one party in securing an acceptance of an offer to exchange he uses no discretion and may take a commission from both parties. (Jauman v. McCussick, 166 Cal. 517; Gunn v. Bank of California, 99 Cal. 349; Carothers v. Caine, 38 Cal. App. 

72; King v. Reed, 24 Cal. App. 229; Glenn v. Rice, 174 Cal. 269; 80-

Clark v. Allen, 125 Cal. 276; Hladik v. Allen, 26 Cal. App. 509where principal consented to agent receiving a double commission.) 

Q. Is the addendum to a contract placed below the signature a part of the contract?

A. Yes, unless it appears it was not so intended. (Eldridge v. Mowry, 24 Cal. App. 184.) 

Q. Is an agreement of exchange a contract?

A. Yes, as it contains all the elements of a contract. (Heslin v. Lapham, 77 Cal. App. 137, 246 Pac. 150; Jauran v. McCussick, 166 Cal. 522; Lundeen v. Otis, 164 Cal. 186.)

Q. What is the statutory period of limitation within which an action may be brought on an agreement of exchange? 

A. Four years. (C. C. P. 337; Heslin v. Lapham, 77 Cal. App. 

137-writing signed by one party, the party to be charged, a quasicontract-Melone v. Ruffino, 129 Cal. 525.)

Q. Does an agreement of exchange fulfill all the requirements of the statute of frauds?

A. Yes, and the agreement may be read into the evidence even though the instrument does not indicate the amount of plaintiff's commission. (C. C. 1614; Tooney v. Dunphy, 36 Cal. 639.)

Q. May the plaintiff broker recover on the theory of a special contract for the benefit of a third party?

A. Yes, before the obligee has rescinded. (C. C. 1559; Cole v. 

Low, 52 Cal. App. Dec. 674.)

Q. Is it material when the contract was signed by the respective parties?

A. No, as both parties are offerors and acceptors, it is a mutual contract as between them for the benefit of a third party. (Green v. Robertson, 64 Cal. 75.) 

Q. Is it necessary for the broker to deliver the contract to the defendant?

A. No, that is not the practice among brokers. (Goodrich v. 

Turney, supra.) 

Q. Is parol evidence admissible to identify the land? (Oral, verbal, speech, not expressed in writing.)

A. Yes, also to prove the amount of the compensation, the true date of the contract, the performance of services, and the time of payment. (Ayres v. S. P. Co., 173 Cal. 74; C. C. P. 1856; C. C. 1860; 

Goodrich v. Turney, supra.) 

Q. Is the agreement of exchange admissible?

A. Yes, to prove the obligation. (Naylor v. Adams, 15 Cal. 

App. 548.)

Q. Where no compensation is stated in the agreement what compensation is the plaintiff broker allowed?

A. A reasonable rate of compensation by implication and operation of the law, the usual or ordinary charge made under like cases. Court may fix compensation without expert testimony. (Naylor v. Adams, 15 Cal. App. 548, 120 Cal. 551, 8 Cal. App. 378; Muney v. Thompson, 26 Cal. App. 634.) -81-

Q. Is the broker entitled to reimbursement for expenditures, including a reasonable sum for abstract? 

A. Yes. (Kicks v. Post, 154 Cal. 22; Quitzow v. Perrin, 120 Cal. 

Q. When does a broker make out a prima facie case of his status as a broker A. When he produces a certified copy of the license entitling him to act as a broker at the time of the transaction. (C. C. P. 

1919; Tolossano v. Will, 62 Cal. App. 622.)

Q. Must a contract authorizing an agent to sell a leasehold interest be in writing?

A. No, as a leasehold interest is not "real estate," only a chattel real or personal property. (Guy v. Brennan, 60 Cal. App. 452.)

Q. Must a real estate broker allege and prove he was a duly licensed broker at the time he acted as such and for which he seeks compensation? 

A. Yes.

Q. Will the broker lose his commission because of defective title of either party signatories? 

A. No. (Martin v. Ede, 103 Cal. 157; Justy v. Ero, 16 Cal." 

App. 519.)

Q. What is the nature of the obligations of the parties signing an agreement of exchange?

A. Joint and several, and hence the broker may sue either or both for his commission. (C. C. 1659; Wood v. Longyear, 71 Cal. 

Dec. 110; Goodrich v. Turney, supra.)

Q. Is parol admissible to prove performance of a written contract! 

A. Yes. (Haberman v. Sawall, 72 Cal. App. 576.)

Q. Is a formal contract necessary to bind a party to pay a commission?

A. No. (Arnold v. La Belle Oil Co., 47 Cal. App. 290, 190 Pac. 

815.) 

Q. What must the broker prove to be entitled to recover his commission?

A. The obligation or debt incurred by proving the employment. 

The burden then shifts to the defendant to prove payment of the debt. (Melone v. Ruffine, 14 Cal. App. 300-payment is an affirmative defense which must be specially pleaded to prove it-Green v. Palmer, 15 Cal. 412-defendant has burden of proving payment.) 

Q. May the defendant attempt to prove fraud to avoid the obligation?

A. No, not unless he has pleaded it specially. (McKiernen v. 

Lenzen, 56 Cal. 61.) 

Q. May the defendant attempt to prove forfeiture?

A. No, not unless he has specially pleaded it. (Gaskill v. 

Moore, 4 Cal. 233.)

Q. May a broker bring an action on an agreement for exchange made for his benefit and signed by the exchange parties? -82-

A. Yes, and it is not necessary that additional consideration run to the broker to support the action. (Lawrence v. Fox, 20 N. Y. 

268, Court of Appeals; Heelin v. Lapham, Cal. 77, App. 137; Malone v. Crescent City M. & T. Co., 77 Cal. 38.)

Q. What is the best evidence of the value of properties exchanged?

A. The value agreed upon in the agreement or at the time of the transaction. (Kirkpatrick v. Downing, 58 Mo. 32; Dean v. 

Hawes, 29 Cal. App. 689; Beverly v. Blackwood, 102 Cal. 83; Vulcan 

Iron Works Co. v. Roquemore, 175 Fed. 11; Brooks v. Hubbard, 3 Conn. 58; Wills v. Marshall, 1 N. Zeland L. R. 28, Rents paid for use of property are relevant to show value.) 

building?

May an unlicensed architect recover for construction of a 

A. The rule is he cannot. (77 Cal. 400.) 

Q. When is a broker's contract cancelled? 

A. See 72 Cal. App. 497, Tolosano v. Will (1923), 62 Cal.

App. 622; Prima Facie case of status; Plaintiff brought an action to recover a 5% commission under a contract executed between himself and defendant for the sale of certain property described as being near Fresno. Allegations of the complaint were: (1) Execution of the contract, (2) Producing of a purchaser, ready, able, and willing by plaintiff under said contract, (3) Refusal of the defendant to consummate the contract. The evidence was conflicting. 

Plaintiff offered a certified copy of his license to sell real estate, for the purpose of meeting the statutory requirement. Question: was the proof sufficient? Held yes, it showed a prima facie case that the plaintiff was a duly licensed real estate broker, and it then became the duty of the defendant to contest the proof if he could do so; (Jauman v. McCussick, (1913), 166 Cal. 517)) Double commission with knowledge; Plaintiff assignee of a firm of brokers brought this action to recover commission for services in securing the acceptance of an agreement of exchange of certain real property.

The action was based on the usual "Agreement for Exchange" and a second instrument by which the second party accepted the offer of the first party. Both documents were subscribed by the parties to be charged. Defense that the plaintiff never secured a purchaser, ready, able, and willing. Question: was the commission earned by the broker plaintiff? Held, yes, on the signing of the acceptance by the defendant. The executed offer and acceptance constituted an agreement of exchange (Lundeen v. Otis, 164 Cal. 187.) (Lundeen v. Otis (1912), 164 Cal. 183.) Reformation of agreement of exchange. Action upon a written agreement by which Otis promised to pay Lundeen a commission of $2933.00 for securing an acceptance by W. A. Graham of a written offer to Otis to exchange certain parcels of land belonging to Graham for certain parcels of land belonging to Otis. The offer was the usual agreement of exchange signed by Otis and Lundeen. Graham signed a written acceptance on a different instrument and subsequently refused to perform. Defense, that the first instrument should be reformed to suit -83-

the facts by striking out the words "when he has secured an acceptance of the written proposition" and inserting instead thereof, the words, "upon the consummation of said erchange." Question: 

Were the facts a defense to the action? Held not, (1) The written instrument could be reformed only by impeachment or set aside by showing its erecution was obtained by duress, menace, fraud, or mistake (C. C. 1567) or that it was without consideration. (Cavanaugh v. Casselman (1891), 88 Cal. 543.) Requirement of Statute of Frauds:

Plaintiff brought an action for damages as a party beneficiary on a written memorandum signed by the defendant and wife, by which the latter parties promised to perform certain acts and convey lands. Plaintiff offered the contract in evidence, but objec tion was offered that it was not a consummated agreement and became merged in a subsequent agreement and hence did not satisfy the statute of frauds. Question: Was the memorandum admissible?

Held, It was, as it satisfied the statute. It was operative on the signing of defendants in the absence of an understanding that the plaintiff was to sign. (1) It names the parties; (2) States the price, (3) Gives a complete description of the property to be conveyed; (4) And subscribed by the parties to be charged. Such is a complete list of the elements necessary to satisfy the statute. (Toomey v. Dumphy is authority that the price need not be stated.) Green v. Robertson (1883), 64 Cal. 75. Judgment on the pleadings. 

Action on a written instrument signed by the party to be charged, Complaint alleged: (1) Execution of the instrument; (2)

Balance of purchase price paid by second party to be written instrument. Defendant admitted: (1) The employment; (2) Services; (3) Execution of the instrument; (4) Payment of the balance of the purchase price. Motion for judgment on the pleadings by the plaintiff Held: The plaintiff was entitled to judgment on the pleadings as neither defense was sufficient to prevent recovery of the plaintiff. The contract to pay money upon the contingency, the payment of the balance of the purchase price matured on the instant the contingency happened. It makes no difference when defendant signed the contract.

Ryan v. Tomlinson (1870), 39 Cal. 639. Oral agreement executed; The plaintiff and defendant made an oral agreement of exchange and the contract was subsequently executed. Later the 

Court pronounced one of the deeds void. In an action to enforce the agreement, plaintiff offered the deed in evidence to prove the consummation of the deal. Question: Was the deed admissible? 

Held, yes. The exchange agreement was carried into effect after the oral agreement, and hence was not void under the statute of frauds. See also the following cases: Marriner v. Dennison, 78 

Cal. 207; Kennedy v. Morickel, Cal. 8, App. 378; Myers v. Holton, 9 Cal. App. 115.

Muncy v. Thompson (1915), 26 Cal. App. 634. Reasonable Compensation;

Action on a written instrument, the usual agreement for exchange in which the amount of the commission was left bank. -84-

The instrument purported to appoint plaintiff as broker, Question: Was the plaintiff authorized to negotiate the exchange? Held, yes. It is not necessary to state the amount of commission as an agent is entitled to a reasonable commission in the absence of a stipulated sum. 

Clark v. Allen (1899), 125 Cal. 278. What is not variance of proof:

Action for the recovery of a commission for an exchange of real estate between defendant and another. Defense: That the plaintiff would be receiving a double commission without the defendant's knowledge. Question: Is the broker entitled to a double commission? Held, yes; (1) Here he acts as a middleman and not as an agent stricti juris, (2) Both parties had knowledge of the double commission, (3) The case accords with sound public policy, (4) The broker does not represent conflicting interests in such a case, as he only brings the parties together for the purpose of making a deal, (5) Evidence showing an exchange instead of procuring a purchaser, ready, able, and willing is not a variance of the proof with the complaint, where the latter alleges plaintiff procured a purchased, ready, able, and willing. 

Ayers v. S. P. R. R. Co. (1916), 173 Cal. 74. Parcel evidence varying the contract is not admissible. 

Defendant Company planned a subdivision, adopting a general scheme by which it prohibited the sale or use of intoxicating liquor on the premises for all time to come, and made the same public. 

Plaintiff signed a contract of purchase omitting the liquor clause, but was assured by the company's representative that no liquor would be sold on the premises. Plaintiff relied upon the parol representations. Breach that saloons were erected in violation of said representations. Question: Could the plaintiff recover damage for the breach? Held, not, as the representation of the agent was without authority, and ultra vires the power of the corporation, as the state itself, had no power to guarantee intoxicating liquors would never be sold on the premises (C. C., 1856). The parol evidence was not admissible. 

Toomey v. Dumphy (1890), 89 Cal. 639. Reasonable compensa tion-Employment: 

Action to recover the reasonable value of services rendered in procuring a purchaser for the defendant's ranch. The appointment consisted of a letter appointing Toomey to arrange for the sale of the defendant's ranch in Nevada in so many words, signed by Dumphy. Plaintiff offered evidence that: (1) He was a real estate broker at the time of the transaction; (2) Execution and delivery of the memorandum letter; (3) Plaintiff found a purchaser, ready, able, and willing to purchase at the purchase price; (4) Plaintiff's services were reasonably worth $18,750.00 on the purchase price of $150,000.00. Question: Did the memorandum satisfy the statute of frauds? Held, yes, and was admissible to prove the employment. (1) All the evidence offered by the plaintiff was admissible; (2) C. C. 1624 (6) was added to the statute of frauds in 1878 to prevent assertion of false claims a remedial -85-

measure; (3) Employment is the chief element under C. C. 1624 (6); (4) It is not necessary to state the amount of the compensation as a written instrument is presumptive evidence of a consideration, (C. C. 1614; C. C. 2308).

Rucker v. Hubler (1922), 56 Cal. App. 771. Commission earned. 

Plaintiff Rucker sued to recover a commission for having represented defendant Hubler and having secured the execution of an agreement of exchange between defendant and another. Defense: 

The third party who accepted the exchange offer did not own the property which he promised to convey. Question: Did plaintiff earn the commission? Held, yes, the commission was due the instant the defendant accepted the agreement by signing the same. 

Naylor v. Adams (1911), 15 Cal. App. 548. Computation of reasonable commission.

Action: (1) Indebitatus assumpsit (common count); (2) On the special contract for recovery of a broker's commission for sale of defendant's property. Defendant Adams appointed plaintiff by letter which he signed. Question: Was the appointment within the status of frauds? Held, yes; Amount of commission is 5% on value of exchange; 22% on cash exchanged. The contract was made for $600.00 commission which was evidence of the reasonable value of the services rendered. 

Beverley v. Blackwood (1894), 102 Cal. 93. Equitable conversion and value.

Plaintiff and defendant effected an exchange of land, and defendant elected to stand on the exchange. Plaintiff gave back a mortgage to the defendant. Both plaintiff and defendant signed the agreement at the foot thereof. Defendant kept his land and offered to foreclose the mortgage. Question: Will the court cancel the mortgage? Held, yes; (1) Equitable conversion, the defendant ought to exchange his land on the basis of the agreement, and the court will consider he has done so; (2) He could not therefore foreclose his mortgage; (3) Valuation of land in a contract is the best evidence of its value. ance. 

Sanchez v. Yorba (1908), 8 Cal. App. 495. Effect of perform 

Plaintiff's assignee brought an action to recover a real estate broker's commission for services alleged to have been performed in making a sale of certain lands owned by the defendant and his sister. Plaintiff proved appointment, and that defendant gave an option on the land as a result of which he later conveyed. Defense: That the plaintiff did not procure a purchaser, ready, able, and willing. Plaintiff showed actual performance, completion of the deal. Question: Was the plaintiff's assignor entitled to the commission. Held, yes. Complete performance on the part of the plaintiff's assignor at a price satisfactory to the defendant, was a conclusive answer to the defendant. 

Melone v. Ruffino (1900), 129 Cal. 518. Burden of proving payment.

Action on a contract for the sale of land to recover a deposit made by the plaintiff on account of the purchase price. Plaintiff -86-

proved the existence of the debt. Defendant failed to establish non payment. Held, that burden was on the defendant to prove payment, an affirmative plea, and when he failed to do so, plaintiff was entitled to have his deposit returned. 

Martin v. Ede (1894), 130 Cal. 157. Interest on commission.

Plaintiff brought this action to recover a commission due him as a broker for effecting the sale of defendant's property. Title of defendant proved defective and he could not perform. Question: 

Was the plaintiff entitled to the commission with interest? Held, yes; (1) Plaintiff did not contract with defendant with respect to title, but he promised only, to secure a purchaser, ready, able, and willing, which he did; (2) Interest commences at the date the commission becomes due and payable, if the commission is capable of computation (C. C. 3287. See also, Ratzloff v. Trainor-Desmond 

Co., Cal. 41, App. 595; Glenn v. Rice, 174 Cal. 270). (Rate of interest is 7% in California.) 

Waterman v. Baltinghouse (1890), 82 Cal. 659. Exclusive right to sale.

Action by the plaintiff to recover commissions for an alleged sale of land. Plaintiff never produced a purchaser, ready, able, and willing. Plaintiff had the exclusive right to sell for a term, and defendant, himself, elected the sale during the said term. Question: 

Could plaintiff recover on the sale? Held, not; He never produced a purchaser under the contract and under his authority under C. C. 

1624 (6); McCarthy v. Loupo, 62 Cal. 299; See also Zeimer v.

Antesell, 75 Cal. 509. As to when brokers commissions are earned see 139 Am. States Rep. 225. In the above case the plaintiff would have been entitled to recover if he had produced a competent purchaser, as his failure to sell would then have been excused by an act of the defendant, and the defendant may not defeat the right of recovery in the plaintiff by his refusal to accept his purchaser, able, ready, and willing.

Pettibone v. Lake View Town Co. (1901), 134 Cal. 227. Personal services. 

Action to recover on personal services under an alleged contract in writing constituting plaintiff exclusive agent on salary and commissions. An acceptance clause was not signed. Question: Did the contract come within the statute of frauds? Held, not, as the contract was for personal services, and added clause was not part of contract. Note: An unexecuted clause appended to the executed contract after the signatures thereto does not make the executed contract inchoate. tion. 

MacKnight v. Davitt (1918), 27 Cal. App. Dec. 116. Descrip 

Plaintiff secured an acceptance of the usual offer to exchange by which the defendant promised to pay a commission of $375.00. 

Plaintiff brought an action for the recovery of the commission. 

Defense: Defective description. Question: May the plaintiff remedy the defect by parol? Held, yes; The courts allow such parol evidence quite liberally; (2) In such a contract the essential part is the employment. The property was described as being a cer- 87-

tain distance west of Fresno on which defendant lived with improvements and stock. (See also Ontario D. F. C. Assn. v. Cutting 

F. P. Co., 134 Cal. 25; Marriner v. Dennison, 73 Cal. 207.)

Goodrich v. Turney (1919), 44 Cal. App. 517. A case in point on exchange. 

Plaintiff brought the usual action for the recovery of a commission basing his right for the said commission on an agreement of exchange after he had secured an acceptance of the same. 

Question: Did plaintiff earn the commission? Held, yes; When he secured the acceptance; (1) In this case there were two instruments making up the contract; (2) Defendant raised an objection that the contract was not consummated because his wife refused to sign the agreement, and that the commission was not earned; but held, that the Sec. 172a of the civil code of California, did not apply to agreements of exchange; (3) The defendant was liable for the commission when the plaintiff secured an acceptance of defendant's offer even though the "deal" was not consummated; (4) Oral evidence was admissible to make perfect an insufficient description for the purpose of identifying the property described, "My" farm located at a general point of identification is a latent ambiguity capable of being made certain, and hence parol is admissble; but "a" farm in a stated county where defendant has two farms, may not be capable of identification, and parol is not admissible to cure the ambiguity; (5) Actual knowledge of defendant and consummation of the "deal" cures defect in description; (6) The written agreement is admissible to prove the contract under the statute of frauds without the signature of the broker; (7) It is not necessary for the plaintiff broker to secure a person; ready, able, and willing under the usual agreement for exchange as the plaintiff is appointed for the purpose of securing an acceptance of the offer to exchange; (8) The broker is duly appointed and authorized when the defendant signs, and on that instant the commission becomes due; (9) It is not necessary to deliver the contract to the defendant, as the universal practice among brokers is to retain the agreement.

Landlord and Tenant 

(See Regulations under Office of Price Administration During 

Wartime Emergency contained herein)

The scope of this section pertains to the hiring of real property for compensation, the creation and termination of the relation of the Landlord and Tenant. The carrying out of the terms of the contract of hire, the rights and liability to the parties, both as to each other and to third persons, and the remedies available to those aggrieved. All of this being in conformity with the laws of the State of California and subject to the regulations of the 

Office of Price Administration of the United States of America during wartime. 

Q. Who is a landlord?

A. A landlord is one who has, owns or represents an estate in real property. 

Q. Who is a tenant?

A. A tenant is one who hires or rents real property from the landlord for a fixed term or period of time at an agreed rental. 

Q. How is the relation of landlord and tenant created?

A. The relation of landlord and tenant is created by an agreement between them, wherein the landlord agrees to let the premises to the tenant, which agreement is called a Lease. 

Q. Define a Lease. 

LEASES 

A. A Lease is an oral, or written agreement binding owner, or lessor, and tenant, or lessee, to fulfill certain covenants or agreements. 

Q. Are Leases required to be in any particular form?

A. No. 

Q. What are the necessary elements of a Lease? 

A. A Lease must show an intent to lease. It must indicate the names of the parties thereto; designate the premises by a proper description thereof and set forth the amount of rental to be paid therefor, and determine a period of time for which the premises are leased.

Q. For what period of time may property be leased by an oral Lease?

A. An oral Lease of real property may be made for a period, or term of one year, or less. 

Q. When must Leases be in writing?

A. Leases for a term of more than one year must be in writing, duly signed by the lessor, or his duly authorized agent or representative, whose authority must also be properly executed in writing. 

Q. Is it necessary for a lessee to sign the Lease?

A. It is not necessary for lessee to sign the Lease, since delivery to him of the Lease and acceptance thereof by him is sufficient. However, it is better practice to have the Lease signed by both parties and in the event the parties, or either of them, are -90-

married, it is good practice to have their respective spouse or spouses also sign.

Q. When and how does the lessee accept a Lease? 

A. The lessee accepts a Lease upon delivery of the same to him by taking possession of the premises and paying rent therefor. 

Q. Who may lease?

A. All persons are capable of contracting, except minors, persons of unsound mind and persons deprived of civil rights. 

Q. What should be required by a lessor or lessee when either or both are a corporation?

A. To make the parties to such a lease legally liable copy of resolution of the board of directors should be attached and the corporate seal be impressed on all instruments affecting the lease. 

Q. Is the lessor of property liable for repairs on the property leased?

A. Not unless provision to that effect is contained in the lease. 

Q. Lessee has notified lessor that he will vacate the premises at a certain time but fails to do so. What demand may the lessor make for rental in such case? 

A. Three times normal rent. (C. C. 3344-3345.)

Q. When a tenant fails to pay rent how may landlord secure immediate possession of premises?

A. By putting up a bond landlord can now obtain immediate possession of real property for non-payment of rent whereas, prior to August 26, 1937, it was necessary to wait until the conclusion of an unlawful detainer suit. In such case it may be necessary to show the court that the tenant is insolvent or using the premises for illegal purposes. (See O.P.A. regulations.)

Q. Tenant fails to pay rent promptly and receives notice from landlord to surrender possession of premises or pay the rent. If the tenant vacates the premises is he liable for the rent for the balance of his term of lease?

A. No, the landlord has merely exercised his option to break the lease because of failure of the tenant to comply with terms contained therein.

Q. (a) Define a lessor. (b) Define a lessee. 

A. (a) A lessor is one who leases the property, usually the owner. (b) A lessee is a person (or corporation) to whom property is leased. 

Q. How may property of minors and incompetents be leased?

A. Minors and incompetents may act through their legally appointed guardian.

Q. For what period of time may the property of minors or persons of unsound mind be leased?

A. The property of a minor, or person of unsound mind, may be leased for a period not to exceed ten years, excepting that a Lease for the production of minerals, oil, gas and other hydrocarbon substances, the Lease may be fixed for a period of not to -91-

exceed twenty years and so long thereafter as minerals, oil, gas and other hydrocarbon substances are produced in paying quantities from the property leased. 

Q. What is essential to the validity of a Lease to minors or incompetents?

A. Leases obtained through guardians of minors and incompetents are subject to approval and order of the court having jurisdiction of the guardianship. 

Q. Who are persons deprived of their Civil Rights?

A. Those persons under sentence of imprisonment in a State 

Prison for any term less than life and under suspension of all their Civil Rights. However, a person sentenced to imprisonment in a 

State Prison for life is thereafter deemed civilly dead. 

Q. May persons deprived of Civil Rights be restored?

A. Persons deprived of their Civil Rights may be restoreed when placed on parole by the Board of Prison Directors, or by a pardon granted by the Governor. 

Q. For what period of time may agricultural lands be leased?

A. No lease or grant of land for agricultural or horticultural purposes for a longer period than fifteen years, in which shall be reserved any rent or service of any kind shall be valid. 

Q. For what period of time may property in cities or towns be leased?

A. No Lease of any city or town lot for a longer period than ninety-nine years in which shall be reserved any rent or service of any kind shall be valid.

Q. For what period of time may municipally owned property be leased?

A. The property of any municipality shall not be leased for a period longer than ten years, excepting that water and sewage discharged from the Municipal Sewer System, the property and equipment used in treating, or disposing of such sewage and the sewer farm of a municipality and all water and sewage used and discharged thereon may be leased for a period not to exceed twenty-five years, and tide-lands and submerged lands granted to any municipality by the State may be leased for a period not to exceed fifty years, subject to the provisions of the grant, and property of any municipality not acquired for park purposes may be leased for the production of minerals, gas, oil, or other hydrocarbon substances for a period not exceeding thirty-five years. 

Q. What is a sub-lease?

A. A sub-lease is one in which the original lessee continues liable on the Lease, but sublets a part or all of the premises to another at an agreed rental. The sub-lessee is bound by all of the covenants of the Lease on which the original lessee is held. 

Q. Is a sub-lease an assignment of the original Lease? 

A. No. 

-92-

How may a Lease be construed?

A. A Lease must be construed according to the intent of the parties to it, such intent to be gathered from the language of the Lease. Since Leases are dual in their character, in that they present the aspect of the contract, as well as that of conveyance, consequently a Lease has two sets of rights and obligations, those based on the privity of estate, growing out of the relation of landlord and tenant, and those based on the privity of contract, growing out of the expressed stipulations of the Lease Agreement. 

Q. What are the requirements of a lessee where the Lease is for particular purposes?

A. When premises are let for a particular purpose, the lessee must not use it for any other purpose, and if he does, he is liable to the lessor for all damages resulting from such use, or the lessor may treat the Lease as thereby rescinded. 

Q. What are the presumptions of a term of hiring where no limit is fixed?

A. Hiring of real property, other than lodging and dwelling houses, in places where there is no custom or usage on the subject, the hiring is presumed to be for one year from its commencement, unless otherwise expressed in the hiring. 

Q. What are the presumptions of a hiring of lodgings and dwelling houses for an indefinite term?

A. A hiring of lodgings or dwelling houses for an indefinite, or unspecified term are presumed to have been made for such length of time as the parties adopt for the estimation of the rent. Thus, a hiring at a weekly rate of rent is presumed to be for one week; at a monthly rate of rent, is presumed to be for one month. In the absence of any agreement respecting the length of time or the rent, the hiring is presumed to be monthly.

Q. What is the doctrine of an estoppel of a tenant to deny landlord's title!

A. A tenant is not permitted to deny the title of his landlord at the time of the commencement of the relation of landlord and tenant.

Q. What is the effect of the attornment of a tenant to a stranger?

A. An agreement of a tenant to become the tenant to a stranger, as the new owner or landlord, is void, unless it is made with the consent of the landlord, or in consequence of a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction. 

Q. How should a Lease be renewed?

A. Upon renewal of a Lease, a new Lease Agreement should be executed by the parties. 

Q. What is the effect of a lessee holding over after the expiration of the hiring?

A. If a lessee of real property remains in possession thereof, after the expiration of the hiring, and the lessor accepts rent from lessee, the parties are presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one month, when the rent is payable monthly, or in any case for a period longer than one year. -93-

Q. 

What is an extension of a Lease? 

A. An extension of a Lease is the continuation in possession by and under the terms and conditions of the original Lease, after due notice has been given in accordance with its terms and conditions.

Q. What are the duties of a lessor of premises to be used for the occupancy by human beings? 

A. The lessor of a building intended for the occupation of human beings must, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, put it into condition fit for such occupation and repair all subsequent dilapidation thereof, which render it untenantable, except that the lessee must repair all deteriorations or injuries thereto occasioned by his want of ordinary care. 

Q. What are the duties of a lessor as to the tenant's quiet and peaceful possession of the property?

A. The lessor agreed to secure the lessee the quiet and peaceful possession and enjoyment of the premises during the term of the Lease against all persons lawfully claiming the same. 

Q. What, if any, liens can be claimed by the landlord?

A. Excepting in the case of Innkeepers, Hotels, Boarding 

Houses, furnished Apartment Houses and furnished Bungalow 

Courts who have liens upon the baggage and other property of their tenants for rent and other charges, landlords do not have a lien for rent and other charges generally, unless by express agreement between the parties it is specifically agreed to the contrary. 

Q. What degree of care is incumbent upon the lessee? 

A. The lessee of premises must use ordinary care for its preservation in safety and in good condition.

Q. When and how may the lessee make necessary repairs? 

A. If, within a reasonable time after notice to the lessor of dilapidations which he ought to repair, if he neglects to do so, the lessee may repair the same himself, where the cost of such repairs does not require an expenditure greater than one month's rent of the premises, and deduct the expenses of such repairs from the rent, or the lessee may vacate the premises, in which case he shall be discharged from further payments of rent, or performance of other conditions. 

Q. How may a Lease be modified, or its terms changed?

A. Any change of the terms and conditions of a Lease may be made by mutual agreement of the parties. However, in the case of a written Lease such change must also be in writing, properly executed by the parties thereto. 

Q. What are the rights of a tenant at will and a tenant for years?

A. A tenant for years, or at will, unless he is a wrongdoer by holding over, may occupy the buildings, take the annual products of the soil, work mines and quarries open at the commencement of his tenancy; otherwise, he has no other rights to the property than such as are given to him by the agreement or instrument by which his tenancy is acquired. -94-

Q. May a Lease be assigned?

A. Unless there is an agreement to the contrary, Leases are assignable without the consent or approval of the other party, and in the event of an assignment by the lessee without consent of the lessor, and lessor accepting rent from the assignee, as such, although there is an agreement stipulating that any assignment must first be approved by the lessor, the acceptance of the assignee by the lessor would be sufficient consent thereto. 

Q. What are the remedies of lessor against assignee of lessee?

A. Whatever remedies the lessor of any real property has against his immediate lessee for breach of any agreement in the Lease, or for recovery of the possession, he has against the assignee of the lessee, for any cause of action accruing while they are such assignees, except where the assignment is made by way of security for a loan, and is not accompanied by possession of the premises. 

Q. What are the remedies of the lessee against assignees of the lessor?

A. Whatever remedies the lessee of any real property may have against his immediate lessor, for the breach of any agreement in the Lease, he may have against the assigns of the lessor, and the assigns of the lessee may have against the lessor and his assigns, except upon covenants against encumbrances or relating to the title or possession of the premises. 

Q. When and how may notice of change of terms be given? 

A. In all Leases of lands or tenements, or of any interest therein, from week to week, or from month to month, the landlord may, upon giving notice in writing to the tenant, change the terms of the Lease to take effect upon the expiration of a period as long as the term of the hiring itself, but if such change takes effect within a rental term, the rent accruing from the first day of such term to the date of such change shall be computed at the rental rate which obtained immediately prior to such change, provided, however, that it shall be competent for the parties to provide by an agreement in writing that a notice changing the terms thereof may be given at any time, not less than seven days before the expiration of a term, to be effective upon the expiration of such term. The notice, when served upon a tenant, shall of itself operate and be effectual to create and establish, as a part of the Lease, the terms, rents and conditions specified in the notice, if the tenant shall continue to hold the premises after said notice takes effect. 

Q. How may a tenancy or an estate at will be terminated?

A. A tenancy, or other estate at will, however created, may be terminated by the landlord giving a notice in writing to the tenant to remove from the premises within a period of not less than thirty days, to be specified in the notice. (The manner prescribed by 

Section 1162 of the California Code of Civil Procedure, should be followed.) -95-

Q. What is the effect of such notice?

A. After such notice has been served, and the period specified by such notice has expired, but not before, the landlord may reenter, or proceed, according to law, to recover possession. 

Q. When and how is re-entry to be made? 

A. Whenever the right of re-entry is given to a grantor, or lessor in any grant or Lease, or otherwise, such re-entry may be made at any time after the right has accrued, upon three days' notice, as provided in Sections 1161 and 1162 of the California Code of Civil Procedure, provided, however, that the three days' notice shall not be necessary, or required in cases where the hiring of real property is for a term not specified by the parties and where such hiring was terminated by proper notice. 

Q. What procedure is necessary to evict a tenant upon his failure to perform under a Lease?

A. He must be served with a three days' notice in writing to perform, or comply with the terms of his Lease, or quit the premises. Should he fail to conform with the requirements of said notice he would thereby be guilty of unlawful detainer of the premises and summary reaction may be brought against him without further notice. 

Q. Can a landlord let family?

A. No.

Q. How is the forcible detainer defined?

A. Every person is guilty of a forcible detainer who either by force, or by menaces and threats of violence, unlawfully holds and keeps the possession of any real property, whether the same was acquired peaceably or otherwise, or who in the night-time, or during the absence of the occupant of any land, unlawfully enters upon real property, and who, after demand made for the surrender thereof, for the period of five days, refuses to surrender the same to such former occupant. The occupant of real property, within the meaning of this subdivision, is one who, within five days preceding such unlawful entry was in the peaceable and undisturbed possession of such lands. 

Q. How is an unlawful detainer defined?

A. A tenant of real property, for a term less than life, is guilty of unlawful detainer: 

1. When he continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, of the property, or any part thereof, after the expiration of the term for which it is let to him, without the permission of his landlord, or the successor in estate of his landlord, if any there be; including the case where the person to be removed became the occupant of the premises as a servant, employee, agent, or licensee and the relation of master and -96—

servant or employer and employee or principal and agent or licensor and licensee has been lawfully terminated or the time fixed for such occupancy by the agreement between the parties has expired; but nothing in this subdivision contained shall be construed as preventing the removal of such occupant in any other lawful manner; but in case of a tenancy at will, it must first be terminated by notice, as prescribed in the 

Civil Code. 

2. When he continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of his landlord, or the successor in estate of his landlord, if any there be, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the Lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount which is due, or possession of the property, shall have been served upon him and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon such subtenant. 

Such notice may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due. In all cases of tenancy upon agricultural lands, where the tenant has held over and retained possession for more than sixty days after the expiration of the term without any demand of possession or notice to quit by the landlord, or the successor in estate of his landlord, if any there be, he shall be deemed to be holding by permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of his landlord, if any there be, and shall be entitled to hold under the terms of the Lease for another full year, and shall not be guilty of an unlawful detainer during said year, and such holding over for the period aforesaid shall be taken and construed as a consent on the part of a tenant to hold for another year. 

3. When he continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, after a neglect or failure to perform other conditions or covenants of the Lease or agreement under which the property is held, including any covenant not to assign or sublet, than the one for the payment of rent, and three days' notice, in writing, requiring the performance of such conditions or covenants, or the possession of the property shall have been served upon him, and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also, upon such subtenant. Within three days. after the service of the notice, the tenant, or any subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, or any mortgagee of the term, or other person interested in its continuance, may perform the conditions or covenants of the Lease or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the Lease from forfeiture; provided if the conditions and covenants of the Lease, violated by the lessee, cannot afterward be performed, then no notice, as last prescribed herein, need be given to said lessee or his subtenant, demanding the performance of the violated conditions or covenants of the Lease. -97-

A tenant may take proceedings, similar to those prescribed in this chapter, to obtain possession of the premises let to a subtenant or held by servant, employee, agent, or licensee, in case of his unlawful detention of the premises underlet to him or held by him. 

4. Any tenant or subtenant assigning or subletting or committing waste upon the demised premises, contrary to the conditions or covenants of his Lease, thereby terminates the Lease, and the landlord, or his successor in estate, shall upon service of three days' notice to quit upon the person or persons in possession, be entitled to restitution of possession of such demised premises under the provision of this chapter. 

Q. When must a person holding over vacate the property?

A. In either of the following cases, a person who holds over and continues in possession of real property, after a three-day written notice to quit the same, shall have been served upon him, or if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon such subtenant, as prescribed in Section 1162 of the Code of Civil Procedure, may be removed therefrom as prescribed in this chapter. 

1. Where the property has been duly sold by virtue of an execution against him, or a person under whom he claims, and the title under the sale has been duly perfected. 

2. Where the property has been duly sold, upon the foreclosure, by proceedings taken as prescribed in this code, of a mortgage, or under an express power of sale contained therein, executed by him, or a person under whom he claims, and the title under the foreclosure has been duly perfected. 

4. Where the property has been duly sold by him, or a person under whom he claims, and the title under the sale has been duly perfected. 

Q. How may service of notice be made?

A. The notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a may be served, either: 

1. By delivering a copy to the tenant personally; or, 2. If he be absent from his place of residence, and from his usual place of business, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at either place, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at his place of residence; or, 3. If such place of residence and business cannot be ascertained, or a person of suitable age or discretion there cannot be found, thereby affixing a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, and also delivering a copy to a person there residing, if such person can be found; and also sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the place where the

property is situated. Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner.

A. It would have the effect of terminating the Lease. 

Q. Could rents be demanded by notice to tenant without making demand of payment thereof, or the possession of said premises? 

A. Yes. A notice demanding the payment of rent and indicating that it is not the intention of the lessor or landlord to terminate the Lease.

Q. What remedy, if any, does the landlord have, as against the tenant, after service of any of the foregoing notices in proper form?

A. His remedy to enforce the mandates of such notices are for possession of the premises and may be enforced by summary reaction in the court.

Q. In what court should an action of forcible entry, or unlawful detainer be commenced?

A. In the Superior Court where the rental value is more than $200.00 per month and the whole amount of damage claimed is in excess of $2000.00. In the Municipal Court where the rental value is $200.00, or less, per month and where the whole amount of damage claimed is $2000.00, or less. In Class A Justice Court when the rental value is $100.00, or less, per month, and where the whole amount of damage claimed is $1000.00, or less, and in Class B Justice Court where the rental value is $75.00, or less, per month and the whole amount of damage claimed is $300.00, or less. -101-

OPTIONS  

Q. What is an option?

A. A contract whereby one is given the right for a certain time, at his election, to demand and receive, or to deliver property at a stated price. law? 

Q. Is a consideration necessary to render an option binding! Yes.

A. 

Q. What are the essentials of an option under the California

A. (a) A consideration. (b) Essential provisions of a sale deposit receipt or other contract of sale. (c) Legal description of the property, or street number will do. (d) Price and terms stated same as in a contract. (e) Optioner to furnish guarantee of title. (f) Specify time for examination of title, also when notice shall be given by optionee in case he elects to exercise his option. 

Q. Notice should be given how?

A. By a written instrument delivered personally, or by registered mail. 

Q. What is one of the most important features of an option?

A. Time. It is necessary that the time in which it may be exercised be specifically stated. The failure to exercise option agreement within the time stated absolutely terminates the rights of the optionee. 

Q. Must an option be exercised within the time limit?

A. There must be a new consideration for any extension of time, regardless of the time the extension is granted. Any extension of time is in fact a new option. 

Q. Is it necessary to record an option?

A. Only in extreme cases. The failure to record same will not affect it.

An option is such an interest in land that it may when properly acknowledged be recorded. The option contract can be made to bind the owner and all persons who acquire an interest by, through or under him. 

Q. When is the right of option waived?

A. When either party to a contract of sale has an option as to time, place, or manner of delivery, he must give the other party reasonable notice of his choice; and if he does not give such notice within a reasonable time, his right of option is waived. (C. C. 1756.) 

Q. Are option contracts assignable? 

A. Yes, unless the right is expressly given to one person only and the agreement states that it is non-assignable, or where the consideration is a note.

The holder of an option has a valuable right but prior to his election to purchase has no legal or equitable interest in the land. -103-

Q. What is the liability of the optionee? 

A. Option contracts usually provide that if the prospective purchaser, known as the "optionee" does not elect to exercise his option, that the money paid by him for the option is forfeited, and that the forfeiture constitutes the limit of his liability. 

Q. Has the optionee any claim against the owner for the money paid!

A. No, except as the owner may be unable to deliver good title, and he may elect to rescind the contract. 

Q. Will equity require the specific performance of an option contract of purchase the same as an ordinary sales or installment contract? 

A. Yes.

Q. The owner of real property, in the presence of witnesses, orally authorizes real estate broker to sell his property. Upon consummation of deal, seller refuses to pay broker's commission. Can broker collect his commission?

A. An agreement authorizing or employing an agent or broker to purchase or sell real estate for a compensation or a commission must be in writing. The statutes provide that any action for collection of commission for sale of real property cannot be sustained unless authorization is given in writing.

POWER OF ATTORNEY  

Q. Does power of attorney authorizing agent to mortgage a certain property also imply right to borrow on it by trust deed? 

Explain your answer.

A. No. Attorney in fact acting under power of attorney cannot execute deed of trust in behalf of his principal when a mortgage only is authorized because terms and conditions of T. D. less favorable for a borrower than are terms of mortgage. 

Q. Can a real estate broker legally execute a deed for client? 

If so, under what conditions?

A. Not unless specifically authorized by a power of attorney. 

The common form of authority to sell certain property merely authorizes broker to find a buyer for it.
