EVICTION OF TENANT Occupancy by Purchaser (Section 6(b)(2) of the Rent Regulation for Housing) Section 6(b) (2) of the Rent Regulation for Housing sets forth a certain procedure which must be followed and certain requirements which must be complied with in a case where either a vendor or a purchaser seeks to evict a tenant of the vendor for occupancy by a purchaser who acquired his rights in the housing accommodations on or after November 1, 1942.

A. 

The procedure which must be followed and the requirements which must be complied with in a case of this type are: 

1. After the contract of sale and the down payment have been made, either the vendor or the purchaser may file, with this -137-

office and on forms provided by this office, a petition for a certificate relating to eviction. 

2. If the petition shows that the payment of principal made by the purchaser, excluding any payment made from funds borrowed for the purpose of making such principal payment, amounts to 20 per cent or more of the purchase price, and that the purchaser intends in good faith to use the accommodations as his own home, a certificate may be issued by this office. 

3. The certificate may authorize either the vendor or the purchaser, at the expiration of three months after the date of issuance of the certificate, to pursue his remedies for removal or eviction of the tenant, for occupancy by the purchaser, in accordance with the requirements of the State Law. 

B. The 20 per cent payment requirement, or the three months' waiting period requirement, or both such requirements, may be waived where it appears that: 

1. The vendor has or had a substantial necessity requiring the sale, and a reasonable sale or disposition of the housing accommodations could not have been made without removal or eviction of the tenant; or 

2. Equivalent accommodations are available for rent, into which accommodations the tenant can move without substantial hardship or loss; or 

3. Other special hardship would result. (Note: The fact that the purchaser is without adequate housing, or the fact that the purchaser is subject to eviction from his present housing, ordinarily does not constitute such a "special hardship" as to permit a waiver of the 20 per cent payment requirement or of the three months' waiting period requirement.)

The following points should be noted in connection with Section 6(b)(2) of the Regulation:

The meaning of the term "purchase price" may be illustrated by an example. Let us suppose that the purchaser of a house pays $500.00 in cash and assumes a $5,000.00 mortgage indebtedness. 

The purchase price includes the amount of the mortgage debt assumed by the purchaser and is, therefore, $5,500.00. The purchaser has not paid 20 per cent of the purchase price. A certificate relating to eviction may not be issued.

The term "borrowed funds" may be illustrated by an example. 

Let us suppose that the purchaser of a house pays $1,000.00 in cash and agrees to pay $4,000.00, the balance of the purchase price, in monthly installments. The purchaser, in order to make the $1,- 

000.00 cash payment, borrows the $1,000.00, giving as security a mortgage on another house which the purchaser owns or on the house which he is purchasing. The purchaser has made the required 20 per cent payment, but has made such payment from borrowed funds. A certificate relating to eviction may not be issued. 

A single "down" payment of 20 per cent is not required. If the down payment does not amount to 20 per cent of the purchase price, a certificate may be issued when, by reason of subsequent -138-

payments, the purchaser has brought his principal payments up to 

20 per cent of the purchase price.

The vendor and the purchaser must act in good faith; that is, the vendor or the purchaser must not evict or attempt to evict the tenant under Section 6(b) (2), except for the purpose of providing the purchaser with a home. Section 6(b) (2) may not be used as a pretext for removing the tenant or for otherwise evading the 

Rent Regulation. 

The Notice to Vacate 

The following points should be noted in connection with the notice to vacate given to the tenant in a case involving Section 

6(b)(2) of the Regulation: 

1. Neither the vendor nor the purchaser may give the tenant a notice to vacate until the certificate relating to eviction is received by the vendor or the purchaser. 

2. A copy of the notice to vacate need not be sent to the Area 

Rent Office. 

3. The Rent Regulation contains no requirement as to the length of time or as to the form of the notice to vacate. Care should be exercised to comply with requirements of the State Law. 

4. If the certificate relating to eviction authorizes the vendor or the purchaser to pursue his remedies under the State Law at the expiration of three months from the date of the certificate, the notice to vacate may not require the tenant to surrender possession before the expiration of such three-month period. However, the notice to vacate may be served upon the tenant during such threemonth period, and must be served sufficiently in advance of the expiration of such three-month period so that the tenant will be on notice for the length of time required by the State Law. 

Court Action 

If the vendor or the purchaser commences a court action to evict the tenant, the vendor or the purchaser must, at the time of commencing such action, give a written notice thereof to the Area Rent Office. This notice must state the title of the case, the number of the case, if that is possible, the court in which the case is filed, the name and address of the tenant, and the ground upon which the vendor or the purchaser seeks to evict the tenant. The vendor or the purchaser may comply with this requirement by sending to the Office of Price Administration a copy of the complaint filed in the action to evict the tenant. Caution

If legal assistance is necessary in connection with matters of State Law, such as the length of time or the manner of service of the notice to vacate, or the proper court in which to file an action, it is suggested that a private attorney be consulted, since this office is not in a position to render such assistance. In this connection it should be noted that many eviction cases have been dismissed by the local courts because of defective, "home-made," notices. -139-

The certificate relating to eviction does not constitute a notice to the tenant to vacate. In order to acquire the legal right to evict a tenant, the vendor or the purchaser must give the tenant notice to vacate as required by the State Law. If the tenant does not surrender possession pursuant to the notice to vacate, the vendor or the purchaser may enforce his rights by filing a proper action in the proper local court.

The final decision as to the right of the vendor or the purchaser to evict the tenant rests with the local courts, which must decide questions of law and of fact, including any defense which the tenant may raise with respect to the sufficiency of the notice to vacate.

The Office of Price Administration does not represent either landlord or tenant. "Setting Maximum Rents by Dates"

The basis of establishing the base rental is the highest rental at which living quarters were rented during the period January 31st to and including March 1, 1942. In the event that there was not a natural rental or offer of rental of the living quarters during the period January 31st, to and including March 1, 1942, then the first rental at which the living quarters were rented after March 1, 1942, shall be the base rental applying to such living quarters so rented after March 1, 1942.

Pursuant to the foregoing, such base rents as were established under either of the above two circumstances become the base rent to which the Landlord must adhere on and after November 1, 1942. 

June 1942 Quota

It has been held by certain local units of the Office of Price Administration, that the number of units rented on a weekly and/or monthly basis must be held available through the period commencing November 1, 1942, providing that there exists or existed a de mand for the same unit and/or units as existed on the same basis during June 1942. The same certain units of the Office of Price 

Administration have also held that where occupancy has extended over a period of sixty days or more that the tenant shall be given the benefit of a monthly basis of rental irrespective of the basis of rental which has originally applied, such as a daily or weekly basis. 

CHANGES MADE BY STABILIZATION EXTENSION ACT OF 1944 WHICH AMENDS THE EMERGENCY PRICE CONTROL ACT OF 1942. 

The following new provisions have been created in the above indicated Act, which became Law as of July 1, 1944: 

1. Provision for the individual adjustment of hardship rent basis particularly where property taxes and other costs have increased in defense rental areas. The provisions of this change are interpreted to impose upon the Administrator the giving of consideration to rents and applicable costs as of or -140-

about April 1, 1941, as compared to rentals and applicable costs during the period in which an adjustment is sought. 

2. Provision is made, particularly with respect to Defense rental areas, that where the availability of adequate rental housing accommodations and other relevant factors are such as to make rent control unnecessary for the purpose of eliminating speculative, unwarranted and abnormal increases in rents and of preventing profiteering and speculative and other disruptive practices resulting from abnormal market conditions caused by congestion, the controls imposed upon rents by authority of this Act, in such defense rental areas, shall forthwith be abolished. (Heretofore such provision has been provided to be applicable only in non-defense areas.) 

3. Provision is made for the creation of a Board of Review consisting of one or more officers or employees of the Office of Price Administration for the purpose of hearing and reviewing rent adjustment protests and/or petitions. 

4. Provision is made to prohibit changes in established rental practices except where such action is found to be necessary in order to prevent circumvention or evasion of any regulation, order, price schedule or requirement under the "Stabil ization Extension Act of 1944." 

5. Provision is made that such regulation or order shall not require the determination of costs or rentals otherwise than in accordance with established accounting methods. 

6. Provision is made strengthening and broadening the facilities of Industry Advisory Committees, toward the end that Administrative officials of the Office of Price Administration shall give proper consideration to the recommendations of such Industry Advisory Committees. 

7. Provision is made that persons subpoenaed in investigations conducted by the Rent Control Division of the Office of Price Administration may have council and may be furnished with a record of their testimony. 

8. Provision is made with respect to the treble-damage provision, as applicable to overcharges, that provides that such overcharges shall be not less than $25.00, nor more than $50.00, as the court in its discretion may determine; with the further provision that such amount shall be the amount of the overcharge or overcharges, or $25.00, whichever is greater, if the defendant proves that the violation of the Regulation, Order or Price Schedule in question was neither wilful nor the result of failure to take practicable precautions against the occurrence of the violation. 

9. Provision is made whereby, instead of the filing of protests against rent orders the regulations being limited to the heretofore sixty day period, such protests may now be filed at any time after the issuance of the involved order or determination of the Office of Price Administration. -141-

Section IV Property and Ownership 

Property may be defined in two classes: 

Real-The earth and all things attached thereto or contained therein.

Personal-All things that are not real property. Some things may be "real property" at one time and "personal" at another.

Example: a building attached to the ground is real property, but when detached for moving it is personal. 

ALIENS 

Q. Who is eligible to own real property in California? ..

A. All persons who are not ineligible aliens may acquire and own property in California as freely as United States citizens. 

Q. Who are ineligible aliens?

A. Ineligible aliens are Japanese, Hindus, and, generally speaking, all Asiatics except Chinese. (Chinese were granted right of citizenship in 1943) .. 

Q. Explain the difference between real and personal property. 

A. Real property is broadly defined as the land and all things attached permanently to it and included within it in its natural state. All other types of property are classed as personal property. 

For instance, a house, fence, tree or garage is real property. Furniture, clothing, jewelry and automobiles are personal property. A lease or mortgage on real property would be termed personal property. Of course, there are many border line items which are classified with greater difficulty.

Q. Can an article which is personal property become real property? 

A. Yes. A lock, door or fixture, although personal property before installation in a house becomes real property when permanently affixed.

Q. Are shrubs and vines growing in a yard classified as real or personal property?

A. Shrubs and vines, as well as trees, are classified as real property. Potted plants are considered personal property. Another exception often made is growing grain and other crops which are planted and gathered annually. Even these should be covered by specific agreement.

Q. Is a movable steel gasoline service station building which is bolted to a cement foundation real or personal property? Could it be either? -142-

A. This is one of the border line cases we mentioned. It would ordinarily be classed as real property, but usually is designated personal property in the lease contract. 

Q. How would you classify a field of growing corn? As real or personal property?

A. Personal. Growing corn is an annual crop. Should be covered by Specific Agreement. 

Q. In selling the home furnished is mere mention in the grant deed of furnishings a good and sufficient conveyance of them? Explain.

A. Furniture, furnishings and fittings of home are personal property and should be conveyed by bill of sale. Bill of sale should be delivered through escrow with grant deed.

Q. May a tenant who rents a store building for the purpose of establishing a grocery business remove his fixtures at a later date if such removal does not injure the building, even though he has firmly affixed them to the building? 

A. Yes. But if they are in any way anchored to the building, arrangements for their removal should be definitely made in the lease. Failure at this point has caused and will cause expensive litigation. Generally speaking, they are considered personal property but the above precautions should always be taken. 

Q. Indicate what is personal and what real property: (a) 

Window shades. (b) Electric chandeliers. (c) Linoleum glued to floor. (d) Gas grate setting in fireplace. (e) Awnings fastened in place with screws. (f) Potted plants. (g) Radiators as part of heating system.

A. (a) Fastened with screws-personal. (b) Real. (c) Real. (d) Personal. (e) Real. (f) Personal. (g) Real.

Q. Designate which is real and which is personal property: (a) ripe crop on trees; (b) window shades; (c) flowers and rare plants which seller wanted; (d) linoleum cut to fit kitchen floor; (e) potted plants; (f) garden hose.

A. (a) Difference of opinion, if probable harvest is expected within escrow period, better be safe with agreement; (b) personal; (c) if growing on the land, real, unless reserved by agreement; (d) personal, unless secured to floor; (e) and (f) personal. 

Q. Recite four ways in which real property may be owned.

A. 1. In severalty (individually.) 2. As tenants in common (undivided interests owned without right of survivorship.) 3. Joint tenancy (undivided interests owned with right of survivorship.) 

4. As community property. 

Q. Does the ownership of real estate in California give the owner all right and benefits in the property without any restrictions? 

A. Ownership in fee contemplates the greatest present and future benefits possible under our form of government. Use of the land, however, is always subject to city, county, State and Federal laws. Zoning and use restrictions imposed under police power are in effect and restrict use. Deed restrictions may also be present. In short, all ownership is subject to use restrictions of some kind. -143-

REAL PROPERTY 

Real property may be owned IN SEVERALTY, i. e., Property which is held by tenant (owner) in his own right only, without any other being joined or connected with him in point of interest during his tenancy. Individually. As sole and separate property. 

Q. Why is it good practice to require the wife to sign a mortgage given by the husband on his separate property?

A. Separate property of the husband is presumptively community property, in other words the burden of proof is on the husband to show that his separate property is actually separate property. It is therefore better in order to avoid any subsequent controversies, to have the wife sign a mortgage or trust deed given by the husband on his separate property. This practice, however, is not absolutely essential to the validity of the instrument. 

Q. How should a deed indicate that the property is the separate property of the grantor? 

A. Grantor's name is sometimes followed by the words "as his (or her) separate property." These words or words of similar import cannot always be relied upon as vesting title in the grantee as his or her separate property.

Q. In what circumstances may real estate be the separate property of wife or husband?

A. All property owned by either before marriage and that acquired by either after marriage by gift, bequest, devise or descent, and that conveyed by either husband or wife to the other, is his or her separate property.

IN JOINT TENANCY, i. e., Property held by two or more persons as joint tenants with joint interests and providing that at death such property becomes the absolute property of the survivor, without probate. Property held in Joint Tenancy does not become a part of the estate of the deceased. The distinguishing feature of Joint Tenancy is its right of survivorship. (Questions and Answers) 

Q. What right do husband and wife possess in property owned in joint tenancy which they did not have as tenants in common? 

A. Right of survivorship.

Q. What is the distinguishing difference between an ordinary ૨. tenancy in common and a joint tenancy? 

A. Right of survivorship in case of joint tenancy.

TENANCY IN COMMON, i. e., Property held in "partnership" according to the proportionate ownership of the tenants (ownership need not be equal). At death of owner his share becomes a part of his estate and reverts to his heirs. -144

Q. Do tenants in common own undivided interests? Must their interests be equal?

A. They own undivided interests but they need not be equal. 

Q. Would you classify interests of partners in a partnership as tenancy in common?

A. A partnership interest is in effect an interest as a tenant in common.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY, i. e., Property held by husband and wife which is not separate property. (Questions and Answers)

Q. Must community property be held by man and wife as joint tenants?

A. Not necessarily. Title is often held in name of one spouse. 

Must be so stated in deed if held as joint tenants. Otherwise, no right of survivorship. 

Q. May a husband, without the signature of his wife, make an assignment of a note and mortgage constituting community property?

A. Yes, the husband may make an assignment for an adequate consideration without the wife's signature. (Personal Property only.) 

Q. Are the earnings of a minor the community property of the husband and wife?

A. Generally speaking they are, presuming that the husband and wife are living together and that the minor child is under their jurisdiction. 

Q. Is money received as damages for personal injuries to husband or wife community property? 

A. Yes. 

Q. Are the earnings of a wife liable for the debts of her husband?

A. No. (C. C. 168.) 

Q. Does a wife's earnings in California constitute her separate income which may be reported in her separate income tax returns?

A. Yes, where there was an oral agreement between husband and wife that their earnings should be their separate property and such earnings were deposited in separate bank accounts. (I. T. 2352.)

Q. How are the earnings of a minor classified under the laws of California?

A. Unless there is other evidence than an agreement not to appropriate a minor's earnings, that the parents have relinquished -145-

their parental authority, such earnings are community income, to be reported by the husband and wife in their joint returns, or, if separate returns are filed, then in the separate return of the husband. (I. T. 2352.) 

Q. Where property is purchased partly with the wife's separate funds and the balance community funds and deed taken in name of husband and wife, what is the status? 

A. One-half is the separate property of the wife and one-half community property. (C. C. 161; 62 Cal. Dec. 57.)

Q. Suppose a man in Kansas sold his property, and he and his wife moved to California, and he invested the proceeds of said sale in land, would the latter be community property? 

A. No. Held that the property was not community property in Kansas and would not become community property in California. (136 Cal. 113.) 

Q. What is the separate property of the husband or wife?

A. It is all of the property of either owned before marriage and that acquired afterward by gift, devise, bequest or descent, or with the profits, rents or issues thereof. (C. C. 162-163.)

Q. Whenever any property is conveyed to a married woman by an instrument in writing is the title presumed to vest in her as her separate property? 

A. Yes. (154 Cal. 672.)

Q. If a married woman acquired title to property before May 

19, 1889, can her husband or his heirs maintain an action to show that the property was community property? 

A. No. (C. C. 164; 154 Cal. 672.)

Q. What effect has a conveyance from one spouse to the other?

A. To vest the property in the spouse receiving it as separate property, subject to rules regulating confidential relationships. (C. C. 158-159.)

Q. Do marriage settlements have to be in writing, executed, acknowledged and recorded the same as a grant of land! 

A. Yes. (C. C. 178-179-180.)

Q. Can a wife separated from her husband have her community rights established without seeking a divorce? 

A. Yes, -146-

Deeds  

Q. How would you briefly define a deed?

A. An instrument of conveyance which is evidence of transfer of title to real property.

Q. Why is it unnecessary to describe the improvements on lot being conveyed by deed?

A. Improvements unless otherwise reserved by seller are part of real property and need not be mentioned or described in deed. 

That which is secured to the land is a part of the land. 

Q. Are deeds to real property valid when duly executed except as to delivery, but to be delivered upon the death of the grantor? 

Explain your answer.

A. No. A deed has no value unless and until delivered. It may be delivered to a third person, to be delivered to the grantee after the death of the grantor, only if it passes irrevocably out of the possession and is beyond the control of the grantor. A deed cannot be delivered conditionally.

Q. When the grantees named in a deed are joint tenants with right of survivorship, may either convey his own interest to some person not named in the deed? Explain.

A. Yes, but conveyance by one would dissolve joint tenancy. 

Husband holding in joint tenancy with his wife could not convey his community interest to other than his wife without her joining in deed. 

Q. (a) Which of the parties to a deed is the grantor? (b) Which is the grantee!

A. (a) Grantor is party conveying the property. (b) Grantee is the party to whom it is conveyed. 

Q. Name two different kinds of deeds used to convey real property or interest therein, and what interest does each convey? 

A. Grant deed and quit-claim deed. Grant deed passes title in fee simple, unless otherwise qualified and warrants that prior to its delivery, grantor has not conveyed the property to any other person and that property is free from encumbrance, done, made or suffered by the grantor or any person claiming under him during his ownership of it.

A quit-claim deed carries no warranty. It conveys only such title as the grantor may have had at time of its delivery. It is used to remove a cloud from the title or when any person desires to convey and relinquish any claim he may have in the property. 

Q. Is a deed to "Smith and Jones, A Copartnership" a legal conveyance? Explain.

A. No. Names of grantee are uncertain. Deeds should run to "John Smith and Bert Jones, Copartners, doing business under firm name and style of Beach Realty Co." -147-

Q. (a) Where and how may a deed be recorded? (b) What is the purpose of recording a deed?

A. (a) A deed may be recorded by the County Recorder of the 

County wherein the property is situated upon payment of the fee for recordation. (b) A deed is recorded to give constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and encumbrancers of the property.

TORRENS TITLE (Land Registration Act) 

Sir Robert Torrens was an Australian Collector of Customs, and later become General Registrar. The Torrens System was first introduced into California March 17, 1897, and amended Nov. 3, 1914 by direct vote of the people.

It is an act for the certification of land titles and the simplification of the transfer of real estate. As expressed by Judge Shaw of the Supreme Court of Calif. "It purports to establish a system for the registration of titles to land, where the official certificate will always show the state of the title and the person in whom it is vested, and to provide that the original registration and transfer of the land may be made in the manner prescribed in detail in the act." 

To register title to property. 

1. File application in form of verified petition with County 

Clerk in county where property is located. Application is made to the superior court of the county, and at the final order of the court, has the effect of a judgment, which operates directly on the land and vests title thereto. Recorders and ex-officio recorders become 

Registrars and deputy Registrars. The Examiner of Titles or searchers are attorneys admitted to practice before Supreme Court of the State of California for at least five years and must be experienced in the proceedings of this act. They are paid by the county, subject to the approval of the Board of Supervisors. 

2. The official examination of title to determine ownership and liens and claims against it. 

3. Notice of application for registration to all interested parties. (This takes form of action at Law.) 

4. Judicial determination of the title sought to be registered. 

5. Registration of title and issuance of certificate. 

6. An assurance fund out of which losses may be paid. (Through error.) (This fund is exhausted at present.) 

7. Permanency of registration. (no withdrawal.) 

8. Simple and cheap.

This act cannot be amended in any particular, as it is an initiative measure, except by direct vote of the people. 

Remarks 

Deed of grantor does not pass title. Title passes when registrar issues new certificate.

The initial Registrar's Certificate and all certificates thereafter issued are made in duplicate, the original of which is retained in the office of the Registrar of Titles as a permanent record, and the duplicate is delivered to the owner as evidence of his ownership of the property. 

Although perfectly legal and safe, registration of land under the land registration act is not recommended, because of the delay in closing a transaction which often occurs as a result of various -150-

requirements of the act; also because of the fact that a great many purchasers of land and lenders of money will not rely upon a Torrens certificate as evidence of title, choosing to require a policy of title insurance from a reputable title insurance company which in their opinion gives them a more satisfactory protection. 

TRANSFER OF TITLES  

Q. Lady took title as Mary Jones, afterwards married John 

Smith and undertook to sell her property. How should she sign the deed! 

A. Must set forth married name and name under which she acquired title, thus, "Mary Jones Smith, a married woman, who acquired title as Mary Jones, a single woman.' 

Q. (a) How are land purchase contracts most frequently used? (b) When is mortgage usually taken back as security for balance payable! (c) When is trust deed usually given by purchaser to secure a balance?

A. (a) In case of sale of subdivision lots or when property generally is sold under small down payment, followed by monthly installment payments. (b) When it will be a first mortgage against the property and its amount does not exceed about 50% of property value. (c) When down payment and first mortgage (or trust deed) does not equal the consideration or purchase price, a trust deed (second lien) is usually executed for the balance. 

Q. "A" sold five acres to "B"; latter never recorded deed.

Later, traded this 5 acres in on city property owned by "A". Transfer of acreage was made by "B", returning unrecorded deed to "A".

Was this a sufficient conveyance? Explain. 

A. Deed did not reconvey title. Redelivering a deed, or cancelling or destroying it does not operate to retransfer the title. To effect actual delivery, property must be conveyed by a new deed. 

Q. When real property is part of an estate in probate, when would you advise your client desiring to purchase to enter into possession thereof?

A. Only upon receiving deed executed by executor or administrator upon approval of court.

Q. (a) When can a piece of real property be legally sold on a description of lot, block and tract number? (b) Under what conditions would it be necessary to describe such property by metes and bounds?

A. (a) When map covering property has been duly filed in 

County Recorder's office, (b) When map not recorded or when portion of property referred to by lot number or recorded map is involved. 

Q. When a grantor is unable to write his own name, how may he legally execute a deed to real property? -151-

A. By making his mark in the presence of two witnesses, both of whom shall sign or subscribe their names as witnesses, and one of whom at the grantor's request shall sign the grantor's name and indicate that it is his mark. All must be done in the presence of each other and must be in writing (not typed or printed). 

Q. Does conveyance by deed to "Sunset Realty Company" (not incorporated) give legal title? Explain. 

A. Since firm is not a corporation, the name "Sunset Realty

Company" is not sufficient for identification. Full names of all members of firm should be used.

Q. (a) In the case of husband and wife, living together, who can sign a deed legally conveying the separate property of either? (b) Who must sign as to their community property?

A. (a) Husband or wife must sign deed conveying his or her separate property. No legal objection if both sign. (b) Both husband and wife must sign deed conveying community property (real property) acquired since July 26, 1917.

Q. In transfer of a home what three instruments are to be turned over to the cash purchaser?

A. Law requires seller to deliver deed only unless otherwise agreed. In addition to deed, seller often furnishes guarantee or policy of title insurance and assigns fire insurance to buyer. 

SINGLE VERSUS UNMARRIED  

Q. What is the legal difference between a single man (or woman) and an unmarried man (or woman)?

A. A single man (or woman) is one who has never been married, an unmarried man (or woman) is one who has been married but who has since been divorced. 

ALIENATION 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. Does title to real estate always pass by voluntary act of the owner?

A. Decidedly not. Loss by foreclosure of a lien, sale for nonpayment of taxes and loss through condemnation proceedings pass title involuntarily. 

BILL OF SALE 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. What is the instrument called with which personal property, such as furnishings, merchandise, etc., is conveyed? 

A. Bill of sale. 

Q. For what purpose is a bill of sale used?

A. To evidence the conveyance of title to personal property. -152-

CHATTELS 

Q. Define a chattel.

A. An interest in, or possession, of any personal property is known as a chattel. A chattel mortgage is an instrument which makes this interest in personal property the security for the performance of an obligation. -153-

Financing and Loans 

Owing to the decreased demand for capital in industrial lines during the past few years, it has been forced to seek avenues for investment through real estate loans. This, together with the safety afforded the lending institutions by the Federal Housing Administration, and the capital made available through the Government sponsored Federal Savings and Loan Associations, has resulted in a very easy market for real estate financing—particularly on residential property-on more favorable terms to the borrower than has ever been available before. 

Experience has taught the great advantage-both to the borrower and lender of the long-term amortized loan over the former straight three-year term, with its innumerable renewals at heavy expense, and all real estate financing today is on the long-term basis with small monthly amortization.

Real estate loans can be obtained from the Banks, the Federal 

Savings and Loan Associations, Life Insurance Companies, and from private investors. The majority of the loans from the last three sources are obtained through loan brokers, and a commission of 2% to 3% is charged to the borrower.

The greater volume of financing is through the Banks, partially because they charge no commission or brokerage, and with the insurance of their loans by the Federal Housing Administration, they are able to offer very favorable terms-long maturities, low interest rates and small monthly payments. Without the Federal Housing 

Insurance they are permitted to loan up to Sixty Per Cent of the appraised value, amortized over a period of not to exceed ten years. 

With the Federal Housing Administration insurance they can loan on whatever terms the Federal Housing Administration will insure -up to twenty-five years and up to Ninety Per Cent of the appraised value, on certain classes of property, as hereafter explained. 

Such a large portion of residential real estate financing is now being made under the Federal Housing Administration plan that it might be well to briefly review the scope, terms, and costs of loans under this plan.

The Federal Housing Administration is an agency of the United States Government, established in June, 1934, under a Federal act known as the "National Housing Act," for the purpose of, 1st. Stimulating home ownership by making available to the home owner or prospective home-buyer a long-term credit-up to as high as Ninety Per Cent of the property value in some cases-at a minimum cost, payable in easy monthly installments, within the borrower's ability to pay. 

2nd. Stimulating the building trades industry and its allied industries through the increased construction of homes. 

3rd. Improving the quality of home construction and eliminating the dishonest contractor who cheapens or cheats on his work. 

The Federal Housing Administration does not make loans, but underwrites or insures loans made by Banks, Building and Loan -155-

Associations, and other lending agencies, approved by them, which enables these institutions to extend more liberal credit on more favorable terms than has ever before been available. Its activities cover practically the entire field of financing of residential property. Numerous amendments have been made from time to time, some of which have extended its scope and some limiting, as changing conditions have made expedient. The following is a brief resume of the Act as it stands today. 

It is divided into various Sections, covering the different types of financing, as follows:- 

1st. Title I -Property Improvement Loans. 

2nd. Title II-Loans to the individual home owner for the construction, purchase or refinancing of a single family or multiple family dwelling up to four units. 

3rd. Title VI-Construction loans to individuals and contract ors.

A brief outline of the different classifications is as follows: 

PROPERTY IMPROVEMENT LOANS 

These are divided into the three following classifications:

Class I 

-Loans for repairs, modernization, alterations or additions to existing buildings, etc. These loans cannot exceed $2500.00 on any one property-are limited to a maximum of three years thirty-two days, and bear a maximum 5% interest discount rate.

Class II 

-Loans up to $3000.00 for not to exceed three years and thirty-two days, for the construction of buildings exclusive of those used for residental purposes -such as barns, garages, gasoline stations, etc.

These loans bear a maximum 5% discount rate. 

Class III-Loans up to $2500.00 for not to exceed seven years for the construction of residences which comply with certain minimum requirements-in locations not permitted under other sections of the act, such as country districts, mountain or beach cabins, etc. 

The maximum discount rate is 32%. At the present time this section is practically non-operative due to war housing.

TITLE II LOANS 

Under this section are classified loans to the individual home owner for the construction, refinance or purchase of single family or multiple family dwellings up to four units. These must be located in a strictly residential district approved by the Federal Housing Administration. These loans are amortized by monthly payments over a long term of years-up to twenty years for the newer houses and graduated to shorter periods according to the age -156-

of the house. The applicant must meet certain requirements as to income to establish his ability to meet the monthly payments. The monthly installments include the principal amortization, interest, taxes and fire insurance, and in most cases are less than the rental value of the property. The maximum interest rate is 5%, and in addition a 1% charge is made by the Federal Housing Administration as a premium for the mortgage insurance, which is included in the monthly payments.

Loans under Title II are divided into three classifications, as follows: 

1st.-Loans up to $5400.00 on new, owner-occupied single family residences-up to 90% of the appraised value. 

For example, the maximum loan on a property having an appraised value of $5000.00 would be $4500.00 and the monthly payments would be @ 5% and F.H.A. Insurance....$36.47

TITLE VI LOANS 

All loans for construction purposes are now being made under this Section. This section was added to the Act especially to provide homes for defense workers. An individual defense worker can obtain a loan under the favorable terms of this section for the construction of his home; or a contractor can obtain loans for the construction of a number of houses to be rented and sold to defense workers. The terms of these loans are very favorable-up to 90% of the value of the property; for a 25 year term, with an interest rate of 4% plus 2 of 1% for mortgage insurance.

The maximum amount of these loans is limited to $5400.00 for a single family residence. 

7500.00 for a two family residence. 

9500.00 for a three-family residence. 

12000.00 for a four family residence.

A builder can finance the construction of a number of houses -after obtaining a priority from the War Production Board. He can sell one-third of these houses to defense workers only; but must rent the remaining two-thirds to defense workers only for a period of at least sixty days. After a sixty-day rental period he is permitted to sell the house to a defense worker who can qualify as to income.

The appraisal of residential INCOME properties by the Federal Housing Administration is not based upon market value or replacement cost, although they are factors in determining value, but upon the estimated income of the property for the life of the loan, and may vary considerably from the market or replacement value. 

All Federal Housing Loans must be "one-paper" loans—that is, there must be no secondary or junior financing involved in the transaction, and if the applicant is purchasing the property he must make an actual investment of the cost price in excess of the loan proceeds.

In the case of a construction loan, three rigid inspections are made at certain stages of construction to see that the work is properly done, according to the plans and specifications and no inferior materials are used.

In the case of an existing house, the building must meet certain required standards, and if the F. H. A. inspection discloses defects, these must be corrected to bring the building up to the required standards before the loan is consummated. 

Q. Can an F. H. A. insured loan be paid prior to maturity, or larger payments be made than originally agreed upon? 

A. Yes. The loan can be paid at any time upon payment of an adjusted premium charge, or bonus, of 1% of the original amount of the loan. However, partial payments of not to exceed 15% of the original face of the note can be made annually without any prepayment bonus. -158-

Q. Must the borrower live in the house in order to obtain an 

F. H. A. loan?

A. Yes. The individual borrower under Title VI and in all cases under Title II, with the exception of Class III under Title II 

the borrower must live in the house. Occupancy by the owner is not necessary in Class III of Title II-the 80% loan on existing homes and residential income. 

Q. Are there any requirements as to eligibility?

Yes. A financial and income statement is contained in the loan application, and a very careful analysis is made by the Federal Housing Administration to determine that the applicant will be able to meet the monthly payments. The borrower must have a satisfactory record for meeting his obligations. While it is not necessary that the borrower have other assets, his resources and liabilities are given careful consideration-particularly in loans in the higher brackets. HIS INCOME is the prime consideration, as it is from this source that the loan payments will have to come. 

It should be at least five times the amount of the loan payments. 

It need not necessarily be from salaries or wages, but the permanency and length of time the applicant has received it is carefully weighed.

Q. Can the owner of a property on which there is an F. H. A. loan sell the property without paying the loan? 

A. Yes. He is not restricted in any way in disposing of the property. However, if he wishes to be relieved of his liability on the note, or intends to apply for another F. H. A. loan on other property, the purchaser will have to file a "Substitution of Liability" form and submit his financial statement, together with a fee of $5.00, to the Federal Housing Administration, through the lending institution, and if eligible the purchaser will be substituted for the former owner, and the latter will be released and is then free to file a loan application on other property. 

Q. Does the age of the borrower have any bearing on the approval of the application, or the maturity of the loan? 

A. Yes. If the applicant is advanced in years the Federal 

Housing Administration will shorten the maturity for which they will insure the loan to coincide with the life and earning expectancy of the applicant. This will, of course, increase the monthly payment. This obstacle is often overcome by having a son or other immediate member of the family, who would normally inherit the property, co-sign the loan papers. 

Q. How do I go about obtaining a Federal Housing Administration Loan, or determine whether I am eligible?

A. The best way is to consult any approved Federal Housing 

Administration lending institution-either a Bank, Federal Savings and Loan Association, etc. They will be pleased to confer with you and analyze your needs and eligibility and give you complete -159-

information. If it appears feasible that you would be eligible they will fill out the loan application for you and submit it to the 

Federal Housing Administration for a commitment. Your applica tion will have to be accompanied by the F. H. A. fee of 30c per hundred with a minimum of $10.00. The Federal Housing Administration will make a careful analysis of the application and return a firm commitment for insurance of the loan, or decline to insure it. 

As soon as the commitment is received by the lending institution, they will prepare the loan papers and proceed as in the case of any real estate loan.

Q. Will an F. H. A. insured loan on my house prevent me from selling it or make it more difficult to sell?

A. No. It should be of considerable assistance in view of the favorable terms, the long maturity without any necessity of renewal or the expense of new papers, and in addition the buyer is protected by the rigid inspection of the building by the Federal Housing Administration.

DEEDS OF TRUST 

A new and improved form of trust deed has just been issued by the Great Western Title and Escrow Corporation which will result in a considerable saving in recording charges. This trust deed gives all of the protection, including assignment of rents, afforded by the old form, but the recording charge is only $1.50 as compared with the average recording charge of $3.50 for the old form. This is a saving of $2.00 on each trust deed, and as there are approximately 8000 trust deeds recorded each month, there will be a saving of approximately $16,000.00 per month in recording charges when this form becomes universal. 

This is accomplished by the filing of a Master Copy of the terms and conditions of the trust deed, and eliminating the repetition of these terms in each individual instrument. By reference to the master copy these terms are made a part of each trust deed, thereby giving each trust deed the same security as though the lengthy terms and conditions were detailed in each instrument. 

Another very important feature of this new trust deed is that the maximum foreclosure fee is $50.00 regardless of the amount of the trust deed. The standard trustee's foreclosure fee commences at $66.66 for a $1000.00 trust deed and is graduated up according to the amount of the trust deed, the foreclosure fee for a $10,000.00 trust deed, for example, being $216.66.

Because of the savings in cost of recording, together with time saved in the Recorder's office, both of which are obvious, it is to be hoped that this form of trust deed as inaugurated by the Great Western Title & Escrow Corp. will be put into general use in the immediate future, as a distinct and beneficial step forward in the handling of real estate financing. -160-

DEEDS (of Trust)  

Q. What is meant by the statement that a trustor retains an equitable title to property?

A. Although the legal title to property under a deed of trust is conveyed to a trustee, the borrower is permitted to retain the use and benefit of the property, as long as his control of the property does not jeojardize the security of the note under the deed of trust.

He is, therefore, said to hold an "equitable" title. Under his "equitable" title the borrower can further encumber the property or dispose of any interest he has in it. 

Q. What caused the "deed of trust" to originate in California?

A. During the period of rapid development in California there was need for liberal financing of real property. The delay in acquiring title to property in event of foreclosure, however, made lenders hesitate to lend liberally. The idea of deeding the property to a trustee with power of sale consequently developed. This method of securing loans came rapidly into general use and has not been declared illegal by the Courts, although the practice was originally contrary to existing laws.

Q. What safeguards have been imposed for the protection of the borrower under a deed of trust in recent years by the California Legislature?

A. Under recent legislation no deficiency judgment is allowed in event of foreclosure of a mortgage or deed of trust given to secure the balance of a purchase price. There is also effective at this time a provision whereby unfair deficiency judgments may not be obtained in event of foreclosure. The law provides for an appraisal for the Court to determine the fair value of property which has been foreclosed and the Court may render a judgment for no more than the difference between the fair value of the property and entire amount due the lender. Such judgment however, must not exceed the difference between the sale price and the total indebtedness. 

Deficiency judgment suits must now be brought within three months following the sale of the property.

Q. What two documents are made out by a beneficiary under a deed of trust, in event hè wishes to start a foreclosure proceeding? 

A. The two documents to be made out are a declaration of default and a request for sale. -163-

Q. What is meant by a reconveyance in connection with a trust deed!

A. After the note under a deed of trust is fully satisfied the trustee executes an instrument known as a "reconveyance” and delivers it to the trustor. This instrument, when recorded, releases the lien from the record.

Q. About how long does it take for a beneficiary to secure title to property under a trust deed foreclosure, and why is this time necessary?

A. A beneficiary under a deed of trust may secure title to the property in default in about one hundred and ten days. This includes an advertising period and other periods provided for in the average deed of trust. (See change in law re: New Trust Deeds.) 

Q. In event a trust deed note should outlaw, is the trust deed instrument itself of any value?

A. Yes. A sale could still be maintained under the provisions of the trust deed. The lender, however, would be precluded from recovering any deficiency judgment.

Q. May a property, which is encumbered by a deed of trust be homesteaded?

A. Yes, however, the homestead is not exempt from execution or forced sale in event of the foreclosure of a lien already on the property prior to the declaration of a homestead. 

Q. Name two purposes other than to give security for a loan, for which property is often deeded in trust. 

A. For the purpose of holding legal title to a land subdivision or for purpose of creating a trust under which the person placing his property in trust, called the beneficiary, may enjoy the income. 

Life insurance trusts may be created in a similar way. 

Q. In event a private trustee is named under a trust deed and said trustee dies, what steps must be taken to secure appointment of a new trustee?

A. Unless the trust deed provides for the appointment of another trustee, the Superior Court must appoint a new trustee. 

This is covered by Sections 2287-2289 of the Civil Code. A beneficiary of age has the right to make a nomination of the new trustee. 

Q. When you sell a house for $6,000 upon which there is a $3,000 first mortgage, and your customer pays $500 cash and $60 per month on the balance, would you advise your client (seller) to take back a straight second mortgage for the balance, or a trust deed? 

Explain your answer.

A. Seller should be advised to take back a note secured by a purchase-money trust deed. Principal and interest of note payable in monthly installments of $60 per month. Seller's security increased by monthly payments. Trust deed could be foreclosed in about 4 months without right of redemption. Under mortgage property -164-

could be redeemed within one year after foreclosure sale. In such a sale, a land contract would probably be preferable to either. 

Q. Indicate which of the following can and cannot legally 

convey real property: (a) Single woman under age of 21 years. (b) Married woman 18 years of age. (c) Single man 18 years of age. (d) Married man at what age?

A. (a) Cannot. (b) Can as provided by amendments to Civil 

Code, Sec. 25, effective July 28, 1927. (c) Cannot. (d) At age of 21.

Q. In event an owner who has lost his property under foreclosure of a trust deed fails to vacate the premises after the sale, how can the new owner secure possession of the property? 

A. The new title-holder would have to take regular legal steps to eject a party in possession after the time of the sale, the same action which is taken to eject a tenant who is in default. After securing title through foreclosure of a mortgage this separate action is usually not necessary. 

Q. (a) What is a trust deed? (b) In what respects does it differ from a mortgage?

A. A trust deed (also known as a deed of trust) is an instrument under which an owner, or borrower, called the trustor, or grantor, conveys the legal title to property to a party called the trustee, as security for the payment of a note and the performance of the covenants or agreements contained in the trust deed, for the benefit of a third party called the beneficiary, who is the holder of note and trust deed.

Under a trust deed legal title is conveyed to trustee, whereas under a mortgage legal title to mortgaged property remains in borrower. In event of default, under trust deed, property is sold to satisfy debt by trustee. Mortgage is foreclosed by court action. 

One year of redemption after sale under mortgage; no redemption under trust deed if sold by authority granted in instrument. (See change in law on Trust Deed executed subsequent to 1939.) 

Q. Is it possible to execute a mortgage or trust deed against property which a mortgagor or trustor may subsequently acquire? 

A. Yes. This occasionally happens. Either a mortgage or trust deed may cover property subsequently acquired, provided that the mortgage or trust deed provides that these properties later acquired shall be part of the security.

Q. May a mortgage be used as second encumbrance, i. e., to secure a second loan upon a property, or may only trust deeds be used for this purpose?

A. While it is customary in California to use only deeds of trust to secure a second loan on property, either a mortgage or trust deed may be used for this purpose. The shorter foreclosure period for a deed of trust causes it to be used as a junior lien and very rarely is a mortgage used for this purpose. -165-

Q. Why is it advisable for persons about to lend money on mortgages or trust deeds to determine the interest of the party in possession of the property?

A. The law recognizes that a party in possession of a property is giving constructive notice that he may have some interest in the property. It is therefore very important for persons loaning money on property to determine the rights of those parties in possession. 

As an example, a person might occupy a home for which he has an unrecorded deed. The person actually securing the loan or attempting to secure it might not be the actual owner at all, even though he is the record-owner. The party in possession might also have a lease on the premises, which might be considered detrimental to the safety of the loan. 

Q. What are the three principal instruments used to finance real estate in California?

A. Mortgages, trust deeds, and land contracts are most usually used to finance the purchase of real property in this State. Under the land contract, the purchaser does not usually secure title to the property until the full purchase price is paid, or until a substantial portion is paid and the balance is secured by a mortgage or trust deed.

Q. Do the California statutes provide for the creation of the 

Deed of Trust?

A. No. The Deed of Trust has no statutory origin. It merely came into existence through popular usage and was subsequently upheld by court decisions.

Q. Is a person who lends money secured by a Deed of Trust called a trustor? If not, how is he designated?

A. No. The trustor is the borrower. The person who lends the money upon the property secured by a Deed of Trust is termed the "beneficiary.' 

Q. Is it necessary to have a trust deed and the accompanying note dated on the same day?

A. It is not necessary to have a trust deed or mortgage note dated the same day as the instrument, however, it is generally considered better practice to do this. 

Q. Does destroying a deed or redelivering a deed to the grantor revest the title in the grantor? Explain.

A. No. Property must be conveyed by a new deed. 

MORTGAGES 

Q. Can maker of note and mortgage assign them when he sells property secured by them, and escape guaranteeing holder of the note its payment in full?

A. No; by selling mortgaged property the mortgagor does not relieve himself from his personal liability for payment of the note. -166

He could be relieved of this liability only by a release given by the mortgagee.

Q. How is mortgage and note assigned to another person without assignor's (other than maker's) joint guarantee of payment? 

A. Note should be assigned by a "without recourse" assignment. The phrase "without recourse" added to the assignment signifies that the assignor means to save himself from liability to subsequent holders of the note.

Q. Must a mortgage always secure a money obligation, or may it be used for another purpose?

A. A mortgage may be given for guarantee of the performance of any legal obligation, for instance, for guaranteeing the construction of certain improvements by a specified time, or the drilling of a well, etc. In the latter cases a mortgage serves the purpose of a bond.

Q. Are there the same number of parties to a mortgage and a deed of trust?

A. No. There may be only two parties to a mortgage, the borrower and lender. The borrower is also known as the mortgagor, and the lender as mortgagee. In the case of a trust deed, or deed of trust, there must be at least three parties, the borrower (trustor), the lender (beneficiary) and the trustee. The trustee holds title to the property pending the fulfillment of the obligation. 

Q. What is the difference between taking property "subject to" a mortgage and "assuming" the mortgage?

A. A buyer who takes title subject to a mortgage undertakes no personal obligation to pay the debt but during his ownership of the property must make necessary payments to prevent foreclosure. 

The mortgage is an encumbrance upon his property, but if he parts with title to it, he has no longer any interest in the mortgage. 

Whereas if he assumes the mortgage, he becomes personally liable for the payment of the debt secured by the mortgage. 

Q. When a note secured by mortgage on real estate is assigned what happens to the mortgage?

A. Mortgage has no existence apart from debt it secures. Assignment of note carries with it the security.

Q. Owner deeded property to holder of mortgage for the purpose of extinguishing the debt. What other thing remained to be done?

A. Holder of mortgage should cancel note and deliver to mortgagor and record a release of mortgage and his deed. Mortgagor should give up possession of property. Owner may have title brought down to show his interest acquired under deed free from previous mortgage which was released.

Q. Does a mortgagor retain title to his property during the period of redemption after foreclosure? -167-

A. After the foreclosure suit proceeds to judgment, property is sold to the highest cash bidder by the sheriff, or representative of the Court. A Sheriff's Deed to the property, however, is not issued until 12 months after the sale, if no redemption is made. 

Actual title, therefore, would appear to remain in the mortgagor until a sheriff's deed is issued. Section 707 of the Code of Civil 

Procedure, however, provides for the recovery of rent from the mortgagor in event he maintains possession of the property during the redemption period.

Q. Name two ways in which a recorded mortgage may be discharged (released from record) by the mortgagee. 

A. A mortgage is released from the record by an instrument called a release or satisfaction of mortgage, which describes the mortgage and states it has been paid, satisfied or discharged. It must be signed by the mortgagee or assignee and must be acknowledged for recording. It is then recorded by and at expense of mortgagor in office of County Recorder where mortgage was recorded.

A recorded mortgage may also be released by an entry in the margin of the record thereof, signed by mortgagee or assignee, which is acknowledged by the recorder when he stamps the satisfaction or release clause across the record and on the mortgage. 

In either case note should be stamped paid and returned to mortgagor.

Q. In event a mortgage note becomes outlawed does the mortgage retain any value as a lien?

A. No. In event the mortgage note should outlaw, the lien of the mortgage ceases. 

Q. May anyone but a mortgagor redeem the property, after foreclosure of a mortgage?

A. In addition to the mortgagor there are other redemptioners who may redeem; among these are holders of mechanics' liens, owners of second mortgages, etc. 

Q. Is a mortgagee or beneficiary entitled to recover any sum over the unpaid principal of the note in foreclosure action?

A. Yes. The mortgagee, or beneficiary, is entitled to recover the amount of delinquent interest and any other expenditures made by him in connection with the foreclosure which are allowed by law. 

Q. How may the former owner of a property who has lost same due to foreclosure on a mortgage be dispossessed if he remains in possession after the period of redemption has expired?

A. If the former owner remains in possession after the period of redemption has expired, the mortgagee may through the same action secure a Writ of Assistance with which the sheriff is permitted to eject the persons occupying the property. 

Q. When it is difficult to determine whether a lien is a trust deed or a mortgage, how is it usually considered? -168-

A. Court decisions have held that when there is any doubt as to the nature of a lien, it will be considered a mortgage. 

Q. In the event a borrower gives a lender a deed to his property as security for a loan, is good title transferred to the lender? 

A. No, the Courts cansider that any deed as security for an obligation is to be construed as a mortgage. .Q Mortgagee extended time of payment. What effect did that have upon liens or mortgage secondary to the first extended mortgage?

A. If mortgage contained provision for extension thereof and mortgagee extends note for a period not exceeding four years from its original due date, extension is valid and mortgage still takes priority over subsequent encumbrances. If extended beyond four years from its original due date without consent of holder of subsequent encumbrance their right will take precedence over original mortgage upon expiration of the four year period. 

Q. What is meant by a "purchase money mortgage"?

A. A "purchase money mortgage" is a mortgage given to a seller as part of the purchase price of a property. 

Q. Does a "purchase money mortgage" have priority over judgments against a purchaser?

A. Yes. Upon acquiring a property for which a purchase money mortgage is given as part of the consideration, the mortgage is deemed to attach simultaneously with the transfer and is prior to any judgment or other liens which might attach because of the new owner.

Q. May a mortgagor, or trustor, whose property is under foreclosure pay up the amount of the lien with all accrued charges and have the action dismissed prior to the sale?

A. Yes, the entire amount of the lien and accrued charges may be paid and the action must be dismissed, any time prior to the sale. The lien-holder, however, may refuse to accept any payments of interest or installments, and may insist upon the entire amount being paid.

Q. Why is it desirable to have building loan mortgages properly recorded before any material is delivered on the job, or work done on it?

A. This is very important and individuals and companies engaged in making building loans are very careful to see that no work is done or material delivered to a project before their lien is recorded. The reason for this is that any mechanic's lien for labor or material which attaches to the job would have priority over the mortgage or trust deed if any work was done or material delivered prior to the recordation of the lien. This priority would not only cover liens for work done prior to such recordation, but any work done on that particular job. -169-

Q. What precaution should be taken by a lender who loans money to a corporation on a note, mortgage or trust deed?

A. The lender, in order to protect his interest, should require an authorization from the Board of Directors of the corporation. 

A mere authorization by some officer of the company might not suffice to make the corporation responsible. 

Q. What is meant by the term "Holder in due course"

A. A "Holder in due course" is one who receives a negotiable instrument for value and in the regular course of business and who has full right to make collection on the instrument, free from any defenses by any party.

Q. Could a person who takes a mortgage note by assignment, knowing that said note is in default, be termed a "Holder in due course"?

A. No. A holder in due course must hold the note before it becomes overdue.

ASSIGNMENTS 

Q. What is necessary in order to assign a mortgage or trust deed!

A. Either a mortgage or trust deed may be assigned by merely endorsing the note. This endorsement carries with it the security given by the mortgage or trust deed instrument. Some believe it better practice to use an assignment form in order to assign mortgages and trust deeds. It is now possible to record these assignments. In all cases the original maker of the note should be notified of the assignment, or if the property has been subsequently transferred, the party responsible for the payment of the note should be notified.

Q. Smith held recorded contract upon which he had paid nearly one-half of purchase price. Agent was selling Smith's equity to Jones. State fully how the assignment of this contract should be made.

A. Assuming contract may be assigned by Smith without consent of seller, an assignment clause should be placed on contract. It may read in this order: "For value received, we do hereby assign to Blank Jones (show marital status) all our right, title and interest in the within contract." Assignment should be signed by Smith and wife, if married. They should also deliver an assignment of contract properly signed and acknowledged to Jones who should record it to complete the chain of title, since 

Smith's contract was recorded. 

Q. What is the effect of assignor of a note to write his name on the back thereof and hand it to assignee! 

A. His endorsement is a guarantee of the payment of the note. 

OFFSET STATEMENT 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. What is meant by an offset statement in connection with a mortgage or trust deed! -172-

A. Offset statements are secured when a new purchaser is acquiring a mortgage or trust deed which already exists. These are usually furnished by the owner of the property given as security, and contain a statement of the condition of the lien. These statements usually include unpaid balance of note, condition of interest payments, due date and whether or not the owner has any claims which do not appear in the instrument. Offset statements are sometimes secured from the mortgagee who gives practically the same information. These statements are given so that there is a clear understanding as to obligation of mortgagor to the new owner of the mortgage. 

PARTIAL RELEASE CLAUSE 

Q. What is meant by the term "release clause" in a mortgage on real property?

A. A release clause is a provision in the mortgage under which certain lots or portions of the mortgaged land may be released upon the payment of a certain sum. What is meant by a partial release clause in an encumbrance and why are these clauses important in connection with the sale of subdivision property?

A. A partial release clause is a provision in the written instrument which permits the borrower to release portions of a property from under the lien upon the payment of a specified sum. The California Real Estate Act requires all subdividers to provide for a release clause in these liens so that they may release individual lots or parcels from under the lien when the purchaser has paid in full. If release clauses were not required, the purchaser after paying in full might be unable to secure a clear title from the subdivider.

Q. How are lots in a tract of land, with a blanket mortgage on entire tract, subdivided and sold free from the above referred to mortgage?

A. Blanket mortgage must contain a partial release clause, which provides that a part of the property held as security may be released upon payment of a certain specified sum. 

SUBORDINATION CLAUSE 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. What is meant by a subordination clause in a mortgage or trust deed?

A. Subordination clauses are provided in mortgages and trust deeds, in order that these liens may be renewed or extended without having junior liens become prior to them. Instances have occurred where subordination clauses were not used in the first trust deed or mortgage and the only recourse of the first lien-holder was to foreclose in order to protect his interest, as against the owner of junior liens. -173-

A clause inserted in a mortgage or trust deed which provides that it shall remain subject and subordinate to an existing mortgage and any renewal thereof, or to any new mortgage given to replace it. Clause usually provides that the new mortgage shall not be larger in amount than the one it replaces. 

REDEMPTION 

Q. Does the borrower under a deed of trust have any period in which to redeem his property after it is sold through foreclosure? 

A. There is no period of redemption after the foreclosure sale in connection with a deed of trust if the instrument is foreclosed without court action. If trust deed was executed subsequent to 

1939 and is foreclosed with court action and the property sells for enough to satisfy the unpaid balance due and the costs of foreclosure there is a three month period of redemption allowed. If the property in court action fails to sell for enough to pay all claims under the foreclosure, a deficiency judgment may be secured, but in this case a one year period of redemption is allowed the Trustor. 

Q. Does the borrower under a mortgage have any period of redemption after foreclosure? 

A. Yes, he may redeem at any time within one year.

LIENS  

Q. What are mechanics' liens and how do they originate?

A. Mechanics' liens are liens filed against real property by workmen, contractors or furnishers of materials for unpaid wages or accounts incurred in the construction of improvements. The right to file these liens was provided by the legislature. 

Q. When no notice of completion has been filed in connection with a new building, how long do claimants have in which to file a "mechanic's lien"?

A. All persons have 90 days in which to file their liens. If notice filed, then original contractors have 60 days and all others 

30 days.

Q. How much time does an owner have in which to file notice of completion after actual completion of the building? 

A. Notice must be filed within 10 days.

Q. In connection with mechanics' liens, when is a building considered completed?

A. Completion is indicated in four general ways: (1) Filing of notice of completion with county recorder; (2) Acceptance of the job by the owner; (3) Cessation of labor for 30 days; (4) 

Actual use of the project together with cessation of work. .. What is the maximum time that mechanics' liens are effective after being filed? -174-

A. Suit to recover must be brought within one year in any event. In simple cases, action to foreclose must be brought within 

90 days after filing the lien.

Q. Ordinarily, how much time does a holder of a mechanic's lien have in which to start foreclosure? 

A. 90 days.

Q. Can deficiency judgments be obtained against owners of buildings if the foreclosure of a mechanics' lien does not produce sufficient money to satisfy the lien? 

A. No. Deficiency judgment allowed; no obligation against owner personally.

Q. What is the penalty for making false claims under a mechanic's lien?

A. The lien right may be forfeited. 

Q. Do you consider a deed of trust a lien?

A. A deed of trust, although a transfer of title to property to a trustee, is primarily executed to secure the payment of a debt and may therefore be considered a lien. 

Q. Are liens created by negligence to pay federal taxes usually general or specific liens?

A. Unpaid Federal assessments in effect become automatic judgments and affect all property of the debtor. They are therefore usually general liens. 

Q. Does a lien always affect only one specific piece of property or may it affect all property of a debtor? 

A. General liens, such as money judgments, affect all property of the debtor. Various State and Federal taxes, if unpaid, become general liens against all property of the debtor. Most voluntary liens are specific liens against a particular property. 

Q. A borrower of $2,500 gave first mortgage on the home he was building, but found himself short of funds to complete it. 

Mortgagee did not record this first mortgage until foundation was begun and after the lumber was on the premises. Material men and contractor filed mechanics' liens. Which took precedence, the prior mortgage or liens later filed? Explain. 

A. Mechanics' liens take precedence. To insure priority over mechanics' lien mortgage should have been recorded before work was begun or materials delivered on lot. 

Q. Name two different involuntary liens. 

A. Involuntary liens are those imposed upon property without the necessity of the owner's consent. Taxes and judgments would therefore be two liens of this type. 

Q. Owner sold lot, taking in security a trust deed payable at $50 per month and permitted purchaser to place a prior mortgage for procuring a loan with which to construct a building on the -175-

lot. How would you advise client to save himself from responsibility for possible building liens? 

A. You should advise client to insist upon having contractor furnish contract bond issued by a responsible surety company guaranteeing completion of the building and the payment of all claims for labor and material. Mortgage and deed of trust should be recorded before work begun or materials delivered on the lot. 

The same result (but not as sure) might be had by having the contractor get a waiver and release of mechanics' liens from all persons or firms supplying labor and/or material on the job. 

Q. As a broker you are about to sell for cash a home just completed. The buyer asks you to advise him as to how he may be protected against liens for unpaid labor and material bills. 

What would be your advice?

A. Broker should inform buyer that he can be protected against such liens by closing transaction through escrow. Escrow clerk should be advised that building has just been completed. If search of title shows notice of completion in proper form has been recorded, then right of material dealer and laborers to file liens expires in thirty days from date of recording notice. 

If no liens have been filed by these parties, transaction may then be safely closed by taking a release from the original contractor in consideration of payment in full to him. If no notice was filed, or notice filed did not comply with the law, then all persons have ninety days in which to file liens and escrow clerk would be guided accordingly. Sale deposit receipt should provide property shall be clear of all such liens. 

Q. Why is it important for a person making a building loan to inspect the site of the proposed building before recording his lien?

A. Because if any work has started or material has been delivered upon the job, all workers and material men "connected with the job may file mechanics' liens for sums due them, and the liens have priority over the recorded mortgage or trust deed. -176-

NOTICE OF NON-RESPONSIBILITY  

Q. If lessee made certain alterations and/or repairs to leased property, would owner be liable in case lessee failed to pay, and mechanic's liens were filed against the property? 

A. Yes. 

Q. How could owner of property protect himself against mechanic's liens for work and material supplied on his property at order of tenant?

A. By posting on premises, or publishing, notice of nonre sponsibility.
