STREET IMPROVEMENTS AND ASSESSMENTS 

Generally speaking, assessments are for the purpose of paying for improvements to streets in the cities and counties affected. 

To this end many different acts have been passed in the State of California to authorize the City Council or the County Board of Supervisors to do this work and pay for it by assessments against the real property benefited.  

Q. What type of work would come under the term, "street improvement"? 

A. Grading, paving, installation of curbs, sidewalks, gutters, grade crossings, parkways, underpasses, tunnels, culverts, sewers, fire hydrants, water mains and street lights. 

Q. Who pays for street improvements and how?

A. Owners of property in the district benefited pay by special assessment imposed by the Board of Supervisors or the City Coun cil.

Q. Is there any limit to the number of assessments that may be levied for improvements in a district? 

A. No. Property owners may, however, refuse to sign petitions for the improvement, or may circulate a petition objecting -178-

to such improvement, and if sufficient names are secured, improvement and assessment may be defeated.

Q. Are assessments against property for improvements in the district a lien against the property assessed? 

A. Yes, and upon failure to pay same, the property may be sold by tax sale.

The most generally used improvement acts are: 

THE STREET IMPROVEMENT ACT OF 1911 

(Amended in 1929)

Under the provisions of this act, where the amount of the tax is in excess of $25.00 it automatically goes to bond. Assessments must appear on regular tax bill. Bill provides for penalty of 1% for allowing bonds to become delinquent, and 1% per month as long as they remain delinquent. Chapter 739 of the statute of 

1935 amended the improvement act of 1911 as regard to the priority of liens and bonds. This chapter states "such liens whether a bond or bonds issued to represent the assessment or otherwise shall be subordinate liens previously imposed upon the same property, but it shall have priority over all special assessments liens which may thereafter be created against the said property." 

Q. May property be acquired under the provision of this Act? 

A. No. This Act provides for improvements only. 

Q. Can improvements to streets or roads be made in Counties under this Act?

A. No. Act provides that all improvements must be within 

Municipality. (Exception. Construction of appurtenances to City sewer system on rights of way outside City limits.) (See Fed. 

Const. Co. v. Ensign, 59 C. A. 200.) 

Q. May property owners protest such improvements? 

A. Yes, anyone whose property is to be assessed may file protest. Protest must be in writing and may be filed with the clerk of the City Council up to the hour of the hearing. No particular form is needed. If protest against proposed work is by majority of the property owners in the district, the protest may only be overruled by a four-fifths majority vote of the Council. 

Q. Does assessment always cover entire district?

A. Not necessarily. Unless assessment district is created, assessments to cover cost will be against lots fronting on the improvement.

Q. Suppose the property owner has constructed his own sidewalk, etc., in front of his property, and the City later decides to do the same type of work on the rest of the street, may the property owner get credit for the work he has done? -179-

A. He may be credited for such work provided it conforms to the official grade, and if accepted by the Street Superintendent as satisfactory.

Q. Are owners of the property assessed for the entire cost of the improvements?

A. Not necessarily. In some cases, the Council may pass a resolution authorizing payment of a part or all of such cost to be paid from a fund that it may designate. 

Q. Are assessments paid in cash by property owner, or through the issuance of bonds?

A. Any assessment of $25.00 or more remaining unpaid for thirty days after recordation of warrant may be covered by bond issue if the Council so provides. Interest on such bonds must not exceed ten percent per annum and must not run in excess of fifteen years, and bonds cannot be issued if property owner files statement objecting to same. (Exception.) Bonds may be issued under the improvement bond act of 1915 and they run for a term of fourteen years with a maximum interest rate of 8%.

THE OPENING AND WIDENING ACT OF 1903 

(Made Applicable to Counties in 1923) (Amended 1929)

This act is used mostly for the acquisition of property for extending, widening, opening, or straightening streets and highways. Under this act the improvements may be partly in one or more counties and/or in a municipality. 

Q. By what method is money raised for improvements under this Act?

A. By assessments against property owners in proportion to benefits derived therefrom. Assessments must be paid within thirty days or property is subject to being advertised and sold as for delinquent taxes. 

Q. After sale, may property owner redeem?

A. Property owner may redeem any time within twelve months by paying assessment penalties and charges incident to sale. After twelve months, purchaser under sale gets deed to property. 

Q. Are these assessments ever covered by bond issue?

A. In some cases, they are covered by bonds issued under authority of the Street Opening Bond Act of 1911, and for the 

Improvement Bond Act of 1915. 

Q. How are these bonds issued?

A. By authority of City Council, where assessments exceed $50.00, at option of owner, assessments may go to bond. -180-

Q. These bonds are payable how?

A. In ten or twenty annual installments, interest 7% per annum.

THE ROAD DISTRICT IMPROVEMENT ACT OF 1907 

The road district improvement act of 1907 is applicable only to counties. It may be used for improving highway in the counties or partly within limits of a city (incorporated or unincorporated) when necessary to connect with such highway beyond city limits.

Bonds are issued to cover cost of such improvements and are paid by special tax levy each year against the particular property affected, and paid as are other County Taxes. 

Q. Is the entire cost of work under this Act necessarily borne by the property owners!

A. No, the County may contribute to the payment of such improvements from the road district funds, general funds of the county, or other funds that may be available for such improvements. 

Q. May the owners of property protest such improvements?

A. Yes. Upon written protest by majority of the owners to the Board of Supervisors, the board is prohibited from proceeding for a period of one year. 

Q. Are these improvements paid for by issue of bonds?

A. Yes, after acceptance, bonds are issued by Treasurer upon expiration of twenty days from final order and delivered to contractor. These bonds are payable in annual installments (maximum of 20) and interest rate is fixed by Supervisor. 

Q. How are these bonds paid? 

A. By Special Assessment and collection under general tax levy.

The STREET OPENING BOND ACT OF 1911, and the IM- 

PROVEMENT BOND ACT OF 1915, provide that bonds may be issued whenever city council directs same, subject to approval of owner if amount exceeds $50.00. Bonds are payable in 10 or 20 annual installments; interest 6%. (Questions and Answers) 

Q. What other improvement acts may use the provisions of this act to cover costs of improvements? 

A. Improvement Act of 1911; County Improvement Act of 

1921; Vrooman Act and Opening and Widening Acts of 1903 and 1923.

Q. What is the maximum term of these bonds and the rates of interest?

A. Term of bonds must not exceed fourteen years and interest must not exceed 8%. Bonds are subject to anticipation of payment. -181-

THE VROOMAN ACT OF 1885 

Under the provisions of this act the city council is authorized to grade, regrade, pave or repair streets, install culverts, etc., within the city or county; to construct sewers after calling election providing for issuance of bonds secured by special fund collected by general tax levy. Provides for acquisition of any public utility under ownership of Municipality or County.

Provides that owners of property may elect to do grading of the street himself/herself and be entitled to an offset against assessments for such work done to official grade.  

Q. Who may use this act?

A. Counties and cities may use this Act for any of the improvements specified therein. It may also be used to acquire any public utility for ownership by such county or municipality. 

Q. May a city and county use this act jointly? 

A. No. Must be separate proceeding as there is no provision for joint jurisdiction.

Q. May the owners to be benefited protest against the improvements? 

A. Yes. If a majority of the frontage ownership file protests provided by law, it will stop proceedings for six months. Individual owners within the district to be benefited may file protest proceedings, in which case protest must be passed upon by legislative body.

Q. Is the assessment against the whole district, or against lands fronting on improvement?

A. If district is formed, assessments are levied against whole district, if not, they may be levied against lands fronting on improvements, with certain exceptions, such as intersections, alley crossings or where work is done on one side of street only. 

Q. May owner be credited for doing grade work in front of his property?

A. Yes, where done to official grade. 

Q. Are such assessments a lien on the property! 

A. Yes, for a period of two years from date assessment is recorded, unless paid prior to that time.

THE MATTOON ACT (The Acquisition and Improvement Act of 1925) 

Because of the possible inequality of taxation under this act and the storm of protest that was raised subsequent to its passage, it was repealed in 1933. Bonds sold to the public prior to repeal were naturally protected because the purchasers bought in good faith. The interpretation of this act by the courts has done immeasurable damage to property values in California. Under this -182-

act assessments are levied upon the entire district and the annual levy is apportioned in accordance with the zones fixed by the legislature ordering the improvement. Unlike other improvement acts, this act provides that the tax shall be an Ad Valorum Tax upon the whole district rather than upon a specific property ownership, thus an owner of one lot may find himself responsible for the taxes of all of the owners in the district. (The author is of the opinion that the intent of the author of this act, the Hon. Everett Mattoon, was to improve the laws governing improvements, and had no thought except to benefit Southern California.)

No Questions and Answers are given under this act because it was repealed in 1933. We definitely admonish caution and consideration in the purchase of property which comes under the provisions of the Mattoon Act.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

Q. Why should instruments be acknowledged?

A. To make it eligible for recordation, and to impart constructive notice to those interested. 

Q. Who is a subscribing witness?

A. One who signs his name as a witness in evidence of the faet that he saw a certain writing executed, or heard it acknowledged. 

Q. Who is qualified to take acknowledgments in California?

A. A notary public, a clerk of a court of record, a county recorder, a judge of a supreme court or a superior court, a police court judge, a justice of the peace, or a court commissioner within their jurisdiction. 

Q. How may signatures by mark be authenticated?

A. By having the name of the person executing an instrument signed by another, and signified by a cross mark over which is written, "his mark" and witnessed by the signatures of two or more persons. 

Q. Is it necessary that a deed from husband to wife be acknowledged to make it valid? 

A. No. 

Q. Does acknowledgment of an instrument by a proper official certify the facts contained therein? 

A. No, acknowledgment only certifies that the person executing the instrument has made himself legally liable as to those facts. 

Q. Mary Jones gave John Doe a signed option on a certain property and subsequently decides to sell the property to another party before the option to John Doe expired. Being advised of this fact John Doe wishes to record his option in order to protect -183-

his interests but can not do so because Mary Jones did not acknowledge the same at the time she signed it. How can John Doe protect his option?

A. John Doe may take his option to any proper official qualified to take acknowledgments and himself make acknowledgment that the option was signed in his presence by Mary Jones. The option is then eligible for recordation. Such recordation would give constructive notice of John Doe's interest and cloud the title. 

NOTARY PUBLIC 

Q. To what four facts must a notary public testify in taking a signer's acknowledgment to a deed?

A. That person whose acknowledgment was taken personally appeared before notary, that signer was known to him to be person whose name was subscribed, that signer acknowledges that he excuted the instrument, and that the notary was properly qualified to take acknowledgment.

ADVERSE POSSESSION 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. What constitutes adverse possession?

A. A person holding property for a period of 5 years in absolute possession and who pays all county, city and state taxes, thereon, is presumed to have title by adverse possession. Such continued occupation of the land, while claiming title by such occupation, but not founded upon a written instrument, judgment or decree, any land so occupied is deemed to have been held by adverse possession.

Q. If in doubt as to the validity of your title to property held by adverse possession, what steps would you take to assure yourself of valid title?

A. Hold possession and pay all taxes and assessments for five years, occupy, fence and improve the property. File suit to quiet title. Suit must be filed within five years from time of first occupation.

Q. What are the five essential elements necessary to constitute an Adverse Possession sufficient to effect a bar of the legal title? 

A. (a) The possession must be hostile and under a claim of right. (b) It must be actual. (c) It must be open and notorious. (d) It must be exclusive, and (e) It must be continuous. (63 Cal. 

586.) (Reprint from "California Property Laws.")

Q. Is actual or constructive notice necessary in the holding of land by adverse possession?

A. Yes. California Appellate Court has ruled that the owner must have knowledge of such possession or means of such knowledge. -184-

Q. Can land of the Public Domain be obtained by adverse possession!

A. No. 

Q. Who pays taxes on property held by adverse possession?

A. The one in possession. Failure to pay such taxes regularly for a period of five consecutive years would defeat the claim. 

ALIENS 

Q. What aliens are incapable of acquiring real property in California?

A. Those aliens eligible to citizenship may acquire, own or transfer real property in this State with same freedom as any other citizen. Alien land laws provide aliens not eligible to citizenship may acquire, possess and transfer real property only to extent of existing treaty between our nation and others. Special privilege to unnaturalized Japanese under treaty between Federal Government and Japan which California laws cannot interfere with or abridge.

Special treaty referred to, are covered by special treaty with Japan in 1911 whereby Japanese who are not citizens are prohibited from leasing land for agricultural purposes but may lease for residential purposes. Whether or not it was the intent of this treaty, its interpretation would seem to be that such Japanese may own, lease or occupy houses, factories and shops but may not own the land upon which such buildings stand. 

Q. What races are not eligible for citizenship?

A. Except where covered by special treaty, races not eligible for citizenship are Hindus, Japanese, Malay and possibly all Asiatics. 

The only treaty covering this now in existence is with Japan. (Chinese were granted right of citizenship in 1943.) 

Q. In the event that an ineligible alien acquires property in satisfaction of a mortgage or lien can they hold title to the same? 

A. Yes, but not for longer than two years.

Q. If an alien acquires property in violation of the Alien 

Land Act, to what penalty is he subject? 

A. Escheat to the state and sale as provided by law. Such action is generally taken by the attorney-general. 

RACE RESTRICTIONS 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. (a) Restriction in grant deed forbids grantee to sell, lease, or rent the property to anyone not of the Caucasian race. Explain why such a restraint is void and unenforcible. (b) How could purpose of "use" restriction be lawfully secured?

A. (a) Such a restriction is a restraint on alienation and therefore void. (b) Condition that property shall not be "used" or "occupied" by a person not of Caucasian race is valid, being retraint not upon alienation but upon use. "Use" restrictions running with land for benefit of all buyers for reasonable time could be imposed upon land by seller. -185-

ATTACHMENTS  

જ. May an attachment be issued in a suit for the collection of a mortgage note?

A. Usually no. Only in cases where the property given as security has become of practically no value, will they be issued. 

Q. How may a property owner release his property from an attachment pending a suit to recover money from him? 

A. A property owner may file a bond with the County Sheriff to cover the amount of money involved in the suit, and thus release his property from the attachment lien. 

Q. Does an attachment protect the priority of a subsequent judgment as a general rule? Give exceptions, if any.

A. Yes. As an example, if property were attached on June 

1st, and a mortgage were recorded on June 10th, a judgment rendered on June 15th would have priority over the mortgage by virtue of attachment. This is not true in case of homesteads declared after attachment and prior to judgment. These, due to special legislation, would take priority over the judgment in the aforementioned example.

Q. Is an attachment a lien for a specific amount of money at the time it is created!

A. No. It is merely the seizure of a person's property as security for the payment of a judgment which may later be given by a court.

Q. What papers are necessary to be made out and filed in attachment proceedings?

A. After complaint is filed and summons issued the plaintiff must by his attorney, make out and file an affidavit for attachment (C. C. P. 538); an undertaking on attachment for not less than $200, and not exceeding the demand of the complaint exclusive of costs (C. C. P. 539); and the writ of attachment which the plaintiff desires the clerk to issue (C. C. P. 540).

Note that where the defendant wishes to prevent an attachment he may do so by filing with the attaching officer an undertaking in a sum twice the value of the money demand of the complaint. (C. C. P. 540.)

Instructions to the sheriff must be left with him or his authorized deputy. In the case of attachment of real estate a notice of attachment is required to be recorded and served on the occupant, or posted on the property where there is no occupant. 

Q. What must an affidavit for attachment show?

A. (1) The amount to which the defendant is indebted to plaintiff over and above all counter claims and set-offs, upon a contract express or implied, made or payable in this state, for the direct payment of money and that the payment of same has not been secured by mortgage, lien or pledge; or if originally so se- -186-

cured the security has become valueless as security without any act of the plaintiff; or (2) the amount of the indebtedness and that the defendant is a non-resident; or (3) that the plaintiff's case is one for the recovery of money as damages arising from an injury to property in this state by the negligence, fraud or other wrongful act of the defendant who is a non-resident; and (4) that the attachment is not sought, and the action is not prosecuted to hinder, delay or defraud any creditor of defendant. (Pajaro Valley Bank v. Sourich, 7 Cal. App. 732, wherein an affidavit which failed to further state "or any creditor of either of said defendants" was held to be fatally defective; Fridenberg v. Pierson, 18 

Cal. 152; for insufficient affidavits see Wilke v. Cohn, 54 Cal. 212, affidavit made in the alternative; Winters v. Pearson, 72 Cal. 554, wherein it was held an insufficient affidavit cannot be amended.) 

Q. What must an undertaking on attachment show?

A. (1) The amount of the undertaking (not less than $200 in the Superior Court, or $100 in the Justice of Peace Court, and in the Municipal Court of Los Angeles) and not exceeding the amount claimed by the plaintiff; (2) sufficient sureties; (3) that if the defendant recovers judgment, plaintiff will pay all costs that may be awarded to the defendant and all damages which defendant may sustain by reason of the attachment, not exceeding the sum specified in the undertaking; (4) that if the attachment is discharged on the ground that the plaintiff was not entitled to the same under C. C. P. 537, the plaintiff will pay all damages which the defendant may have sustained by reason of the attachment, not exceeding the sum specified in the undertaking (C. C. P. 

539, providing also for the exception to the bond and the justification thereon); (5) affidavit to stay the bond must state that the sureties are freeholders or householders, and that each is worth the sum specified in the bond, over and above his just debts. (C. C. 

P. 1057; Faze v. Landford, 16 Cal. App. 744.) 

Q. Is an undertaking sufficient to sustain a writ of attachment if the affidavit of the sureties omits to state the material fact that they are freeholders or householders? 

A. No. (Tibbet v. Tom Sue, 122 Cal. 206, wherein an attachment was discharged under C. C. P. 558 for irregularity. It was held that proceedings for attachment are not subject to amendment). 

Q. What must the writ of attachment show?

A. (1) It must be directed to the sheriff (or other execution officer if in other courts) of any county in which property of the defendant may be located; (2) it must require the sheriff (or other attaching officer) to attach and safely keep all the property of the defendant within his county not exempt from execution, or so much thereof as may be sufficient to satisfy plaintiff's demand as stated in the complaint-unless the defendant shall give security by an undertaking of at least two sufficient sureties in an amount to satisfy the plaintiff's demand besides costs, or in an amount equal -187-

to the value of the property of the defendant which has been or is about to be attached, said undertaking to be approved by the judge issuing same. (C. C. P. 540; Ralph v. Burns, 22 Cal. App. 

153; Peterson v. Beggs, 26 Cal. App. 760.)

Q. 

What must a notice of attachment of real estate show? 

A. (1) That it is based upon a writ of attachment; (2) names of the parties; (3) statement of the attachment and a description of the property attached; (4) signature of sheriff (where the action lies in the Superior Court) or of other attaching officer in other courts.

It must be recorded in the office of the recorder of the county where the property is located and a copy of the notice must be left with the occupant or posted on the property. (Schwartz v. 

Cowell, 71 Cal. 306.) 

BUILDING CLASSIFICATION 

(Los Angeles)

Class A building" shall mean any building of fireproof construction throughout, which has a "skeleton" framework of reinforced concrete or of structural steel, fireproofed as elsewhere required in this Article, and which "skeleton" framework consists of columns, girders, beams and similar members carrying and transmitting all external and internal live and dead loads, and all stresses, to the foundation or foundations of the building; provided, however, that for any such building, not exceeding four (4) stories in height, there may be used in lieu of reinforced concrete or structural steel columns at the exterior walls of the building solid masonry piers not less than six (6) feet in width and of the thickness as shown in chart in this article for solid masonry walls for a building of the same height. In lieu of solid masonry walls a Class B building may have grade one concrete hollow tile walls as allowed by Section 91.219 of Building Code. 'Class C building" shall mean any building having its exterior walls of solid masonry of the thickness required by Sections 91.127, 91-133 and 91.134 of Building Code, except for the necessary window, door, or similar openings in the exterior walls, and which building does not comply with the provisions of this Article for a Class A or B building. 91-219 of Building Code.

Every building or structure heretofore erected or constructed which does not conform to the provisions of this Article relating to construction, material or requirement of buildings of Class A, Class B or Class C construction shall be deemed and considered a building or structure of Class D.

CLOUD ON TITLE 

Q. What instrument would you use to secure release of some cloud on a title? 

A. Quitclaim deed.

Q. What is meant by "cloud" on the title, and how can it be removed?

A. Anything that affects title to property. An encumbrance might be a cloud upon the title. Taxes, assessments, liens, building restrictions, etc., affect title. Cloud can be removed by discharge of liens, by quit claim deed, or court action to quiet title. 

COVENANTS 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. What is meant by a covenant in a deed or other legal instrument?

A. A covenant is an agreement included in deeds and other instruments used in connection with real estate, in which the parties to the instrument agree to do certain things. As an illustration, -189-

a clause in a deed in which the parties agree that no intoxicating liquors are to be sold on the premises, is a covenant. In some instances, the covenants are merely implied. For instance, when a grant deed is given in California the law presumes that the grantor covenants with the grantee that he is the lawful owner of the property being conveyed. Briefly, it is an agreement to do or not to do. 

DEFICIENCY JUDGMENTS 

Q. In event a mortgage is foreclosed and the sale of the property does not realize enough to satisfy the claim of the mortgagee, is it necessary for the latter to bring suit to obtain a deficiency judgment?

A. No. If the sale does not realize enough funds, the Court automatically gives deficiency judgment for the difference between the price the property brings and the amount of the obligation. 

This answer should perhaps be qualified, due to the fact that there is recent legislation which protects the property owner from not being given due credit for the true value of the property foreclosed. 

Under certain conditions, the Court will appoint an appraiser and allow a deficiency judgment for only the difference between a fair appraised value of the property and the amount of the obligation. 

It is also not possible at this time to secure a deficiency judgment on purchase money mortgages executed since the recent legislation went into effect. 

Q. Is it necessary to bring a separate suit after the sale of property under a trust deed foreclosure, in order to obtain a deficiency judgment?

A. Yes. Separate suit must be brought in Court to recover a deficiency judgment under trust deed foreclosure. 

Q. For how long is a deficiency judgment effective after being obtained in connection with a trust deed foreclosure? 

A. A deficiency judgment is good for a period of five years after the entry date of the original foreclosure decree. 

DOCUMENTARY STAMPS (Internal Revenue Stamps) UNITED STATES INTERNAL REVENUE DOCUMENTARY STAMPS REQUIRED ON DEEDS OF CONVEYANCE SECTION 725 OF THE REVENUE ACT OF 1932 imposes a tax on all deeds, instruments or writing whereby any real estate is transferred, assigned or otherwise conveyed when the consideration or value of the property or interest conveyed exceeds $100.00. 

This tax is paid by affixing Documentary Stamps to the deedwhen issued. Any party to a taxable transaction is responsible to the Government for affixing and cancelling stamps in the required amount. -190-

HOW TO CALCULATE AMOUNT OF STAMPS REQUIRED: 

In calculating the amount of stamps which must be affixed to a deed of conveyance, the tax is computed upon the full consideration for the transfer, less all encumbrances which rest on the property before the sale and are not removed by the sale. Encumbrances placed on the property in connection with and as a result of the sale or transfer, as well as notes for deferred payments can not be deducted in determining the amount upon which tax is calculated. 

Taxes and assessments which have not been paid at time of sale are deductible only when they have become a lien. 

Deeds to satisfy mortgages and/or trust deeds are taxable for full amount of consideration, which includes any unpaid amount of principal plus accrued interest, plus any additional consideration tendered for transfer.

Corporation stock given for transfer of real estate is a taxable consideration.

STAMP TAX RATES ON DEEDS OF CONVEYANCE: When the full actual consideration is 

Over $ 100.00 and not over $ 500.00........... 500.00 1,000.00 

-- 1,000.00.. 1,500.00..... .55 .1.10 ....1.65 and so on at the same rate-55c additional for each additional $500 or fraction thereof. Deeds where actual consideration is $100 or less-require no stamps. 

SECTION 802 OF THE REVENUE ACT OF 1926 PROVIDES: 

Whoever makes, signs, issues, or accepts, or causes to be made, signed, issued, or accepted, any instrument, document, or paper of any kind or description whatsoever without the full amount of tax thereon being duly paid is guilty of a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof shall pay a fine of not more than $100 for each offense.

BE SURE TO CANCEL ALL STAMPS WHEN AFFIXED: 

The person affixing the stamp shall write or stamp thereon, in ink, his initials and the day, month, and year on which it is affixed, and in addition to the foregoing, stamps of the value of 55c or more shall have three parallel incisions made with a sharp instrument, lengthwise through the stamp. But this is not required where cancelled by perforation.

DEED TO COVER GIFT: A deed issued to cover a pure and bona fide gift of property from husband to wife, or from parent to child, or from an individual to a municipality or other political subdivision, or to the United States, wherein the consideration named is "natural love and affection and $1" "desire to promote public welfare and $1," or "$1 and other valuable considerations" is not taxable. -191-

EMINENT DOMAIN  

Q. May an individual have the power of eminent domain conferred on him?

A. Yes, such power can be conferred by act of the legislature. 

Q. Is there any type of property that is not subject to the exercise and the power of eminent domain? 

A. No. All property of any nature whatsoever, real or personal is subject to eminent domain. There may be an exception in the case of money. 

Q. Does the law permit political subdivisions to take a person's real estate from him under certain conditions? What are these conditions and by what term is the right known?

A. The law does permit political subdivisions to take property under the right of "eminent domain." In order to condemn property under this right, it must be shown that the acquisition is beneficial to public welfare, and the political subdivision must pay the owner a fair compensation for the property thus acquired. 

ENCUMBRANCES 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. An owner of real property agreed to convey same to purchaser free and clear of all encumbrances. He offered a deed showing the land subject to building restrictions. Is such a restriction an encumbrance and was the deed offered in conformity with the agreement of sale?

A. Building restrictions are an encumbrance, hence deed offered was not in conformity with agreement of sale. 

Q. What encumbrances are imposed upon real estate under the police power of the State?

A. These are numerous. Generally speaking, all restrictions to the free use of property imposed by local, county and state laws are imposed by virtue of the "police power of the State." Zoning restrictions, certain building restrictions to eliminate fire hazards, etc., are imposed under the police power of the State for general welfare.

Q. Which is the most comprehensive, the term lien or the term encumbrance?

A. Encumbrance is the broader term. Anything which restricts the rights to fee simple ownership of property without preventing its transfer is termed an encumbrance. A lien is an encumbrance which gives a creditor the right to recover the amount of a debt from the property of the debtor. A specific claim for money is involved in a lien, whereas an encumbrance may be a more abstract restriction or claim, such as a zoning restriction or easement. -192-

Q. Is an easement classified as a lien legally? If not, what is it?

A. An easement is a good example of an encumbrance which is not a lien as it is not imposed for the purpose of securing or satisfying a debt. See above answer.

Q. Define or give an example of an easement pertaining to real property.

A. Easement is right of another to have certain uses of one's property. Examples are rights of way for roads, water or gas mains, poles for electric light or power, or telephone or telegraph service. 

Q. (a) Name four customary encumbrances incident to land. (b) Name four liens on land not named above. 

A. (a) Taxes, assessments, mortgages and restrictions. (b) 

Mechanics' liens, judgments, income taxes, inheritance taxes. 

ESTATES 

Q. Is an "estate" designated as real or personal property, or may an estate be either?

A. An estate may be either real or personal property. Many estates left consist largely, sometimes exclusively, of mortgages, stocks, bonds and such holdings which are personal property. 

Q. Is an estate for life a fee simple estate? Define each.

A. No. A fee simple estate is the greatest interest one may have in real estate whereas an estate for life is an interest in real estate which lasts only as long as the life of the holder. 

Q. Is an "estate at will" simply a form of lease?

A. Yes. The rights to property are limited in accordance with the terms and conditions of the lease. 

HOMESTEADS 

(Questions and Answers)

Q. Under the laws of California what is a declaration of homestead on privately owned home? Explain benefits. How does it differ from the filing for a homestead on United States government lands?

A. A declaration of homestead is an instrument recorded in the office of the County Recorder for the purpose of setting aside certain property for the purpose of a home and protecting such part of its value as does not exceed the statutory exemption against claims of creditors. Exemption is $5,000 for head of family and $1,000 for any other person. Homestead on privately owned property covers property already acquired and upon which homestead claimant must actually reside. On government land signifies intention of becoming owner through filing of homestead and complying with requirements of government. -193-

Q. When a homestead has been properly declared and recorded by the sole owner thereof, what effect on the homestead has the owner's grant deed conveying it?

A. Owner's deed conveying title to homestead property has the effect of abandoning the homestead. 

Q. What is a homestead?

A. It consists of a dwelling house actually occupied by the claimant as his residence and the land on which the same is situated when selected and declared as provided by law. (C. C. 1237; 16 

Cal. 181.) 

Q. How is a homestead designated and established?

A. By recording in the office of the County Recorder where the land is situated a declaration of homestead properly signed and acknowledged, containing (a) a statement showing that the person making it is the head of a family and if married the name of his spouse; (b) a statement that the person making it is residing on the premises and claims the same as a homestead; (c) a description of the premises; (d) an estimate of its cash value; (e) a statement of the character of the property with sufficient detail to show that it is a proper subject of homestead. (C. C. 1244, 1263, 1267.) 

Q. By whom may a declaration of homestead be made?

A. By the head of a family or by the wife if her husband has not selected a homestead, or by any other person. (C. C. 1260, 1262.) 

Q. How may a person other than the head of a family select a homestead?

A. Must execute and acknowledge in the same manner as a grant of real property is acknowledged. (C. C. 1266.) 

Q. From what property can a homestead be selected?

A. From the community property, or separate property of husband, or by consent of the wife it may be taken from her separate estate, or from any of the property of one not married but the head of a family. (C. C. 1238; 94 Cal. 66; 76 Cal. 315.) 

Q. Who is considered the head of a family?

A. (a) The husband, or (b) every person who has residing on premises with him or her and under his or her care and maintenance, either his or her minor child, minor grandchild, minor brother, minor sister, or minor child of a deceased brother or sister, or father, mother, grandfather or grandmother of the deceased husband or wife, or an unmarried sister, or such relatives who have attained the age of majority and are unable to take care of or support themselves. (C. C. 1261.)

Q. Is there any limit placed on the value of a homestead for purposes of exemption from execution?

A. Yes, $5,000, if claimant is the head of a family and $1,000 if claimant is any other person. (C. C. 1260.) -194-

Q. What is a probate homestead?

A. A homestead set apart by the court for the use of a surviving husband or wife, and the minor children out of the common property, or of the real estate belonging to the deceased. (In re 

Noah's Estate, 73 Cal. 590, 15 P. 290, 2 Am. St. Rep. 834.)

Q. What is the difference in value of a homestead made and recorded during the married life and a probate homestead? 

A. A selected and recorded homestead cannot exceed $5,000 in value. There is no limitation as to value of probate homestead except the sound discretion of the awarding court. (Est. Walker, 108 Cal. 627; Est. Kennedy, 157 Cal. 517.)

Q. Is there any remedy for creditors when the homestead exceeds the statutory value?

A. Yes, if the application by verified petition is made by judgment creditor within sixty days after levy of execution to the superior court of the county in which the property is located for the appointment of persons to appraise the value thereof. (C. C. 

1245-1259; 79 Cal. 460; 85 Cal. 71.) 

Q. Is a homestead liable to execution?

A. It is not, excepting (a) for the satisfaction of judgment liens obtained before the declaration of homestead was filed for record; (b) on debts secured by mechanics', contractors', sub-contractors', architects', builders', laborers', material men's, or vendors' liens upon the premises; (c) on debts secured by mortgages on the premises executed and recorded before the homestead was filed for record, or (d) on debts secured by mortgage on the premises executed and acknowledged by both husband and wife or by the claimant if unmarried, and (e) taxes and special assessments. 

C. 1241; 119 Cal. 364.) (C. 

Q. Can the homestead be also used for business by the family?

A. It would not cease to be homestead property. (33 Cal. 

220; 171 Cal. 329; 103 Cal. 264; 94 Cal. 291.) 

Q. Can one file a homestead on a mining location? 

A. Yes. (98 Cal. 472.)

Q. Can a homestead be carved out of property held in a joint tenancy or tenancy in common?

A. No, unless the tenancy be between husband and wife. (156 

Cal. 195.) 

Q. Suppose the wife dies and husband remarries. second wife benefit by the homestead declaration? 26.) Would

A. No. A new declaration would have to be filed. (113 Cal. 

Q. When the selection of a homestead is made by a married person from the separate property of the spouse selecting it, in whom does the property vest upon the death of either spouse? -195-

A. The survivor. (C. C. 1265; C. C. P. 1474.) It does not pass by succession and is not subject to testamentary disposition. (178 

Cal. 54.)

Q. Suppose two sisters, both widows, resided on and owned a piece of property jointly, could they homestead it in both their names?

A. Not unless one was dependent on the other, in which case a homestead could be filed for their mutual benefit. (56 Cal. 339.) 

Q. Can the homestead of married persons be encumbered or conveyed!

A. It can if both husband and wife join in execution and acknowledgment of the written instrument. (C. C. 1242; 83 Cal. 657.) 

Q. Can the husband or wife dispose of the homestead without the consent of the other if it is taken from his or her separate property? 

A. No. (C. C. 1242, 1257.) 

Q. Can a homestead be destroyed by divorce?

A. Yes. But if the homestead was selected from the community property it may be assigned by the court to the innocent party, either absolutely or for a limited period, subject in the latter case to the future disposition of the court, or the court may divide it, or it may be sold and proceeds divided. (78 Cal. 310.) 

Q. Does removal from the property work an abandonment?

A. No. A declaration of abandonment or grant deed duly recorded is necessary to extinguish the homestead. (C. C. 12431244.) 

Q. What right has the surviving husband or wife in the homestead? In

A. It vests absolutely in the survivor except that if the homestead was selected from the separate property of either of the husband or wife, without his or her consent, it vests, on the death of the person from whose property it was selected, in his or her heirs or devisees, subject to the power of the superior court to assign it for a limited period to the family of the decedent. either case it is not subject to the payment of any debt or liability contracted by or existing against the husband and wife, or either of them, previous to or at the time of the death of such husband or wife, except as provided in the civil code. (C. C. P. 1474-1486; 

95 Cal. 397; 121 Cal. 92; 231 Pac. 371.)

Q. Of what property of deceased can the court assign a homestead permanently?

A. Only out of community property. (Est. Schmidt, 94 Cal. 334.)

Q. When may an income, other than the homestead, go to the children? -196-

A. When the widow has a maintenance derived from her own property equal to the portion set apart to her for support of the family. (C. C. P. 1464-9, 1470.)

Q. Can a wife declare a homestead partly on separate property and partly on community property? 

A. Yes. (Russell v. Langharn, 20 Fed. 2d, 95.)

Q. The declaration of the wife operates to exempt what title? 

A. The entire title owned, whatever may be the several interests of the husband and wife and the community therein. (Russell v. Langharn, 20 Fed. 2d, 95.)

Q. Suppose the property upon which a homestead is placed by a wife was purchased by funds procured by fraudulent acts of her husband.

A. The wife may not without offering to do equity to the defrauded party, enjoin a sale of the premises upon execution of a judgment in favor of the latter. (Kemp v. Enemark, 194 Cal. 748.)

Q. Suppose a woman without severing the marital relationship with her first husband, remarries and files a declaration of homestead for the joint benefit of herself and her second husband, on her death would second husband share in homestead?

A. No. (Clend v. Parker, 69 Cal. App. 685, 231 Pac. 765.) 

Q. Would a court order be necessary to protect the title of surviving spouse?

A. No, but the title of record remains, in case of death of a husband in the deceased, so that probate proceedings upon the estate of deceased are advisable in order that the record conform to the fact. (Rocha v. Rocha, 197 Cal. 396.)

Q. Does a homestead cease to exist upon death of the surviving spouse without minor children? 

A. Yes. (In re Muntz's Estate, 69 Cal. App. 404.)

Q. Suppose the survivor dies intestate does homestead cease to exist?

A. Descends to his or her heirs. (In re Muntz's Estate, 69 

Cal. App. 404.)

Q. Can a wife enjoin the sale under execution of homesteaded property to satisfy a judgment for money fraudulently obtained by the husband and expended in improvements upon property subsequently exchanged for the property upon which a homestead was declared?

A. No. (Kemp v. Enemark, 194 Cal. 748.) 

Q. A filed a homestead on ten acres a week before filing voluntary petition in bankruptcy. The tract of land was divided into two unequal parcels by a highway, on the smaller parcel a small house was maintained, on the larger parcel across the street there had been erected a small building used as a store and filling station with a few tourists' cabins which were rented out. Would -197-

the entire tract be impressed with the homestead and exempt from the creditors? 

A. Held, yes, Read (Heathman v. Holmes, 94 Cal. 291).

Q. Suppose husband and wife guaranteed a bail bond, both signed the usual agreement waiving all rights to claim any of their property, including homestead rights should an attachment follow. The bond is jumped and bonding company attaches the property. Homestead is declared immediately by owners, would it hold? 

A. Yes. Judge Gould (Superior Court) recently ruled that a guarantor's house is safe from attachment up to $5,000.00 no matter what kind of a paper he has signed to the contrary. (Torres v. Seaboard Surety Co.)

MINORS 

(See Incompetent)  

Q. Would you as a broker advise a buyer of real property to purchase same from an owner who is a minor, insane or incompetent? If so, under what conditions?

A. Yes, only if purchase made through person's guardian with permission and by order of court. 

Q. Define Minors? 

A. All persons under the age of twenty-one years. Exception 

A married woman over eighteen years of age is not legally a minor. 

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. Are mortgage and trust deed notes negotiable? What is meant by a negotiable instrument?

A. The state laws specify that mortgages and trust deed notes are negotiable. In order to be negotiable, instruments must conform to certain requirements. By a negotiable instrument is meant one which may be transferred by indorsement, giving the ultimate holder the right to collect the due sum as if he were the original payee. 

Q. Is a non-negotiable instrument transferable?

A. Yes. It may be transferred, but only subject to the defenses and offsets of previous holders. 

NOTES 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. What is meant by a joint note?

A. It is a note signed by two or more persons jointly, that is, they must assume joint responsibility for the payment of the note, and if suit is necessary, they must be sued jointly. 

Q. Define a "joint and several" note.

A. It is a note for which the makers are individually and collectively responsible for payment, and can be sued either singly or jointly. 

Q. In the case of a "joint note," what right does a maker have who has paid more than his proportionate share of the money due on the note?

A. A maker under these circumstances may sue the other makers and collect a proportionate amount of the money from them. 

Q. What is meant by endorsing a note "without recourse"?

A. Endorsing without recourse means that the endorser is passing title without any liability or guarantee. -199-

Q. What liability does a person assume who endorses a note "in blank" A. He is, in effect, making himself a guarantor of the eventual payment of the note.

Q. What is the effect of making a material alteration to a note!

A. It would make the note void unless initialed by the party adversely affected. The law specifies what constitutes a material alteration.

POSSESSION 

Q. The contract purchaser of a lot in a subdivision built and lived on said lot from time of purchase and in actual, open, exclusive and visible possession and not consistent with the record title, as his purchase contract had not been recorded. Under such conditions the record owner of the tract mortgaged same, including above referred to lot. Under such circumstances could lot purchaser lose his equity? Explain. 

A. No. Lot purchaser protected by being in possession. Anybody dealing with property must ascertain rights of party in possession. A lender must look beyond the records when he makes a loan to ascertain facts as to possession. 

"TIME IS THE ESSENCE" 

(Questions and Answers) 

Q. What is the significance of the phrase, "Time is the essence," in a contract for the sale and purchase of real estate?

A. "Time is the essence" means that the parties to the contract, in order to receive the benefit of their rights under the contract, must each carry out his part of the contract within the time specified. -200

Section V 

Escrows and Their Use

In transactions involving the sale of real property, or the borrowing of money, the repayment of which is secured by mortgages or trust deeds, some time must of necessity elapse between the finding of the proposed purchaser or lender and the final consummation of the deal. The title to the real property must be examined, and policy of title insurance must be furnished for the protection of such purchaser or mortgagee.

No one can be expected to part with his money until he has the assurance that he will receive the title to the real property involved in the form and condition agreed on; and frequently it is necessary to use the purchaser's or lender's money to pay off existing liens and encumbrances to place the title in the required condition,

It is to cover this lapse of time and to make more certain the final closing of the deal that escrows have come into favor. 

Where two or more persons deposit money and instruments with a third person, to be delivered on a certain contingency, or the happening of a certain event, such money and instruments are said to be in escrow, and the party with whom they are deposited is said to be the escrow holder. 

The escrow holder may be considered as a stake-holder, or clearing-house, where all of the parties owning estates, interests, claims or liens on property may deposit their instruments transferring or releasing their claims, and receive therefor their compensation or the amount of their demands for such conveyances or releases. The party purchasing the property, or lending the money thereon, may deposit his money in escrow, to be delivered when the escrow holder shall have received for him either the title to the property demanded, or such lien as he may be seeking. 

ESCROWS COVERING REAL PROPERTY 

Taking the simplest form of transfer as an illustration: The owner of a piece of property desires to sell, and having found a purchaser, comes into the escrow office with him. The seller brings with him such evidence of title as he may already have, and other instruments, such as fire insurance policies, etc. He executes and deposits in escrow a grant deed of the property, authorizes the issuance of a new policy of title insurance, and delivery of the deed on payment for his account of a specified sum of money within a definite time limit, and out of the proceeds thus collected authorizes the pay off of such incumbrances as may exist against the property to place it in the required condition as agreed on by the terms of the sale.

The purchaser deposits in escrow the money called for by the agreement of sale and gives authority to place that money to the account of the seller when an examination of the record title of the -201-

property shows it to be in such condition that by recording the deed, the title will vest in the purchaser in the condition required, provided the same can be done within the time specified in the escrow instructions. 

As to who is to furnish the evidence of title is a matter of custom. In nearly all parts of the United States it is customary for the seller to furnish satisfactory evidence of title and this custom prevails in Southern California.

When an escrow is started, the seller orders his policy of title insurance to show the present condition of the title, and to assure the buyer that the title is clear, or in the condition required. 

The title company begins its search of the title in the county in which the property is located, including all judgments, divorce proceedings, insanity commitments, and any and all such matters of record as would affect the title to or interest of the owners of the property in question. Often complications are met with. 

After the completion of the examination of all deeds, mortgages, judgments, etc., of record which may affect the title of the property involved, if all instruments are in hand to place the title in the condition required, the instruments are caused to be filed for record in the proper county offices, and the escrow is closed. 

The title insurance company thereupon causes the policy of title insurance (which includes a map of the property) to be written, and after this has been carefully checked, it is ready for delivery to the person for whose benefit it has been made. 

ESCROWS COVERING LOAN TRANSACTIONS 

The conditions of handling a loan escrow are very similar; that is, the party borrowing the money brings in his instruments and papers, together with the new mortgage or deed of trust and note, and authorizes their delivery upon collection of a specified sum of money for his account, out of which the escrow agent pays the charges, costs and expenses, and pays off any encumbrances necessary to be cleared to place the title in the required condition. 

The lender deposits his money, authorizing delivery thereof to the account of the borrower when the title insurance company can issue a policy of title insurance insuring the title to be in the borrower, subject to the new mortgage or deed of trust, on terms and conditions stated.

These are illustrations of the simplest forms of escrows. You can readily understand that where there is an existing encumbrance to be paid off, in case of a sale, it is necessary to have the mortgagee, who is being paid, deposit in escrow such papers and instruments as he may have in his possession, and furnish a release of the mortgage, a release of his interest in the fire insurance, etc., to be delivered when collection can be made for him the amount of the mortgage debt including interest to the date of payment. 

Likewise if there are any attachments, judgments, or other encumbrances shown by the search of the title that would be liens against the property being transferred, the holders of such encum- -202-

brances would deposit their claims in escrow, with proper satisfactions thereof, with instructions to collect the money due for such releases or satisfactions, and the instructions of the grantor would in each instance specify what amounts were to be paid for each of such releases.

There are instances in which the party acquiring the title to the property agrees to take it subject to certain existing encumbrances, in which case it is customary to secure statements from the holders of such encumbrances as to the present status of the same, and to adjust interest, etc., based on such statements. 

Then, also, there are cases where property has been leased or rented, and the rents are to be adjusted through escrow, based on statements made by the parties leasing, giving the name of the lessee, the term of the lease, the rate thereof, and to when rent is paid.

TWO GENERAL CLASSES OF ESCROWS 

There are two general classes of escrows in use at the present time-one which might be designated as an escrow based on good faith alone, and the other as a perfect or binding escrow. 

An escrow based on good faith alone does not contain the essentials of a perfect escrow, and is not one, ordinarily speaking, that could be enforced, or that is binding, until it has been acted on by the escrow holder by the delivery of the instruments and money, in accordance with the instructions, or until the conditions have been met, at which time it becomes final. 

A perfect escrow is one that contains all the necessary instructions which show a complete meeting of the minds on all of the essential requirements of the deal. If properly drawn and executed, it becomes an enforceable contract, binding on all the parties. It must be executed by all the proper parties, or if executed on their behalf, all parties so executing must have adequate written authority from the proper parties filed in the escrow, clearly authorizing the agent or attorney to act for them. 

It must contain a definite subject matter-i. e., the description of the property must be accurate and complete, sufficient to thoroughly and positively identify the property, and such as could not be confused with nor fit the description of any other parcel of land. 

A perfect escrow cannot be made where a vague and indefinite description is given.

The condition of the title must be agreed on as to the encumbrances subject to which the same is to be taken-taxes and assessments, rights-of-way, reservations, restrictions or any other matters -and the terms of any such encumbrances, showing clearly that the parties have considered the subject and that their minds have met, and that such matters have not been left open for a later agreement between them.

The amount of the consideration must be agreed on, and not be subject to any reservation of a right to change the same through any whim or fancy of either of the parties. It must be definite and -203-

not subject to a later modification or change through the separate calculations of one of the parties to the escrow, or subject to a later agreement between the parties. 

For these reasons it is necessary and advisable that all parties to an escrow should meet in the escrow office at the inception of the deal that all matters may be discussed and all questions agreed on. 

That there may be a perfect meeting of the minds when all parties are thus assembled, the parties should have with them the existing policy of title insurance, fire insurance policies, a copy of any existing lease, and any other instruments required to give the exact condition of the title, that the escrow clerk may be in a position to draft instructions that will cover all of the essential points. 

It is obvious that at this stage all instruments should be drawn, signed by the proper parties, acknowledged and placed in the escrow, together with appropriate instructions. All money should be placed in the escrow to be used in accordance with the signed escrow instructions. All this can be done if the information is in hand.

If the money and instruments are not deposited at the inception of the deal, it is manifest that after the examination of title has been completed it will be necessary to write the parties to deposit the balance of the money and instruments. This, with the time necessary to clear a check through the bank, will consume from five to ten days' additional time, depending on the promptness of the response, and if the check should chance to be on an eastern bank, it would take much longer. It is the experience of those handling escrows that over fifty per cent of the time lost in closing escrows is due to the instru ments and money not having been deposited prior to the completion of the examination of title. 

Therefore, if time is material in the closing of any deal, it can be seen that the rule of depositing the instruments and money promptly is of the greatest importance. 

ESCROW HOLDER PROTECTS ALL PARTIES 

The escrow holder is not a mere agent. It is not subject to the laws and rules governing agency. It must be a neutral party, entirely inconsistent with agency. It is in a class by itself, charged with certain responsibilities, which, in the case of a perfect escrow, make the instructions irrevocable, unless with the consent of all parties.

The escrow holder cannot make your deal for you, but can, however, be of material assistance in so drafting the escrow instructions that both sides of the escrow may have a maximum of protection, and that the intent of all parties may be clearly expressed. A complete knowledge of the laws of real property, and long experience in the handling of escrows is essential to enable the escrow holder to give this protection. 

When you take your escrows to a reliable escrow holder, you do so for the protection you believe it is able to give you, and while -204-

the escrow holder must be a neutral party, it cannot be expected to remain silent and permit the signing of instructions which do not clearly express the intent of the parties through failure on the part of someone to understand them.

A properly drafted set of escrow instructions should cover every essential point of the deal; should provide for the payment of agent's commission; should clearly set forth a summary of the entire transaction; the purchase price, the nature and amount of incumbrances existing of record and to remain; how much is to be paid in cash; how much is to be evidenced by a purchase money mortgage, or trust deed, and the full terms and conditions thereof; the date to and from which taxes, rents, and insurance, are to be adjusted, and every detail of the transaction. 

THE PROCEDURE IN MAKING AN ESCROW 

When you are ready to make an escrow, keep the following suggestions in mind: (1) Whenever possible have all the parties to the escrow meet in the escrow office.

It is quite evident how necessary it is to have all parties to the escrow meet in the escrow office, that there may be a perfect meeting of the minds, and that all escrow instructions may be made to agree in all details. With all present it is possible to discuss all angles of the deal, iron out any objections that may be raised and obviate the necessity of recalling the parties into the office for alterations and amendments, and prevent, by having a perfect meeting of the minds, the deal from afterward falling down because of a party refusing to waive some material point which afterwards develops. (2) Bring with you the title policy, fire insurance policies, and any further instruments required.

If the old title policy, fire insurance policies, etc., are brought in, there will be in hand all data necessary to draft instructions in the form of a perfect escrow. There will be no question as to the description of the property; the exceptions that are shown in the title will be known, with the book and page reference to the same; and it will not be necessary to sign instructions until all parties have satisfied themselves as to all of such exceptions that are to be shown. (3) Before the parties leave the escrow office, all new instruments should be drawn and executed, if possible. 

If you have in your possession the papers called for under the second suggestion, it will be possible to have the new instruments properly executed at once and placed in escrow, thus avoiding the chance of failure to secure the instruments later, through the parties changing their minds, leaving town, or otherwise becoming incapacitated. (4) Have all instructions fully drawn and properly signed. 

The suggestion as to having all instructions fully drawn and properly signed carries with it the suggestions that all parties agree -205-

as to just how rents shall be adjusted, how taxes shall be prorated, if necessary to prorate same; and if fire insurance is to be transferred, just what insurance it is and how it is to be prorated; and if a bill of sale is called for, just what articles are to be covered by that bill of sale. (5) Anyone acting under power of attorney, or as an authorized agent, should bring into escrow satisfactory evidence of authority.

This is an important suggestion, and must be considered seriously. Under the laws of California, any instrument conveying a right in real property, other than a lease for a term less than one year, must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged therewith. This power can be delegated, if done in accordance with the law, to an attorney in fact, but likewise, that power must be in writing, must clearly define the powers of the attorney in fact, and must be executed in due form. Certain matters may also be delegated to an agent, but those powers, likewise, when affecting title to real property and dealing with the transfer of same, must be in writing and properly executed by the proper party. To make a good and binding escrow a perfect escrow-every care should be exercised to carry out the letter and intent of the law, and to see that the escrow instructions are properly signed by persons authorized to bind the principals. (6) Each party should place in escrow at once all instruments and everything called for by the instructions. 

It is obvious that if all instruments, money, etc., are placed in escrow at once, it will save time and greatly insure the prompt and successful closing of the escrow. (7) Do not ask, expect, nor wait to be notified to bring into escrow anything that, according to the instructions, you should deposit.

The following of this suggestion will save the time of the customer, and of the escrow clerk, and assure the successful closing of the escrow. It will make it more binding on the parties to the deal, prevent unnecessary delays and lessen the possibility of one of the parties changing his mind. (8) Instructions should be read before being signed, to be sure the intention of the parties is clearly expressed. 

All instructions should be thoroughly understood, and to make certain that they are, they should be read carefully by the persons signing them. If there are any questions, or if the meaning of the instructions is not clear, or the intent not properly expressed, the time to make such corrections is prior to signing. (9) Do not attempt to modify, alter or change your instructions to the possible detriment of the other parties to the escrow. 

It is obvious that an agreement between two parties, made in good faith and for a consideration, cannot be altered, modified or changed by one person without the consent of the other. (10) Do not forget that every delay on the part of anyone delays work on the escrow. -206-

(11) Answer all communications relative to your escrow promptly.

When it is necessary to communicate with the parties to the escrow, a prompt reply will facilitate the early closing of the transaction. When you receive a communication relative to an escrow, every half day saved in giving it attention will be a half day saved in the closing of the escrow.

STATEMENT OF IDENTITY 

Q. What is the purpose of the statement of Identity?

A. To give title companies facts regarding the personal history of the parties to a real estate transaction to facilitate the issuance of title policies or other instruments pertinent to the transaction at hand.

ESCROWS 

Before going to escrow, the broker should Have a complete meeting of the minds and agreement between buyer and seller.

Have a complete description of the property, including exact street address and legal description. Description should be procured from a prior deed, or prior policy of title insurance. 

Have complete information regarding taxes, insurance, rents, encumbrances and interest thereon, and how amortized. 

Have the complete name and address of the principals to the transaction, including the name and address of any encumbrance holder.

Know how the buyers wish to take title, i. e., in severalty, in joint tenancy or tenancy in common. 

Have the sellers take to the escrow their last tax receipt, their records of the encumbrance, if any, their insurance policies on the -208-

property, old title or old deed, rent statement and OPA statements, if income property.

It frequently happens that the seller is a surviving joint tenant, in which case the following procedure is necessary: 

1. Procure a certified copy of death certificate. 

2. Procure an affidavit terminating Joint Tenancy. 

The certified copy of death certificate is then attached to the affidavit and filed in the escrow for recording. 

3. Procure an inheritance tax release; the Inheritance Tax 

Office require the following: 

A. A copy of the title report.

B. Any tax receipt covering the property involved. 

C. An Inheritance Tax Affidavit, Form No. 22 (said form can be procured at any escrow office.)

The Inheritance Tax release should then be filed with the escrow.

In the case of a sale of the property, the customary charges of the seller are:

Title policy charge 

Seller's escrow fee

Drawing any documents he executes Recording any documents in his favor 

Revenue stamps Notarization crow. 

Insurance transfer fees.

The customary charges of the buyer are: 

Buyer's escrow fee

Recording any documents in his favor Drawing any documents he executes 

Notarization 

Insurance mortgage clauses.

In the case of a loan, the borrower pays all expense of the es In paying off an HOLC loan, it is well to have the owner of the property sign a letter directed to the HOLC, advising them that it is his desire that the loan be paid. Otherwise, the escrow holder will write to the HOLC for their papers and demand; the HOLC will then write to the owner asking whether it is his desire that the loan be paid; the owner will then write the HOLC that it is his desire, and the HOLC will then furnish their demand to the escrow. 

Considerable delay is occasioned by the correspondence back and forth.

The broker should carry a complete copy of all original escrow instructions, of the principals to the transaction, for the reason that the principals will refer to their broker regarding any question that might come up relative to their escrow. -209-

Q. Deal was closed as of March 31. Seller was to adjust and prorate with buyer following terms: ($2,000 mortgage at 7% interest, payable quarterly from January 1; $5,000 insurance policy, rate 

80c per $100, paid for three years from January 1; taxes for fiscal year which begins July 1, $150. Show in figures how adjustments were made. 

A. Buyer should pay: Insurance premium for balance of period from March 31, 2 years and nine months, $36.67; taxes, March 31 to June 30, inclusive, $37.50; a total of $74.17. 

Seller should pay: Interest on mortgage from January 1 to 

March 31, $35; insurance from January 1 to March 31, $3.33; a total of $38.33.

Escrow holder will enter debits and credits to take care of these adjustments.. 

Q. Does the escrow system used in California eliminate the need for real estate brokers and salesmen to understand the rudimentary principles of agency and conveyancing? Discuss. 

A. No. The escrow is primarily for carrying out instructions, not to give advice. Too many agents take a transaction to escrow with the hope that the escrow officer will "tuck in the loose ends" in other words, close the sale or exchange. Furthermore, some transactions are not escrowed, and responsibility for a clear understanding of the transaction falls upon the agent. Without knowledge of the rudimentary laws of conveyancing the agent can do much harm to his clients.

Q. What is the purpose of an escrow, and when is it completed!

A. To facilitate the safe and efficient handling of monies and instruments involved in a sale or transfer of real property. Complete when instructions are mutally agreed upon, signed and fully complied with, by all parties to the transaction. 

Q. How would you protect buyer against possibility of having to pay seller's personal property tax which may be attached to real property, when the buyer is assuming taxes made payable in the future?

A. A condition that would arise only with sales made between the first Monday in March and third Monday in October. A settlement of this item in escrow, based perhaps on previous year's levy, would expedite and be most satisfactory. 

Q. In agreeing to prorate the taxes "now a lien and payable hereafter," from what date should they be pro rated?

A. County taxes and municipal taxes, if collected therewith, should be pro rated from July 1st. -210-
