Section VI Title Insurance TITLE SEARCH 

Most land titles in private ownership in the United States, were derived from the Federal or State Governments. In California and some other western states titles to real estate in many cases antedate the patent and must be traced back to the original owner who came into possession over a hundred years ago, when great ranchos were granted to "caballeros" by Spain and Mexico. Every deedevery transaction-affecting land from the time of the patent or the grant must be authentic, or present day titles are jeopardized! It is the assembling of these records-plus the added security of title insurance that protects you from loss of investment. 

COVERAGE 

A Policy of Title Insurance insures against loss which the insured may suffer, not only by reason of any defects arising upon the face of the records, but indemnifies him as well for loss which may arise as the result of the forgery of any recorded instrument, or by reason of false personation of a party to an instrument.

Title Insurance also protects against risks of former bankruptcies, former moratoria, and former tax sales; defects in former foreclosure proceedings, former judgments and former United States tax liens, and—against the risks occasioned by recent legislation. 

TITLE PLANT 

Because of the complexity of land title records, a title company cannot give adequate, efficient service, and proper protection, without a title plant. To attempt to do so is to invite disaster to the company and to those it purports to protect. A title plant is an index to all county, state, and Federal Government and certain municipal records that must be located and examined before the title to a property can be properly determined. These records are found in many different offices and courts. A title plant is never finished. 

Each day these records grow, and countless lawsuits are filed affecting land titles. Every year taxes are levied-land is sold for delinquent taxes or is redeemed from delinquent tax sales; every session of the legislature, every session of Congress, adds to the great mass of law affecting real estate; the courts are continuously rendering decrees affecting land ownership.

Each day every title company must keep abreast of this great mass of new recordings, new laws, new lawsuits, new decisions, and each day all these events must be noted in the title plant. The plant must be complete in order that title policies can be issued, correctly reflecting the condition of each title at the very minute that any transaction is completed. Unceasingly the task of keeping those records complete goes on, so that a service may be rendered, and a protection afforded to purchasers of land and to lenders who make loans with land as security. -240

-- 
SUPERVISION 

Title Insurance companies are controlled by state insurance laws. They are required to deposit cash or securities with the state and in addition to set apart a "title insurance surplus fund” as a 'guarantee fund" for the payment of losses. This is the additional assurance of protection you have in dealing with a Title Insurance Company. In the State of California are the most efficient, complete, and responsible companies in the United States issuing title insurance. They give the utmost in security and protection—yet the cost of this insurance in California is less than in any other state in which comparable insurance is written. 

Q. Is it safe for a buyer of real property to accept a deed not based upon a search of title? Explain your answer.

A. No. For the protection of the buyer it is necessary that a search of title be made to determine whether grantor in deed is owner of property and the nature of liens and encumbrances against it.

Q. In California who customarily pays for usual policy of title insurance?

A. In Northern California buyer ordinarily pays. In Southern California it is customary for seller to pay for cost of bringing title down to date of delivery of deed and buyer pays new owner's fee for showing title in his name and charge for showing in title any mortgage or deed of trust given as part of purchase price. 

Q. Purchaser wanted the title insurance raised $10,000 above the purchase price of the lot which he intended improving. Who should pay for vesting title in buyer and paying for the added guarantee of title? Explain. 

A. Buyer would pay for charges as he is one who will receive protection.

Q. (a) What added protection does a policy of title insurance give over a mere guarantee of title? (b) What, if any, exceptions are noted in a policy of title insurance against which a purchaser of a mortgage is not protected?

A. A guarantee of title is based solely upon the public records and does not insure against any latent defects in any instrument or in any link of the chain of title not disclosed by such records. Policy of title insurance is broader in its terms, in that it goes beyond the mere record title, and, unless qualified by exceptions, insures the actual title and ownership of the property against all defects in chain of title. It is particularly desirable because it protects against forgery. (b) Depends upon form of policy. Some policies do not insure against rights of parties in possession unless disclosed by public records, protect against violation of building restrictions or zoning ordinances, or as to position of building with respect to lot lines. -241-

COVERAGE OF POLICIES OF TITLE INSURANCE THE JOINT PROTECTION POLICY INSURES BOTH 

the owner of land and the insured owner of any indebtedness secured by a mortgage or deed of trust thereon against loss or damage not exceeding a stated amount which any insured may sustain by reason of the title being vested otherwise than as set forth in the policy, or by reason of unmarketability of such title, or by reason of any defect in the execution, insofar as it af fects the lien or charge upon the land, of any insured mortgage or deed of trust, or by reason of defect in, or lien or encumbrance on the title other than as shown.in the policy. 

This policy does not insure against any facts which a correct survey or inspection of the land would show, claims or title to water, water rights, mining claims, rights or claims of parties in possession of the land, liens or encumbrances not disclosed by the records, or against the effect of governmental regulations, such as zoning ordinances.

Insurance against these matters may be secured under the fullcoverage policies hereinafter described, or by the elimination of one or more of the standard exceptions.

The insurance under this policy insures to the benefit of the successor in ownership of any indebtedness and any owner thereof who acquires the land by foreclosure or other legal manner in satisfaction of the debt.

FULL-COVERAGE FEE POLICY 

Insures the owner and lender, or either.

It eliminates all exceptions except the one relating to governmental regulations.

It has all the advantages of the Joint Protection form, and, in addition, includes insurance of survey and insurance against: mechanic's liens and similar unrecorded liens or encumbrances. rights of parties in possession, violation of conditions, restrictions, encroachments, and overlaps of improvements.

STANDARD LOAN FORM 

is used by many banks, building and loan companies, and other lenders of money. It insures lenders only against loss or damage not exceeding a stated amount which the insured lender may sustain by reason of the title being vested otherwise than as set forth in the policy, or by reason of unmarketability of such title, or by reason of any defect in the execution of the mortgage or -242-

deed of trust insofar as it affects the lien or charge on the land, or by reason of defect in, or lien or encumbrance on the title other than as shown in the policy. 

This policy does not insure against any facts which a correct survey or inspection of land would show, claims or title to water, water rights, mining claims, rights or claims of parties in possession of the land, liens or encumbrances not disclosed by the records, or against the effect of governmental regulations, such as zoning ordinances.

Insurance against these matters may be secured under a fullcoverage policy, or by the elimination of one or more of the standard exceptions.

The insurance under this policy inures to the benefit of the successor in ownership of the indebtedness and any owner thereof who acquires the land by foreclosure or other legal manner in satisfaction of the debt. 

"AMERICAN TITLE ASSOCIATION” POLICY 

The "American Title Association" standard form policy is a full-coverage loan form in which all exceptions are eliminated, except the one relating to governmental regulations. 

It includes insurance of survey, insurance against mechanics' liens, and other unrecorded liens or encumbrances, rights of parties in possession, existing violations of covenants, conditions, and restrictions, encroachments, and overlaps of improvements.

This form of policy is required by most non-resident lenders, life insurance companies, mortgage companies, and financial institutions lending money on real estate in California, and is preferred by many local lenders. -243-

Section VII Land Measurements  

Among the changes recently incorporated in both broker and salesmen's examinations is a test of the applicant's knowledge of 

"LAND MEASUREMENTS"-township and section maps. 

PUBLIC LANDS-HOW DIVIDED AND DESCRIBED: Pub lic domain of United States is divided by North and South lines, 6 miles apart, into strips called RANGES; these strips are again divided by East and West lines, 6 miles apart, into squares (36 square miles) called TOWNSHIPS.

RANGES are numbered East and West from some principal meridian; TOWNSHIPS are numbered both North and South from a certain Base Line. 

There are 36 sections in each township, numbered "1" from

N/E, corner consecutively West, then back on second tier East, then West on third tier, etc., alternating direction in each tier, No. 

36 being the S/E section.

A TOWNSHIP contains 36 sections-a section contains 640 

acres, or one square mile.

In California there are three points from which surveys are made-Humboldt Peak Base and Meridian line in Northern California; Mt. Diablo Base and Meridian line in Central California and the San Bernardino Base and Meridian line in Southern California. Surveys from these points cover the entire State. 

Study of these charts and practice on the following questions will prepare you for similar questions in the examination. 

Q. How many square feet in an acre? 

A. 43,560.

Q. Plot all sections in a township. By this is meant to draw a township and number the sections correctly. Start in N/E corner with "1" and end in S/E corner with 36, as is done on chart. 

Q. Indicate (in pencil) on Township and Section plots the location of the following described 20 acre parcel of land. N½ of 

S/E 14 of S/W 14 of Section 6. Simply "black out." 

Q. Refer to "map of section" on page showing "LAND

MEASUREMENTS." And describe the 5-acre parcel in the N/E 

corner. 

A. East 5 acres of N/E 14 of N/E 4 of N/E 14 of Section. 

Q. How many acres in the N/E ¼ of the S/E 4 of a Section? 

A. 40 acres. 

Q. (Refer to Township plot.) A railroad right-of-way cut diagonally across the S/E corner of Township, entering at exactly the N/E corner of Section 13 and leaving at exactly the S/W corner -244-

of Section 35. Approximately how many acres are there in the wedge-shaped piece of land thus formed? 

A. A total of four sections of 640 acres each or 2,560 acres. 

METES AND BOUNDS 

Q. When is land generally described by "Metes and Bounds"?

A. Legal description by "metes and bounds" are used when the property referred to, is not covered by a duly recorded map or where it is in such shape as to make it impracticable to describe by section, township and range. "Metes and bounds" descriptions are sometimes used, and are perfectly legal, in connection with property which could be legally described otherwise. 

Q. Is the front line of the property measured from the curb line or inside of the sidewalk?

A. City lots are measured from inside of sidewalk. Farm lands (not subdivided) which are described by section, township and range, from center of road.

Section VIII Land Economics and Appraising  

Q. Define a market value.

A. In a California court case, Sacramento Southern R. R. Company v. Heilbron, 156 Cal. 408, the following definition was given; it is often used in expert testimony regarding value: "Market value is the highest price estimated in terms of money which the land will bring if exposed for sale in the open market, with a reasonable time allowed to find a purchaser, buying with full knowledge of all the uses and purposes to which it is adapted, and for which it is capable of being used." 

Comment: There are many definitions of market value, none of them perfect, and there is much confusion of thought on the subject. Similar terms are also used, such as fair market value, fair cash market value, intrinsic value, justified value, use value, utility value, warranted value, or merely the one word, value. All of these expressions, in a general non-technical sense, may be considered to mean the same as market value. Expert witnesses in 

California courts are accustomed to use the term, market value; appraisers, outside of court, often use the expression, warranted value; and many real estate dealers use the words, fair cash market value. 

Q. Distinguish between market value and market price.

A. Market value, as defined above, is based, in part, upon the following elements: 

1. Fair efforts to sell, with proper publicity; being "exposed for sale." 

2. Not under forced conditions, but "in the open market.' 

3. "A reasonable time allowed to find a purchaser." In a prolonged depression, "a reasonable time" might be construed to be a long period. 

4. "Buying with full knowledge of all the uses and purposes" a fully informed purchaser, who takes into consideration the highest and best use (the most profitable use) of the property. 

Market value may or may not be equal to market price. The price merely reflects the market level at a particular time and generally is not based upon all of the four elements outlined above. 

A conclusion and opinion as to market price is based, in part, upon asking prices, selling prices, and offers to buy. It contemplates an actual sale of the property at a price which may be higher or lower than its market value. 

On a distressed market, the typical buyer will not buy at the market value but at price lower than the market value, because it is not an "open market. 

During a boom, the typical seller will not accept a price equal to the market value as he expects to get a price which is higher -249-

than the market value. Under such conditions, market prices may be temporarily set by speculators, or other purchasers, lacking information on real market values, or failing to exercise intelligent judgment in the matter.

Over a period of years, the market values of a property may be represented by a smooth line on a chart indicating long-time trend of values, while the market prices of the property may be represented by a series of lines, irregular in direction, sometimes above and sometimes below this smooth line. 

Q. What is the difference between buying property on specu lation and on investment basis?

A. Speculation involves risk in the hope of making a profit. 

Property is bought on speculation with the intent of reselling at a profit. The incentive is to attain an appreciation of principal rather than mere security. Investment represents a quest for safety of principal and assured regularity of income. 

Q. Agent advised patron to purchase newly built_garage, terms as follows: Price, $12,000 (lot was 50x100 feet, and valued at $5,000). First mortgage to be assumed, $6,000 at 7 % interest. 

Trust deed second lien, $3,000 at 8% interest. For how much must the garage rent to assure buyer at least 8% net interest on his investment? Analyze answer.

A. Assuming property is to earn 8% net per annum on the actual cash investment of the owner, the garage should bring in a gross rent of $1,704.32 per year. Analysis: 

Interest on $6,000 mortgage at 7%..... $ 420.00 

Interest on $3,000 trust deed at 8%.. 240.00 

Interest on $3,000 equity at 8%...... 240.00 

Taxes 12% of $12,000..... 180.00 

Repairs 1% of value of bldg. only, $7,000... 

Depreciation on bldg. 4% of $7,000... 70.00 280.00 

Fire Insurance 80c, 3 yrs. rate......... 18.67

.$1,448.67

Allowing for vacancy of 15% of gross annual rent. $1,448.67 is 85% of income which must be received. 

Divide $1,448.67 by 85 is $17.0432 or 1% of necessary income. 

Multiply by 100 is $1,704.32 or 100% of necessary total income.

Q. What benefit is it to a city to limit by law the height of buildings in the business section?

A. Height restrictions prevent traffic congestion, stabilize land value over a wide area, insure better light to buildings in district and make fire-fighting easier.

Q. What are the parties to a lease called, and define each. 

A. Lessor and lessee. Lessor is an owner (or tenant) who leases property. Lessee is a person or organization to whom property is leased. -250-

Q. What, if any, difference in rate of interest should be expected from lease of ground, and of improvements thereon? Explain.

A. A higher rate is justified on improvements because of greater risk, wear and tear, and a larger burden of management. 

Rate on buildings usually about 2 points higher than on land. 

Q. Smith owns a corner in the path of rapid business development which he wishes to bequeath to his children. He had opportunity to lease it for ten years for gas filling station at $1,800 per annum straight or from year to year at $1,200 per annum. 

As an agent, what would you advise Smith?

A. Would advise Smith to employ a competent appraiser to make a study of the property and report as to the earning expectancy of the property during the next ten years, under its highest and best use.

Q. Enumerate interior changes usually necessary to make, in an old office building, to delay its obsolescence to point of its economic usefulness.

A. Install modern high-speed elevators, modern lighting fix tures, improve appearance of entrance, and thoroughly redecorate interiors, clean outside of building and place in hands of competent building manager.

Q. What provision should be made in a lease of stores and office rooms to protect lessor against undesirable sublessees? 

A. Include covenants in the lease against subletting without owner's consent in writing. 

Q. Store building on Lot "C" 50x100 feet is leased at rate $40 per front foot. A small store 15x25 feet on portion of Lot "D" adjoining first store referred to is for rent or lease. What would seem a fair rental for the smaller store? Show figures. 

A. Building on Lot "D" is only 25 feet deep. According to ratio of value of 25 foot lot to lot 100 feet in depth, as shown by typical depth tables, building on Lot "D" should rent for 37.5 per cent of Lot "C" or at $15 per front foot. 

Q. How would you determine, by a simple process, the ground value per front foot in the center of a block which is all built up with modern stores of varying sizes and heights in the central business district?

A. (1) Estimate value of building in its present condition. (2) Ascertain or estimate stabilized gross rentals of property making due allowance for vacancies. (3) Ascertain taxes. (4) Ascertain insurance. (5) Estimate depreciation on building based upon its probable remaining economic life. (6) Estimate maintenance and management expenses, etc. (7) Compute interest on present worth of building, say at 7 to 12% per annum, using rate justified by risk involved in investment. (8) Compute net income by deducting items 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, from item 2. This net income represents earnings of the land. (9) Compute value of land by capitalizing net- -251-

income at current interest rate, say 5, 6, or 7%, using rate justified by risk involved in investment. (10) Compute value per front foot by dividing total value of lot so found by its width.

Q. Agents were predicting a probable resale of the lots in their single family subdivision for laborers in nearby factories. 

Initial prices averaged about $2,000 per lot. Discuss the possibilities of their resale predictions.

A. Resale possibilities at profit not founded on facts. Original price is too high for the purpose. Prices on resale will undoubtedly be lower than original selling prices. 

Q. What is meant by "percentage" basis of fixing rents?

Discuss its advantages to lessee and to lessor. Offset this by pointing out disadvantages.

A. A "percentage" lease is one under which the amount of rent to be paid by tenant is a fixed percentage of his gross sales. 

Advantages: 1. Percentage lease offers a compromise between tenant's and owner's differences regarding rental values. 

2. Percentage lease does not lend itself to speculation. 3. It encourages the proper utilization of real estate. 

Disadvantages: 1. Success under percentage lease is dependent on tenant. The tenant may die or become incapacitated. 

He may be content with a modest business and lie down on the job without being penalized as under regular lease. 2. It encourages tenants who are not trained merchants to take a chance at the expense of the property owner. 3. There is no percentage lease written that a dishonest tenant cannot take advantage of. 

Q. What factors force small specialty shops to the fringes of highest rental value districts?

A. Small volume of sales with corresponding high percentages of overhead expense. -252-

Q. About how much purchase value per 100 persons is usually attributed to sidewalk traffic in shopping districts? 

A. Approximately $2 for each 100 persons passing store.

Q. (a) What are customary street widths in typical average residential districts? (b) How much does it usually cost per square foot for hard-surface paving? (c) How much is the usual assessment for paving per fifty-foot lot? (d) About what is cost of putting in sidewalk and curb per fifty-foot lot?

A. (a) Sixty feet between property lines. (b) Five-inch about 

20c per square foot. (c) Assuming street forty feet wide between curbs, area charged against fifty-foot lot would be 20x50 or 1,000 square feet at about 20c would be approximately $200. (d) Approximately $50.

Q. What is the relative value to shops of volume of pedestrian traffic to character of such traffic?

A. The type of pedestrian traffic is very important. Sites which are passed by poorer classes or by those not in a buying mood are not so valuable. A high-class retail store could not be conducted profitably in a poor section; nor the average cheap store to best advantage in an exclusive section. 

Q. Proprietor of men's clothing store agreed to pay rental on basis of 6% gross receipts. Sidewalk traffic averaged 2,000 persons per hour of 8-hour day and 26 days per month. Careful check showed value to merchant of this traffic to be at rate of $2.00 per 

100 persons per hour. Show by figures how much rent tenant should pay for use of store. 

A. Sidewalk traffic is 16,000 persons per 8-hour day. Gross receipts at $2 for each 100 persons equals $320 per day, or $8,320 per month of 26 days. 6% of gross receipts is $499.20 per month, the amount of rent which should be paid. 

Q. When a lease of ground is for only 10 years, what other income from the improvements lessee erects must he obtain over and above taxes, ground rent and maintenance, in order to avoid loss?

A. In addition to items mentioned, rent should be sufficient to cover: (1) Interest on capital invested, that is, on amount expended in erecting and financing on building. (2) An amount sufficient to amortize cost of building (or whatever loss on building lessee will sustain) during term of lease. (3) A sufficient amount over and above all the foregoing charges to compensate the operator for his services and the risk involved in the undertaking. 

Q. When a vacant lot is leased what customary safeguard does lessor require to guarantee payments?

A. Lessor should require lessee to furnish surety bond to guarantee payment of rent and the erection of any building agreed to be built by lessee. Sometimes in lieu of bond, lessee deposits securities or cash in escrow. -253-

Q. Upon what premise or basis of income to owner of property is a long-term lease made? 

A. Long-term lease is made on basis of yielding the owner a reasonable net return over the period of lease. Five or six per cent net to owner (not including income and inheritance taxes) is usually considered reasonable return on land leased for a long period. 

Q. Customer had $15,000 to invest in, preferably, a garage. 

Agent found suitable site 50x100 feet. Also found tenant who would take secured lease and pay $175 per month rent for 5 years. (a) How much should the garage cost to build? (b) How much could be allowed for lot? (c) How much and what items should be allowed for carriage and overhead? (d) After these deductions, what net interest would the $15,000 investment be earning? 

A. (a) One-story brick garage to cover lot would cost about $9,000 or 60% of investment. (b) $6,000 or 40% of investment. (c) Taxes, 12% on $15,000........... 

Repairs, 1% on $9,000...... 

Depreciation, 4% of $9,000.

Q. Name three prime needs of an industrial building site. 

A. Transportation facilities, ample water supply, proximity to markets and location that is favorable with respect to labor. 

Q. In subdividing a forty-acre tract, about how many fiftyfoot lots could be properly secured? Explain. 

A. Allowing five lots, 50x125 feet per acre, forty acres would develop into 200 lots. If lots cut to 50x100 about six lots per acre, or 240 lots total. These calculations assume street sixty feet in width between property lines. 

Q. Here are two adjoining subdivisions; both have identical street improvements, and lots are equal in size. (a) One is building up with homes costing an average of $4,000 each-the minimum restrictions. The other tract has minimum building restrictions of $6,000 single family homes. In which tract should lots sell higher? 

Why? (b) About what will be the maximum economic value of lots in each tract during its present restricted use? 

A. (a) Lots should sell higher in tract carrying the higher restrictions since value of lots should be in proportion to the value of the improvements. (b) According to surveys made in Los Angeles and Southern California, lots valued at $2,500 or less should represent about 32% of property value; lots valued from $2,500 to $5,000 about 36%. On this basis, a $4,000 house would represent 

68% of total value of property, which is $5,882. Value of lot is then 32% or $1,882. Similarly, $6,000 equals 64% of $9,375, value of property. Value of lot then is $3,375. -254

Q.

(a) Why should close-in single family building restrictions 

in fast-growing city be limited in years to time estimated to practically build up the tract? (b) And how can such restrictions be extended if desirable?

A. (a) A restriction should not extend into the future so far as to prevent or impede the proper economic utilization of the property for a different use when the normal change of conditions brings about the need. (b) By recording of a new set of restrictions executed by the owners of the property to be protected. All other persons having an interest in the property will need to give consent to new restrictions. Restrictions should be drawn by competent attorney co-operating with a title company since search of title will be required to ascertain names of all parties having an interest in the properties. 

Q. What price residence would you recommend to a family consisting of husband and wife and two children, the sole support of the family being the husband's income which is $150 per month? Explain.

A. Price of home should not exceed two and one-half times annual income. Would recommend property costing about $3,800 to $4,000, for house and lot. 

Q. (a) In what way do zoning ordinances encumber real property? (b) Are they beneficial? Explain.

A. Zoning regulates use to which property may be put; may establish maximum height of any building, may regulate percentage of lot areas to be covered, or establish minimum lot areas. (b) Yes, usually so. Zoning ordinances tend to stabilize values and contribute generally to the comfort, health and prosperity of the community. They are a modern economic necessity. 

Q. Gross income of furnished ten-unit apartments was at rate of $8,400 per annum. Lot fairly worth $15,000; apartment new, and cost $30,000; furnishings cost $5,000; total investment, $50,000. (a) Name six major items of proper deduction from the gross income to indicate the net income. (b) Show what amount represents the net income. (c) What rate of net income upon the value does the property earn?

A. (a) Taxes, insurance, repairs, depreciation on furniture, depreciation on buildings, vacancies: 

Taxes, 1% on $50,000.. 

Fire Insurance, 27c per $100 per year.. 

Depreciation on building ($30,000 value). 

Repairs, 1% on building... $ 750.00 94.50 1,000.00 300.00 

Depreciation on furniture (allowing 7 yrs. life).. 714.00 Vacancies-15%

(b) $4,281.50. (c) 8.56 per cent. 

1,260.00 .$4,118.50 -255-

Q. Agent advised novice buyer to build duplex bungalow of four rooms per, on lot 50x125 feet, selling for $10,000. The street was rapidly building up with two to four story flats. What would you have advised?

A. Land too high for duplex. If demand justifies, should build flats that are in keeping with neighborhood as to size, cost and design.

Q. The gross income of certain unfurnished flats is $3,600 per annum. Name four items of proper deduction in order to ascertain the net income of these flats, and what per cent of income do you allow for (1) vacancies, (2) management, (3) depreciation, 

(4) maintenance. 

A. Items of deduction and percentages estimated as follows: 

(1) Taxes 1% of total value per year. (2) Insurance, 27c per $100 per year. (3) Depreciation, 4% of building value per year. (4) Vacancies, 15%. (5) Repairs, 1% of building value per year. (6) Management, including collection of rents 5% of gross rents. 

Q. Name five items of proper deduction from the gross income to determine the net income of a furnished apartment house when lot is also conveyed. 

A. Taxes, repairs, insurance, depreciation and vacancies. 

Q. About what may be the maximum market value of a 50x120 foot lot in a workingman's tract building up with $2,500 houses? 

Explain. 

A. According to surveys made in Los Angeles and Southern 

California, lots valued at approximately $2,500 or less should represent about 32% of complete property value. On this basis above $2,500 house would represent 68% of total value of property, which is $3,676. Value of lot is then 32% or about $1,176. 

Q. If gross income from furnished flats is $900 per month, name the items of proper deduction to ascertain what the net income is when you are listing the lease and sale of furnishings only. 

A. Taxes, insurance and depreciation on furniture and furnishings, management, vacancies, rent, janitor, water, light and power, telephone, advertising and general repairs and maintenance expense, except as to exterior of building. 

Q. Having sold the lease and furnishings of an apartment house, recite in chronological order, beginning with taking a deposit, how to close the deal. 

A. Take deposit, draw deposit receipt, have signed by seller and buyer, get agreement for commission. Then upon collecting balance of purchase price deliver bill of sale, copy of lease duly assigned, fire-insurance policy properly assigned, rent statement and keys, to buyer. Then make adjustments of rents, taxes and other items of expense as agreed upon. Notify tenants of new owner and give up possession.

Q. 

What is meant by "The City Directional Growth" and what effect does it have upon real estate values?

-256-

A. "The City Directional Growth" refers to the manner and direction in which a city tends to grow. Property in the direction of growth in different sections of a city tends to increase in value, especially if growth is steady and rapid. 

Q. (a) When do County-state taxes become a lien? (b) When is first installment due and payable?

A. (c) When does first installment become delinquent? (d) In what month does second installment become due? (e) When does second installment become delinquent? (a) First Monday in March at noon. (b) November 1st. (c) December 5th. (d) January 20th. (e) April 20th.

Q. To ascertain the net income of property, what are the main items usually charged against the gross income of such property? 

A. Taxes, insurance, depreciation, repairs, vacancies, management.

Q. What do the state housing laws require with respect to building a home near the dividing lot lines? (b) Why then is a lot only 25 feet wide undesirable for residential purposes in a typical tract?

A. (a) Require four feet between side of building and lot line if windows on that side; eaves may project eight inches beyond side of buildings. If no windows, building may be built up to lot line. (Eaves must not overhang adjoining lot.) (b) If windows on both sides, house could only be seventeen feet wide. A 25 foot lot would not permit very good room arrangement in one story house. Lower floors likely to be dark in two story home on this width lot.

Q. By what public procedure are street improvements and other utilities often installed? Enumerate the main features of at least two public improvement acts.

A. Through procedure conducted under provisions of public improvement acts. See Street Improvement. 

Q. What would you examine to justify owner's listing price of two homes of equal floor space on equal size lots in the same subdivision, one house at $8,000 and the other at $10,000? 

A. Design and construction of buildings, plan of houses, character of workmanship, condition of building and interior fixtures, number of bath rooms, quality of plumbing, heating, and electric fixtures, interior decoration, lawn and landscaping, kind of roof. 

Q. How would you determine the true value of a home you are listing?

A. Determine value of lot and present value of building after making due allowance for depreciation. Compare value so determined with value of similar properties in immediate neighbor- -257-

hood. Check as to actual sales and assessed values of the properties used in comparison. Estimate cost of replacement and deduct for age.

Q. What is meant by set-back building ordinances or restrictions?

A. A set-back ordinance is one passed by the county or city to establish the distance buildings must set back from front property line on the streets which are subject to the ordinance. Setback is not necessarily uniform.

Q. Why is it bad practice to sell old people lots in a tract in their expectation of resale for profit?

A. Because vacant lots yield no income and are an expense to carry. If not sold at a profit, may work hardship on owners. 

Q. How can subdivider help to enhance value of lots in the tract?

A. By installing improvements and utilities, by placing restrictions and enforcing same, by building a few houses to start and influence development. 

Q. What precaution would you take in selling a person a lot on easy terms?

A. Satisfy yourself that prospective buyer understands contract and is able to handle payments. 

Q. On what grounds could you safely predict resale of lots in a subdivision at a profit?

A. It is very unwise and hazardous to make any positive prediction or promise as to the probable resale of a property at a profit. If business conditions in community are good, population in district constantly increasing, subdivision in hands of a concern having good reputation, lots well located and property restricted, street improvements and public utilities in and original selling prices moderate, it is reasonable to believe that favorable and satisfactory turn-over can be made, but avoid an absolute promise, (and trouble).

Q. After the subdivider has sold out his tract who can enforce the tract restrictions?

A. Lot owners, provided restrictions were properly imposed. 

Q. Should assessment to be assumed against a lot be figured in as part of the purchase price? Explain.

A. Yes. Assessment assumed must be paid by buyer and should be added to purchase price.

Q. Name some advantages to a lot purchaser, also some objections to street and other improvements having to be assumed. 

A. Lots subject to assessments are usually sold on smaller down payment. Default in payment of assessments will cause entire unpaid balance of assessment to become due and payable and buyer might lose equity in foreclosure of assessment. Added payments to keep up assessments may make undue burden on buyer. -258-

Q. What improvements should be installed in a high class residential subdivision where building restrictions call for houses costing upward of $7,500? 

A. Pavement, sidewalk, sewer, public utilities and trees (if they are to be cared for during building up of subdivision). 

Q. What minimum improvements are necessary to be installed before a lot can be used for residential purposes? 

A. Reasonably good streets and water. 

Q. What is a "key" lot? Why is it less preferred and how can its objection be overcome by subdivider and by builder upon the "key" lot?

A. A "key" lot is one that adjoins a corner lot, but at right angles to same and fronting on the intersecting street. The greatest objection to the "key" lot is the possible disregard of the corner owner to agreeably care for or improve the rear of his lot; this can be overcome by the subdivider imposing certain restrictions on the corner lot as to the placement of and location of improvements and plantings. Builder on "key" lot can lessen objections by plan of house, position of driveway and shrubbery. 

Q. Name the compass exposures or fronts in their order considered preferred for corner lots in residence property. Explain reasons.

A. A question to bring forth a host of answers and arguments, both for and against. While in the East and Mid-West, the South and East fronts are the most preferred, the California buyers find an equal desirability for West and North fronts, especially if there is a valley or mountain view involved. The answer should resolve itself to the particular wishes of the buyer we have in hand, or the particular corner property we are trying to sell. 

Q. Assuming all street work paid in full how much, if any, more is corner residence lot generally worth than inside of equal size?

A. If purely residential property, approximately 20% more than same size inside lot.

Q. (a) Why should close-in single family building restrictions in fast-growing city be limited in years to time estimated to practically build up the tract? (b) And how can such restrictions be extended if desirable?

A. (a) To provide a higher use for property, when demand arrives. (b) Restrictions can be extended by united action of owners in tract. 

Q. By what authority and by what method of financing are tract public improvements often installed, and which requires lot purchasers to assume the assessment?

A. Improvements are usually installed under provisions of improvement bonding acts by authority of County Board of Supervisors or City Council. -259-

Q. Name the chief characteristics of the: (a) Str. Imp. Act. of 1911; (b) Mattoon Act. (The Acquisition and Improvement Act of 1925); (c) County Road District Improvement Act of 1907. Point out outstanding difference between them.

A. (a) This is a State law which provides for construction within municipalities of all kinds of work in public streets, such as pavements, curbs, sidewalks, gutters, sanitary sewers and storm drains, and for the installation of ornamental lighting systems and facilities for domestic water supply. It constitutes a specific lien. 

Upon completion of work and its acceptance by the City, the property that abuts the improvement is then assessed upon a frontage basis for cost of work, each lot bearing its proportionate part. 

The assessment is a specific lien on particular lot. 

When assessment is less than $25, the owner must pay cash. 

When it exceeds $25, owner may pay in cash or allow a bond to be issued. Each year on January 2, one-tenth of the principal of bond is payable and interest at rate of 7% is payable January and July 

2nd of each year. (b) Mattoon Act (A and I Act of 1925) was repealed by the 1933 legislature, but it is essential that agents be informed of its provisions because so many properties are within the Districts created under it.

The act provides a procedure for the acquisition and improvement of public ways and parks whether lying within a city or county or partly within both. Bonds issued under this act are not liens against separate and specific pieces of property but are obligations of an improvement or acquisition district. 

The principal and interest amounts of bonds are paid from special assessment taxes and are collected in same manner as general municipal or county taxes. Bonds are issued to mature in -260-

series and may run for thirty years. Bonds usually run for ten years. They constitute a general lien. (c) Under this act Board of Supervisors are vested with power to establish road improvement districts outside of incorporated cities or towns, to construct roads in said districts, to issue bonds to cover their cost, and to constitute a fund by levying taxes on the lands of the district. Bonds may be issued to run as long as 25 years. Interest is payable semi-annually on January and July 2nd.

The bonds are a direct and ad valorem tax lien on all lands in district. 

Q. Merchant pays $500 per month for a store 20x100 feet, situated 100 feet from corner. On this basis how much should an adjoining storeroom 15x50 rent for? Show figures, or explain. 

A. First 50 feet toward front of store is worth about two-thirds of the whole depth of 100 feet. Small store is only 4 of width of other one. On this basis, rent of small store would be ¾4xx$500 equals $250 per month. Sometimes there is limited demand for small stores at high rentals so rent might be considerably less. One should not use a depth table arbitrarily but merely as a guide or a check. 

Q. When could the term "Obsolete" be aptly applied to a building?

A. A building would be considered obsolete when its appointments, style and convenience are no longer up to modern requirements and demand. 

Q. Name the four cardinal factors in all real estate valuations.

A. Location, Utility, Size and Shape. 

Q. Has there been any accepted or adopted method or rule in real estate appraising?

A. No. One method may properly be used in one case and totally unfitted for application in another. 

Q. Name some of the systems, methods or rules that have been involved. 

A. (a) Hoffman Rule. (b) Neill Rule. (c) Sumner's Rule. (d) Davies Rule. (e) Zangerle's Method.

The two most widely known of these are the Hoffman Rule and the Davies Rule. The Hoffman Rule considers lots of no more than 100 feet in depth while the Davies Rule is applicable to lots 200 feet in depth, and hence is a more satisfactory rule for California property as the lots are generally more than 100 feet in depth. -261-

Q. Does the interest rate affect the value of land?

A. No factor is so clear in affecting its value. Q. 

What controls the rate of interest?

A. The market rate of money in industry and finance. Q. 

What would you consider the main factor in land value?

A. The condition of general business. 

Q. What directly affects the value of land? 

A. Cost of building and the cost of labor.

Section IX Economics---Agricultural  

Q. (a) How many cuttings and how many tons per acre alfalfa does land yield annually in your district? (b) What is the fair value of such lands? (c) What are the items of cost to produce alfalfa?

A. 6 to 9 cuttings, 8 to 10 tons per acre. (b) The value of the land is 10 times the net return; in general, alfalfa ranches sell at $100 to $300 per acre. (c) Chief items of cost are water and labor of cutting, baling and handling.

Q. Acreage developers depended upon water well with average lift of 100 feet. Discuss what crops they could economically raise on the land, as far as cost of water is concerned, assuming project to be suitable, soil favorable and 100 miles from main markets: Answer "yes" or "no" in blanks. 

A. Alfalfa-Yes. Cotton-Yes. Deciduous fruits-Yes. Truck garden-onions, lettuce-Yes. Vineyard-wine grapes, Yes; raisin grapes, Yes. Citrus fruit-Yes.

Q. According to history in this State over a period of about 

5 years what is the average annual net income of 1500 hen poultry plant? What is about the right number of hens for one-man-care plant? What is your authority for these figures?

A. Farm Advisor of Los Angeles County states that net return per hen per year has averaged from $1 to $1.50. Taking $1.25 per hen, a 1500 hen plant would return $1375. These figures make allowance for wages of one man.

One man can take care of 2000 to 2500 hen plant. A plant of at least 2000 hens is recommended.

Q. If you were intending to deal in poultry, fruit and small rabbit ranches, what sort of information would you want, and where would you obtain it upon which to base your selling arguments?

A. Would want to know the kind of soil for particular fruit, district in which particular fruit is successful. Would want to ascertain which poultry or rabbit stock pays best, market possibilities, probable profit and how to care for them. 

Information could be had from University of California, agricultural department, or from local farm bureau. Would also get any reports available from State Real Estate Department or from 

United States Department of Agriculture. 

Q. What factors determine the value of: (a) Dairy farm. 

(b) Cattle Ranch. (c) Fruit grove. (d) Root crops, such as truck gardens?

A. (a) Character of soil, whether suitable for hay and grain, water supply for cattle and crops, proximity to market, climatic -263-

conditions, labor conditions in district, kind of cattle and their general condition. (b) Ample water supply and land suitable for raising hay. (c) Suitability of soil, water supply and cost of water, climatic conditions with special reference to frosts and protection against frost, condition of trees and their age. (d) Suitability of soil, water supply and cost of water, proximity to market and labor supply. 

Q. (a) What is meant by the term "water table"? (b) About what is the annual rainfall in your part of the State? (c) What is meant by the term "gravity" water?

A. (a) Distance from top of soil to level at which surface water is found, usually expressed in feet. (b) Consult nearest office of the United States Weather Bureau or your local newspaper. 

Following are averages in several cities and towns in Southern 

California: Beaumont, 19.19 inches; Bishop, 6.74; Brawley, 2.44; 

Calexico, 3.10; Fresno, 9.82; Los Angeles, 15.23; Riverside, 10.75; 

San Bernardino, 16.06; Santa Ana, 12; Santa Barbara, 18.68; San

Diego, 10.30. (c) Gravity water is a water supply that does not require pumping for distribution.

Q. Why is California especially interested in a tariff on agricultural products?

A. California is principally an agricultural State and is interested in a tariff on such products in order that it may compete with certain products, such as citrus fruit, raisins, prunes, olives, figs, dates, etc., produced in foreign countries under cheap labor. 

Q. Define a mutual water company. (b) Define irrigation district. Show how these two differ. (c) How are water rights from a stream acquired?

A. A mutual water company is one organized by water users in a given district with the object of securing an ample water supply at a reasonable rate to each user. Shares of stock in company can be assigned only when land is sold or is used as security for loan secured by a mortgage or deed of trust. (b) An irrigation district is the district which is supplied with water from certain sources such as wells or dams. Formation of the district is started through a petition from property owners in proposed district presented to County Board of Supervisors. If proposed district is approved, election is called. If election carries, Board of Supervisors declare district duly organized. Then follows selection of Board of Directors, employment of engineer to develop plans, and calling of bond election for purpose of financing project. (c) Under so-called riparian rights. 

Q. Where land is subdivided into acre units, what, if any, loss does subdivider suffer in dedication of streets? Explain.

A. Subdivider loses no land since he divides the plot into what are known as "commercial acres" and such acres are measured from the center of the road. -264-

Q. (a) What trees are exempt from taxation, and for how long? (b) What vines and crops?

A. (a) All fruit and nut trees under four years old from time of planting in orchard form. (b) All grapevines under 3 years old from time of planting in vineyard form, and all growing crops. 

Q. What kind of soil must the following plantings have? (a) 

Walnut grove. (b) Grapevines. (c) Citrus trees. (d) Beans. (e) 

Deciduous trees. (f) Tomatoes.

A. (a) Sandy loam-6 to 12 feet deep. (b) Depends upon kind of grapes. In general, sandy loam. (c) Sandy loam. (d) 

Sandy loam. (e) Sandy loam desirable but those trees do well in almost any good soil. (f) Any good soil.

Q. (a) Name at least 4 fruits of tree and vine in production of which California leads all other states combined. (b) Name those which come in competition with European products, and state how it is possible to compete with them. 

A. (a) Prunes, oranges, apricots and wine grapes. (b) Prunes, figs, raisins and olives. Competition is helped by suitable tariff and more efficient marketing.

Q. Tenant built a fence around portion of the farm without knowledge of owner. Could tenant remove it before expiration of tenancy, over objection of owner? Explain.

A. No, not unless fence was in portable or movable form. 

When a person affixes his property to land of another, without an agreement permitting him to remove it, the thing affixed belongs to owner of land unless he chooses to require the former to remove it. (See Sec. 1013 Civil Code.) 

Q. (a) What is understood by the term "dry farming" in 

California? (b) What products are generally grown by "dry farming" in California? 

A. (a) Farming done without irrigation. (b) Grain and beans. 

Q. Name places or zones in California generally devoted to: (a) Alfalfa farming. (b) Walnut growing. (c) Prune orchards. 

(d) Peaches. (e) Lima beans. (f) Grapes. (g) Figs. 

A. (a) Imperial and San Joaquin valleys. (b) Mostly along coast in Southern California. Particularly in Los Angeles, Ventura and Orange Counties. (c) Santa Clara Valley. (d) Sacramento 

Valley. (e) Ventura County. (f) Southern California and San

Joaquin Valley. (g) San Joaquin Valley. Some in Southern Cali fornia.

Q. In general what are the requirements for successful citrus growing in California? (a) As to climate. (b) As to water. (c) 

As to soils. (d) As to marketing associations.

A. (a) Climate where frost damage and bad winds are rare. (b) Abundance of water for irrigation. (c) Good soil with proper drainage, easily worked. (d) Market associations are necessary to market citrus fruits at a profit. -265-

Q. What is the sale price per acre under typical real estate market conditions of the different commercial farms in Southern California? Good

A. Citrus groves, $1,000 to $3,000 per acre. Alfalfa ranches, $100 to $300 per acre. Lima bean land, $200 to $400 per acre. garden truck farms, $200 to 400 per acre. 

Q. (a) How many square feet are there in an acre? (b) What provision is made in measurement of acreage with reference to county roads?

A. (a) 43,560 square feet. (b) Acres abutting on road are measured from middle of road. 

Q. What is the longest term for which agricultural land can be leased in the State of California? 

A. For not more than fifteen (15) years. pal Lease.)

Section X 

Ethics Professional courtesy and ethics should not stop at those things which have been sanctioned by law. The man who tries only to stay on the border of the law inevitably at some time steps across. The code of conduct of which we have previously spoken is that which a broker must observe. We will now consider what he ought to observe.

The National Association of Real Estate Boards and its constituent boards and state associations form a composite organization of brokers whose object it has been to forward the interests of brokers, disseminate education, and raise the standards of real estate practice and the estimation in which brokers are held by their fellow citizens. To this end, and after study and investigation, a code of ethics was formulated and adopted. It is submitted in this book as the most generally accepted code of ethics for real estate brokers that is available and has the approval of a very large body of brokers in this country. It is recommended that it be carefully studied, and scrupulously observed. 

It will be noted that this code uses the word "Realtor." This is a coined word and no one has the right to use it who does not belong to a constituent board of the National Association of Real Estate Boards. To do so is a violation of the California Real Estate 

Act, subsection 11 of section 12. 

CODE OF ETHICS NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF REAL ESTATE BOARDS PREAMBLE 

Under all is the land. Upon its wise utilization and widely allocated ownership depend the survival and growth of free institutions and of our civilization. The realtor is the instrumentality through which the land resources of the nation reaches its highest use and through which land ownership attains its widest distribution. He is a creator of homes, a builder of cities, a developer of industries and productive farms. 

Such functions impose obligations beyond those of ordinary commerce; they impose grave social responsibility and a patriotic duty to which the realtor should dedicate himself, and for which he should be diligent in preparing himself. The realtor, therefore, is zealous to maintain and improve the standards of his calling and shares with his fellow realtors a common responsibility for its integrity and honor.

In the interpretation of his obligations, he can take no safer guide than that which has been handed down through twenty centuries, embodied in the Golden Rule: "Whatsoever ye would that men should do unto you, do ye also unto them.” -267-

Accepting this standard as his own, every realtor pledges himself to observe its spirit in all his dealings and to conduct his business in accordance with the following Code of Ethics, adopted by the California Real Estate Association and the National Association of Real Estate Boards: 

PART I PROFESSIONAL RELATIONS 

Article 1. In the best interest of society, of his associates, and of his own business, the realtor should be loyal to the real estate board of his community and active in its work; and he should willingly share with his fellow members the lessons of his experience.

Article 2. The realtor should so conduct his business as to avoid controversies with his fellow realtors; but in the event of a controversy between realtors who are members of the same real estate board, such controversy should be submitted for arbitration in accordance with the regulations of their board and not to a suit at law, and the decision in such arbitrations should be accepted as final and binding.

Article 3. Controversies between realtors who are not members of the same real estate board should be submitted for arbitration to an arbitration board consisting of one arbitrator chosen by each realtor from a real estate board to which he belongs and to one other member, or a sufficient number of members to make an odd number, selected by the arbitrators thus chosen. 

Article 4. When a realtor is charged with unethical practice, he should voluntarily place all pertinent facts before the proper tribunal of the real estate board of which he is a member, for investigation and judgment.

Article 5. A realtor should never publicly criticize a competitor; he should never express an opinion of a competitor's transaction unless requested to do so by one of the principals, and his opinion then should be rendered in accordance with strict professional courtesy and integrity.

Article 6. A realtor should never seek information about a competitor's transaction to use for the purpose of closing the transaction himself or diverting the customer to another property. 

Article 7. When a realtor accepts a listing from another broker, the agency of the broker who offers the listing should be respected until it has expired and the property has come to the attention of the accepting realtor from a different source, or until the owner, without solicitation, offers to list with the accepting realtor; furthermore, such a listing should not be passed on to a third broker without the consent of the listing broker.

Article 8. Negotiations concerning property which is listed with one realtor exclusively should be carried on with the listing broker, not with the owner. -268-

Article 9. The schedules of fees established by the various real estate boards are believed to represent fair compensation for services rendered in their communities and should be observed by every realtor.

Article 10. A realtor should not solicit the services of any employee in the organization of a fellow realtor without the knowledge of the employer.

Article 11. No sign should ever be placed on any property by a realtor without the consent of the owner. 

PART II RELATIONS TO CLIENTS 

Article 12. In justice to those who place their interests in his hands, the realtor should endeavor always to be informed regarding the law, proposed legislation, and other essential facts and public policies which affect those interests. 

Article 13. In accepting the agency for property, the realtor pledges himself to be fair to purchaser or tenant, as well as to the owner whom he represents and whose interests he should protect and promote as he would his own. 

Article 14. A realtor should not buy for himself property listed with him, nor should he acquire any interest therein, without first making his true position clearly known to the listing owner. 

Article 15. When asked for an appraisal of real property or an opinion on a real estate problem, the realtor should never give an unconsidered answer; his counsel constitutes a professional service which he should render in writing over his signature and only after having ascertained and weighed the facts, for which he should make a fair charge. The realtor should not undertake to give an appraisal on any property in which he is in any way interested whatsoever, unless such interest is specifically disclosed in the appraisal report, and under no circumstances should he undertake to give an appraisal or opinion when his employment is contingent upon the amount of his appraisal or the character of his opinion.

Article 16. The realtor should encourage the naming of the actual or an obviously nominal consideration in a deed. 

Article 17. When acting as agent in the management of property, a realtor should not accept any commission, rebate, or profit on expenditures made for the owner, without his full knowledge and consent.

Article 18. The exclusive listing of property should be urged and practiced by a realtor as a means of eliminating misunderstanding and dissensions and assuring better service to the owner. 

Article 19. The acceptance by a realtor of an exclusive listing imposes the obligation of rendering skilled and conscientious service; when a realtor is unable to render such services either himself -269-

or with the aid of his fellow realtors, he should not accept the listing.

Article 20. Before offering a property listed with him by the owner, it is the realtor's duty to advise the owner honestly and intelligently regarding its fair market value.

PART III RELATIONS TO CUSTOMERS AND THE PUBLIC 

Article 21. It is the duty of every realtor to protect the public against fraud, misrepresentation, or unethical practices in connection with real estate transactions. 

Article 22. Property should be offered by a realtor solely on its merit without exaggeration, concealment, or any form of deception or misleading representation. 

Article 23.-It is the duty of a realtor to ascertain all pertinent facts concerning every property for which he accepts the agency, so that in offering the property he may avoid error, exaggeration, and misrepresentation.

Article 24. A realtor should never offer a property without the authorization of the owner.

Article 25. The price at which a realtor offers a property should not be higher than that which the owner has openly agreed to take.

Article 26. Before a realtor buys for a client property, in the ownership of which the realtor has an interest, he should disclose his interest to all parties to the transaction. 

Article 27. Before a realtor sells property in the ownership of which he is interested, he should make it clear to the purchaser that he is acting solely for the owner. 

Article 28. A realtor when acting as a broker should make it clear for which party he is acting, and he should not receive compensation from more than one party except with the full knowledge and consent of all parties to the transaction. 

Article 29. Under no circumstances should a realtor permit any property in his charge to be used for illegal or immoral purposes. 

Article 30. In closing transactions, the realtor should advise the use of legal counsel when the interest of any party to the transactions appears to require it; and in all cases he should exercise care in the preparation of documents so that they shall embody the exact agreements reached. 

Article 31. At the time the agreement is reached as to the terms of a transaction the realtor should fully inform each party regarding commissions and other expenses to which each is respectively liable. 

Article 32. Before the closing of a transaction, the realtor should recommend the examination of title and conveyancing papers. -270-

Article 33. All contracts and agreements to which a realtor is a party should be made in writing and should be complete and exact.

Article 34. A realtor should never be instrumental in introducing into a neighborhood a character of property or occupancy, members of any race or nationality, or any individuals whose presence will clearly be detrimental to property values in that neighborhood.

Article 35. No instructions nor inducements from any client or customer relieve the realtor from his responsibility strictly to observe this Code of Ethics.

ADDENDA 

1 

SUGGESTIONS TO THE PUBLIC 

(The following suggestions are made, not as a part of this Code of Ethics, but to indicate to the public how they can cooperate with realtors so as to secure the best service.) 

1-Your relationship with a real estate broker should be considered confidential; it is unfair to a broker for you to quote to others the terms and properties which he has offered you in confidence. 

2-Competent counsel in connection with real estate transactions is valuable and proceeds from years of training and study; it should not be expected gratis. 

3-By retaining the services of a single broker and placing your confidence in him, you enable him to render you more intelligent and satisfactory service. 

4-Do not injure your property nor your broker's chances of serving you by quoting one price to the broker and another to a prospective purchaser. 

5-Do not list your property unless you are willing and ready to sell it. 

6-When you ask a realtor for an opinion, you should expect it to be rendered in accordance with his best judgment, unbiased by your personal preferences.

II The term, client, is used in this code to denote one who retains a realtor to represent his interests in real estate matters. 

The term, customer, is used to denote one who transacts business with a realtor but does not retain his services. 

Q. What is the Realtor's Code of Ethics? 

A. A code adopted by realtors for the purpose of guiding its members and their organizations in their conduct with each other, -271-

with their clients and with the public. It is founded and built upon the Golden Rule. Each Realtor becoming a member of any board must subscribe to and agree to be governed by its code of ethics. 

Q. What should be done when prospective purchaser is willing to buy, but it is apparent that he cannot keep up the monthly payments? 

A. Seller should not sell to him. Should be advised to wait until he is financially able to make payments or buy property requiring smaller payments.

Q. Should prospect's attention be called to undesirable neighbors or other objectionable features before taking deposit? Explain. 

A. Yes; he must not practice deceit by withholding informa tion vital to value of property. See Section 12 of Real Estate Law. 

Q. Why does the State Real Estate Department urge licensees to join a realty board!

A. To promote the standardization of the real estate business, harmony among those engaged in it, and honest and ethical dealing with the public.

BUYER BEWARE 

Q. To what extent and why has the old doctrine of "let the buyer beware" been discarded in the real estate vocation? 

A. By the enactment of the California Real Estate Law, the appointment of a State Real Estate Commissioner, the licensing of Real Estate brokers and salesmen, and the formation of local Realty Boards throughout the State, the business has been brought to a higher plane and the public is more protected against the acts of unscrupulous operators. -272-

Section XI. 

Typical Salesman's Examination READ CAREFULLY: 

This examination is in four sections. The first section consists of statements which are either true or false. Following the statements are the letters "T" and "F," and you are to enclose one of them in parentheses (), which will indicate whether you believe the statement to be true or false. Following is a sample question: 

True False 

Real Estate Brokers are required by the California

Real Estate Law to maintain a definite place of business. (T) F 

You are cautioned to read each statement carefully before indicating your answer. Satisfy yourself that you understand the meaning clearly.

Your grade on the "True and False" section of this examination will be determined by subtracting the number of erroneous answers from the number of correct answers. It is therefore better to guess than to leave blank any statements of which you are not sure, as an unanswered statement counts against your grade as much as a wrong answer.

No changes or additions may be made to any of the questions in this examination. True and false statements must be answered only in the manner above described and no written comments are permitted. Any deviation from these rules will cause the applicant to be graded "0" on the question.

The reverse side of the pages must be used for making computations.

The time limit for this examination is 3 hours.

TYPICAL ILLUSTRATION OF PROBLEMS USED IN BOTH BROKER'S AND SALESMEN'S EXAMINATION 

The Real Estate Commissioner sometime ago submitted the following problem which is typical of those used in the examination to qualify for a real estate license. A problem of this kind counts 

20% of the possible 100% grade. -279-

THE PROBLEM 

Mr. John Randall authorized you to sell an income property, giving you an exclusive agency listing for 60 days at a price of $37,500. The authorization was signed on December 20, 1935, and provided for a 5% commission in event of a sale. The property is a three story building, the ground floor of which consists of four store rooms, one of which is occupied by a radio store, another by a jeweler, another by a haberdasher, and the last by a job printer. 

The upper floors are occupied by 10 furnished apartments. 

The jeweler has a 10-year percentage lease providing for a rental equal to 11% of his gross sales which have averaged $600 per month. The radio dealer pays $55 a month on a 5-year lease. 

The haberdasher, who has only 16 feet frontage on the street pays $30 per month on a month-to-month basis. The printer's rent is $45 per month on a verbal 3-year lease. 

The furnished apartments rent as follows on a monthly basis: 

Three at $35 per month, two at $32.50 per month, two at $30 per month, two at $27.50 per month, and one extra large front apartment at $45 per month. Over a period of several years, they have averaged 11% vacancies. The depreciation allowance for the furniture has been computed at $295 per annum. 

Expenses chargeable to this property are: Repairs and main tenance, $835 per annum; janitor service $42.50 per month (parttime janitor is engaged); electricity, $27.50 per month; water, $18.50 per month; management, $350 per year; taxes, $930 per year. A fair allowance for depreciation and obsolescence on the building has been determined to be $1,425 per annum.

QUESTIONS UPON PROBLEM: 

Answer the following questions in connection with the above 

1. Make a detailed statement of the gross annual income from this property after deduction for vacancies, assuming there are no vacancies in the storerooms on the ground floor. 

2. Make a detailed statement of the total annual expenses on this property, not including the depreciation allowance on the building, but allowing for depreciation on the furniture. 

3. What is the net income earned by this property, assuming that all expense charges have been listed in the problem? 

4. Based on the net income at which you have arrived, what is the value of the property, assuming that the lot is properly and fully improved? 

5. What rate of capitalization did you use and why? 

6. What usual item of operating expense has been omitted in the above tabulation?

You secured a buyer for the above described property who was acceptable to Mr. Randall. The buyer paid $15,000 cash and executed a note for the balance of the listed purchase price which was -280-

secured by a purchase money Deed of Trust on the property. The note becomes due in six years with an interest rate of 52% per annum. 

7. In this case, what would be the amount of your commission? 

8. How much interest would the buyer pay quarterly on the trust deed note? 

9. How much annual net income would the buyer receive upon the money he has invested in the property? 

10. In your opinion, has the buyer made a good investment and does he receive adequate return on the capital invested? (Assuming character of the district will remain the same.) 

11. In event the principal of the trust deed note which the buyer executed is amortized at the rate of $225 per month, (plus interest) how long would it take to fully discharge the obligation? 

12. Would you advise your buyer to amortize the loan at this rate? Why? 

13. In computing a proper depreciation allowance on this building, would you use the straight line method or the sinking fund method? Discuss. 

14. If the buyer defaulted under his deed of trust and Mr. 

Randall started foreclosure action, would he have to resort to court proceedings? Explain. 

15. Could Mr. Randall under any circumstances secure a deficiency judgment against the buyer? Explain. 

16. Would you have been legally entitled to your commission if you had sold the property on February 17, 1936? If Mr. Randall had sold it himself on that date to a buyer unknown to you? 

17. What allowance do you usually make for depreciation on furniture in an apartment property of this kind? 

18. If the buyer of this property added two more stories of apartments, would he necessarily increase his net income? Explain. 

19. If the owner wishes to give the printer notice to vacate, could the printer legally enforce the provisions of his lease? 

ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS UPON PROBLEM: 

The following answers were also submitted by the Department, 'with the following comment:

After working the problem you may be "surprised to find that the property under discussion does not prove to be a profitable venture for the purchaser. This was not prepared as a 'trick' problem, but simply to show that many properties which at first glance seem to be a good investment often will not show adequate return upon being closely analyzed. It is also designed to illustrate that a broker who goes by 'the rule of thumb' in determining values may seriously injure a client. Many of the questions below are not answered as completely as they might be, but the principal points are given and would be considered sufficient in the examination." -281-

Following are the answers: 

1. Gross annual income, $5,876.40. 

2. Total annual expenses, $3,472.00. 

3. Net annual income is $979.40, including depreciation and obsolescence. 

4. Net income capitalized at 7% shows value of $14,000 (in round figures). 

5. 7% would be about average rate. This might be somewhat lower or higher depending upon risk. 

6. Item of insurance. Cost of heating and advertising might also be added. 

7. Commission is $1,875.00. 

8. Quarterly interest on trust deed is $309.38. 

9. The buyer receives no net income on his investment in this property. After paying all expenses including depreciation on the building, he sustains a loss of $258.10 per year. 

10. Purchaser does not secure any return on his investment and would probably lose the property unless he had other assets. 

11. 100 months or 8 years and 4 months. 

12. No. He should not buy it in the first place at this price. 

13. In a property of this size, the sinking fund method of allowing for depreciation is more fair to the property. 

14. No. The trustee is granted power of sale. 

15. No. A deficiency judgment cannot be obtained on a purchase money Deed of Trust executed since 1933. 

16. You would be entitled to your commission if you sold the property on February 17, 1936, as you sold it within the period of your authorization. If Mr. Randall sold the property you would not be entitled to your commission as you had only an exclusive agency listing, which permits the owner to act without liability for the payment of a commission to you. An "Exclusive right to sell" listing would give protection in this case. 

17. Depreciation on furniture is rather high and an allowance of 10% per annum would be conservative. 

18. No. It is possible that the additions would not even pay interest on the additional capital invested. Many people have an idea that the larger the improvements, the better return. The reverse is often true. 

19. The printer has only a verbal lease. This cannot be legally enforced if made for a term of more than a year. -282-

Section XIII "TRUE" AND "FALSE" STATEMENTS 

Answer the following questions by putting the letter "T" or "F" in parentheses () to indicate whether the statement is "true" or "false." Do not explain answer or attempt to list exceptions.

Approximately 60 of this type of questions are usually given in 

Salesmen's examination and around 120 in Brokers. 

True False 1. The cost of inspection of a subdivision is met by the real estate commissioner.

T (F) (It is met by owner or subdivider.) 

2. A real estate broker should keep his license in a safety deposit vault or other safe place so that it cannot be lost or stolen.

T (F) (License must be displayed in prominent location in place of business.) 

3. Community Property is that property owned or set out by a city, county, town, or other community. (Community Property is the property acquired during marriage from the joint or separate earnings of husband and wife.) 

4. A corporation putting a subdivision on the market for sale before obtaining permit to do so is subject to a fine of $2,000.

T (F) T (F) 

5. A revocation of broker's license by the Commissioner is subject to a review. (T) F 6. A joint tenancy is not established without the use of the words "right of survivorship."

T (F) (Joint tenancy automatically carries "Right of survivorship.") 

7. A Warranty Deed is the form in general use in California.

T (F) (Grant deed.) 

8. "Exclusive Listing" is the same as "Exclusive 

Right" to sell.

T (F) (Exclusive listing protects against sales by other brokers only. Exclusive right protects against sale by other brokers and owners.) 

9. A broker may conduct his business in a strictly residential neighborhood.

T (F) (City zoning prohibits.) 

10. A "good" and "valuable" consideration is the same.

T (F) (A "good" consideration may be love and affection. A “valuable" consideration is money or its equivalent.) 11. 

A broker's license cannot be revoked for wrong doing of his salesman unless he has guilty knowledge of the same. (T) F 

12. A forged deed is absolutely void. (T) F 13. A salesman may split a commission with any other licensed salesman or broker.

T (F) (All commissions are payable through broker under whom salesman is licensed.) -287-

14. There are two street and highway improvement acts in California. 

15. A downtown store vacancy is more valuable for an automobile agency and garage than for a high class shoe store. 

16. A trust deed may be foreclosed though the note has been outlawed by time. (T) F T (F) (T) F 17. Broker may, in some circumstances, collect commissions from both the seller and buyer. (T) F 18. Lease of apartment house for 8 months may legally be made orally. (T) F 19. The decision respecting revocation of license is reviewable by the Real Estate Board. T (F) (Reviewable by action to Superior Court.) 

20. The attorney general prosecutes all violations of the subdivision section of the Act. T (F) (City or District Attorney.) 

21. The owner, his agent or subdivider, shall notify the commissioner not only that he is selling lots in parcels in a subdivision, but that he intends to or is offering such, or is leasing or offering to lease such. (T) F 

22. The Commissioner, his deputies, "brokers" and "Salesmen" are all bonded for the faithful performance of their duties.

T (F) (No bond required.) 

23. Quit Claim deed always conveys fee title to Real Estate.

T (F) (Quit claim deed conveys only such title as the executor has.) 

24. Procedure for revocation provides for immediate revocation on filing of complaint.

T (F) (Only after hearing by commissioner or duly appointed deputy.) 

25. Commissioner can revoke a broker's license as well as salesman's if salesman is found guilty of conduct of fraudulent or dishonest dealing.
